hld:url-shortener.prompt: A shortener sees 200M new URLs per month with a 100:1 read-to-write ratio. Using 2.5M seconds per month, roughly how many redirects per second does it serve on average?
hld:url-shortener.explanation: 200M / 2.5M s = 80 writes/s, and 100:1 reads gives about 8,000 redirects/s. 800 forgets the ratio factor of 100 (it would be the write rate times 10); 16,000 doubles the figure for a peak nobody asked about.

hld:url-shortener.prompt: A service stores 2B new URLs per year for 5 years at about 500 B per record, with every record kept on 3 replicas. How much storage does it need in total?
options: 5 TB
50 TB
10 TB
15 TB
hld:url-shortener.explanation: 2B x 5 years = 10B records x 500 B = 5 TB of unique data, and 3 replicas triple it to 15 TB. 5 TB ignores replication; 50 TB is an order-of-magnitude slip (500 B is 0.5 KB, not 5 KB).

hld:url-shortener.prompt: The service expects 6 billion URLs over 5 years. Given 62^5 is about 0.92 billion and 62^6 is about 56.8 billion, what is the shortest Base62 code length with enough distinct codes (ignoring collision handling)?
hld:url-shortener.explanation: Five characters give under 1B codes, which is too few. Six give about 56.8B, which is enough on paper. Real designs often pick 7 (about 3.5T codes) so random or hashed codes rarely collide at only a tiny fraction of the space.

hld:url-shortener.prompt: A team derives each code from the first 7 Base62 characters of MD5(longUrl). Which problem must the design handle?
options: The same long URL gets a different code on every call, so duplicates pile up
Codes come out in increasing order, so anyone can walk the whole space
Two different URLs can map to the same truncated code, so inserts need a collision check and retry
MD5 output cannot be written in Base62, so codes need a different alphabet
hld:url-shortener.explanation: Truncating a hash to 7 characters keeps only about 42 bits, so distinct URLs eventually collide and the write must detect that. The hash is deterministic (same URL, same code), and it is pseudo-random, not sequential.

hld:url-shortener.prompt: Marketing wants accurate per-link click counts. An engineer proposes answering every redirect with 301 to cut server load. What is the consequence?
options: Browsers can cache the 301 and skip the shortener on repeat visits, so those clicks go uncounted
Clicks are counted twice, once by the browser and once by the server
301 forces every request to carry a new code, which breaks the cache
301 cannot carry a Location header, so redirects fail in some clients
hld:url-shortener.explanation: A 301 is a permanent redirect that browsers may cache, so repeat clicks never reach the service and analytics undercount. A 302 keeps every click visible at the cost of more traffic. Both carry Location and neither double-counts.

hld:url-shortener.prompt: Select all real drawbacks of generating codes from one global counter encoded in Base62.
options: Two requests can receive the same code when the counter is correct
The counter is a single point of failure and a write hotspot
Codes are predictable, so people can enumerate them
Codes grow too long to fit in a URL after a few thousand links
hld:url-shortener.explanation: A sequential counter is guessable and every write must pass through one place, so it limits throughput and availability. An atomic counter never hands out the same value twice, and Base62 keeps even huge counts short (7 characters reach trillions).

hld:url-shortener.prompt: One link goes viral and hits the redirect path at tens of times its normal rate. Which response fits the design best?
options: Rate-limit that code so the store is not overwhelmed
Split that key's row across more partitions so reads spread out
Serve it from the cache or a CDN edge, since the mapping never changes
Regenerate a longer code so fewer collisions occur
hld:url-shortener.explanation: A mapping is immutable, so cached copies stay correct and a hot code is served from memory or the edge. A single key lives on one partition and its replicas, so adding partitions does not help; rate-limiting punishes legitimate users; code length is unrelated.

hld:url-shortener.prompt: Incrementing a click counter row in the main URL store inside the redirect request is a good way to keep redirect p99 under 50 ms.
options: True
False
hld:url-shortener.explanation: It puts a synchronous write on the hottest path. The design emits a click event asynchronously (for example to Kafka), returns the redirect at once, and aggregates later in a stream job.

hld:url-shortener.prompt: Supporting custom aliases safely requires an atomic insert-if-absent on the code, because two users may claim the same alias at the same moment.
options: True
False
hld:url-shortener.explanation: A check-then-write sequence races: both callers see the alias as free. A conditional write (or unique constraint) on the code makes exactly one succeed and the other get a conflict response.

hld:url-shortener.prompt: Which part of a URL shortener genuinely needs strong consistency, and which can lag?
options: Both need strong consistency because they share one store
Neither, because redirects tolerate two URLs behind one code
Click counts must be strong, while code uniqueness can be eventual
Code uniqueness on create must be strong, while click counts can be eventual
hld:url-shortener.explanation: Two long URLs must never share a code, so creation needs a strong uniqueness check. Click statistics are aggregated asynchronously and a slightly stale dashboard harms nobody. Duplicate codes would send users to the wrong site.

hld:url-shortener.prompt: Which designs give collision-free codes across many API nodes without a single hot counter? Select all that apply.
options: Snowflake-style IDs (timestamp, machine id, sequence) encoded in Base62
Each node leases a block of IDs from a key-generation service and encodes them in Base62
Each node counts up from 0 on its own and encodes the value in Base62
Each node picks 7 random Base62 characters and inserts without checking for existing codes
hld:url-shortener.explanation: Leased ranges and machine-scoped Snowflake IDs are unique by construction. Independent per-node counters all start at 0 and clash immediately, and unchecked random codes will eventually collide.

hld:url-shortener.prompt: A shortener takes 100M new URLs per month (use 2.5M seconds per month), reads outnumber writes 100:1, and peak traffic is 2.5x the average. Roughly what peak redirect rate must the redirect path handle?
options: About 4,000 redirects/s
About 10,000 redirects/s
About 40,000 redirects/s
About 1,000 redirects/s
hld:url-shortener.explanation: Writes: 100M / 2.5M s = 40/s. Reads: 40 x 100 = 4,000/s on average. Peak: 4,000 x 2.5 = 10,000/s. 4,000/s is the average, not the peak the system must be sized for.

hld:url-shortener.prompt: The store will hold 6B URLs at about 500 B each. You decide to cache the hottest 1% of records in Redis. Roughly how much cache memory is that, before overhead?
options: About 30 GB
About 3 TB
About 3 GB
About 300 GB
hld:url-shortener.explanation: 1% of 6B = 60M records; 60M x 500 B = 30 GB, which fits on a modest Redis cluster. 3 TB is the size of the whole dataset, not the hot 1%.

hld:url-shortener.prompt: A client requests GET /{code} for a link whose expiresAt has passed but whose record still exists. Which response best matches the API contract?
options: 500 Internal Server Error, because the record is in a bad state
410 Gone, signalling the code existed but is no longer available
302 to the long URL, because expiry is only a soft hint
301 to the site homepage so browsers cache the miss
hld:url-shortener.explanation: The API lists 404/410: 410 Gone tells clients and crawlers the resource was intentionally removed. Redirecting anyway ignores the expiry the user set, and a 500 wrongly signals a server fault.

hld:url-shortener.prompt: Interviewer follow-up: "How do you stop people enumerating codes to discover private links?" Which answer is strongest?
options: Serve redirects only over HTTPS so codes can't be sniffed
Answer 404s more slowly than 302s so scanners give up
Keep a sequential counter but start it at a large random offset so codes look arbitrary
Issue non-sequential codes from a large keyspace and rate-limit 404s per client
hld:url-shortener.explanation: Non-sequential codes (random, or an encrypted/shuffled counter) make neighbours unguessable, and rate-limiting misses throttles brute force. A random starting offset still yields consecutive codes once one is known.

hld:url-shortener.prompt: A key-generation service hands each API node a range of 1M IDs. One node crashes after using 200k IDs from its range. What normally happens?
options: The KGS reissues the same range to another node, which is safe because codes are checked later
The KGS blocks new range requests until the node recovers and returns its range
Every code issued by the crashed node becomes invalid and must be regenerated
The remaining 800k IDs are simply skipped, which is fine given a 3.5-trillion keyspace
hld:url-shortener.explanation: The KGS can't know which IDs in the range were used, so the unused tail is abandoned; wasting 800k of ~3.5 trillion codes is negligible. Reissuing the range would risk duplicate codes.

hld:url-shortener.prompt: The urls table is partitioned by code in a KV/wide-column store. Why not partition it by user_id instead?
options: TTL-based expiry stops working when rows are grouped by user
Codes would start colliding, because each user's partition would issue codes independently
KV stores can only partition on string columns, not numeric ids
Redirects look up by code, so each one would need a scatter-gather or secondary index
hld:url-shortener.explanation: The dominant query is GET /{code}; partitioning by code makes it a single-partition point read. Partitioning by user_id doesn't cause collisions; it just makes the hot path expensive.

hld:url-shortener.prompt: Why does the architecture send redirects to a separate redirect service rather than through the shortener API that creates links?
options: Creating links needs a different database engine than reading them
Load balancers cannot route GET and POST requests for the same host to one backend service
Redirects are ~100x more frequent with a tight p99, so they scale and deploy alone
Keeping them apart is required so the key generator can stay stateless
hld:url-shortener.explanation: The read path dominates traffic and has the strict latency SLO, so isolating it lets you scale it, cache aggressively and protect it from write-path incidents. Both paths can share one store.

hld:url-shortener.prompt: To absorb a viral link, 302 responses are cached at a CDN edge for 5 minutes. What do you lose, and how is it usually mitigated?
options: The CDN may rewrite the Location header, so the fix is signing every redirect URL
Edge hits skip your service, so clicks undercount unless you ingest CDN logs or use short TTLs
Browsers start treating the redirect as permanent, so the fix is switching every redirect response to a 307
Deleting a link becomes impossible, so the fix is never allowing deletes
hld:url-shortener.explanation: A cached edge response short-circuits your redirect service, so click events are never emitted; CDN access logs or short TTLs recover them. A shared-cache 302 doesn't become permanent in browsers; deletes just need a purge or short TTL.

hld:url-shortener.prompt: Custom aliases share the namespace with generated 7-character codes. Which conflict must the design prevent, beyond two users claiming the same alias?
options: Aliases expiring sooner than generated codes and confusing analytics
An alias containing uppercase letters that the cache stores in lowercase
A custom alias being longer than 7 characters and breaking Base62 decoding
The key generator later issuing a code that a user already took as an alias
hld:url-shortener.explanation: If the KGS doesn't know about aliases, it can eventually generate the same string. Fixes: insert-if-absent for generated codes too, or keep aliases in a disjoint space (different length or charset). Longer aliases are just strings; nothing decodes them.

hld:url-shortener.prompt: Which choices help the redirect path meet p99 < 50 ms? Select all that apply.
options: Re-scan the long URL with a malware API on every redirect
Partition the URL store by code so a miss is one point read
Emit the click event to Kafka asynchronously after replying
Synchronously insert a click row into SQL before replying
Serve lookups from Redis or a CDN edge with a long TTL
hld:url-shortener.explanation: Caching, async analytics and single-key reads keep the hot path to roughly one cache hit. A synchronous SQL insert or an external scan per click adds network round trips and new failure points to every redirect.

hld:url-shortener.prompt: 7 Base62 characters give about 3.5 trillion codes and the system expects 6B URLs. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
options: 7 hex characters would give a similar number of codes
Random 7-character codes still need a collision check on insert
A random guess hits a live code roughly 1 time in 580
Under 0.2% of the keyspace is used after 5 years
Collisions are impossible once the keyspace exceeds the URL count
hld:url-shortener.explanation: 6e9 / 3.5e12 = 0.17%, and 3.5e12 / 6e9 = ~583, so a guess hits about 1 in 580. Randomness can still repeat (birthday effect), so check on insert. 16^7 = 268M, far fewer than 62^7.

hld:url-shortener.prompt: Clicks flow redirect service -> Kafka -> stream aggregator -> stats store. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
options: Stats may lag redirects by seconds to minutes, which is acceptable here
Keying click events by code keeps one link's events ordered within a partition
Stats should be read from the URL store primary to stay consistent
Kafka by itself guarantees each click is counted exactly once, with no aggregator dedup
If the aggregator is down, redirects still succeed and events wait in Kafka
hld:url-shortener.explanation: Analytics are eventually consistent, the queue decouples aggregation failures from redirects, and Kafka orders by key within a partition. Consumer restarts can replay events, so exactly-once counting needs idempotent or transactional aggregation.

hld:url-shortener.prompt: Because the code-to-URL mapping is immutable, a cached redirect entry only needs invalidating when the link is deleted or expires.
options: True
False
hld:url-shortener.explanation: True. A code never changes its target, so cache entries can live long; only delete or expiry ends them. That's why a long TTL is safe on the read path.

hld:url-shortener.prompt: If expires_at is stored on the URL record, the redirect service never has to think about expiry, even with a long-TTL cache in front of the store.
options: True
False
hld:url-shortener.explanation: False. A cache entry with a long TTL can keep redirecting after expiry. Cap the cache TTL at the link's expiry, or store expires_at in the cache entry and check it on each hit.

hld:key-value-store.prompt: A Dynamo-style store has N=5 replicas per key. Which read/write setting guarantees that every read quorum overlaps the latest acknowledged write quorum?
hld:key-value-store.explanation: The overlap guarantee needs R + W > N. 3 + 3 = 6 > 5 works. W=2,R=3 and W=4,R=1 both sum to exactly 5, so a read set can miss the write set entirely; W=2,R=2 sums to 4.

hld:key-value-store.prompt: A store holds 20 TB of data with replication factor 3, and each node can hold 400 GB. What is the minimum node count, ignoring headroom?
hld:key-value-store.explanation: 20 TB x 3 = 60 TB raw; 60 TB / 400 GB = 150 nodes. 50 forgets replication. 200 would add roughly a third of headroom, which the question excluded.

hld:key-value-store.prompt: The cluster takes 150k client writes per second at RF=3, spread evenly over 120 nodes, and every write is applied on all 3 replicas. About how many replica writes does each node handle per second?
hld:key-value-store.explanation: 150k x 3 = 450k replica writes/s across the cluster; 450k / 120 = 3,750 per node. 1,250 ignores replication; 450,000 is the cluster total, not a per-node figure.

hld:key-value-store.prompt: A cluster of 10 equal nodes places keys with hash(key) mod 10, and an 11th node is added. Roughly what fraction of keys change owner under mod-N versus consistent hashing?
options: About 91% under mod-N, about 9% under consistent hashing
About 91% under both schemes
About 50% under mod-N, about 9% under consistent hashing
About 9% under both schemes
hld:key-value-store.explanation: With mod 10 versus mod 11 only about 1 key in 11 keeps its owner, so around 91% move. Consistent hashing hands the new node roughly 1/11 of the ring, so about 9% of keys move.

hld:key-value-store.prompt: With N=3, W=2 and R=2, two of a key's replicas are down. A sloppy quorum acks the write from one real replica plus a stand-in node outside the replica set. Why does R + W > N no longer guarantee that a later read sees the write?
options: R + W > N only holds when R is larger than W
Hinted writes are discarded once the acknowledgement is sent
The stand-in is not one of the key's replicas, so a read quorum can miss it until the hint is replayed
Coordinators read from stand-in nodes first and return stale data
hld:key-value-store.explanation: Overlap reasoning assumes both quorums are drawn from the same N replicas. A stand-in holding a hint sits outside that set, so reads can hit real replicas that lack the write until handoff completes. Hints are kept, not discarded.

hld:key-value-store.prompt: What can a vector clock tell you about two versions of a value that a wall-clock timestamp cannot?
options: Whether one version causally descends from the other or the two are concurrent
Which version is newer according to the writers' clocks
Which version the application should keep when merging
How many replicas have acknowledged each version
hld:key-value-store.explanation: Vector clocks capture causality: if neither clock dominates the other, the writes were concurrent and become siblings. They detect conflicts but do not resolve them; resolution is last-write-wins or an app-level merge.

hld:key-value-store.prompt: How does a node in a Dynamo/Cassandra-style cluster typically learn that another node is dead?
options: Nodes exchange state with random peers via gossip and suspect a peer whose heartbeat stops advancing
A central master pings every node and publishes a live list
Clients report failed requests to a registry that evicts the node at once
Each node holds a distributed lock whose expiry marks it as dead
hld:key-value-store.explanation: Gossip spreads membership and suspicion peer to peer, so there is no single master to fail. A central pinger or registry reintroduces a single point of failure, and client-reported evictions would flap on transient errors.

hld:key-value-store.prompt: An LSM-tree storage engine makes writes cheap. What is the main cost it pays in return?
options: Every write rewrites a B-tree page in place before the ack
Data in the memtable is lost on a crash because the commit log is optional
Reads may consult the memtable and several SSTables, and background compaction uses disk and CPU
Keys can live in only one SSTable, so range scans are impossible
hld:key-value-store.explanation: Writes append to a commit log and memtable and flush as immutable SSTables, so a read may probe several files and compaction must merge them later. The commit log makes crashes recoverable and range scans work fine.

hld:key-value-store.prompt: With N=3, a write acknowledged at consistency ONE followed by a read at consistency ONE can still return the older value.
options: True
False
hld:key-value-store.explanation: With R=1 and W=1, R + W = 2 which is not greater than N=3, so the read replica may not be the one that took the write. Higher levels such as QUORUM trade latency for overlap.

hld:key-value-store.prompt: Last-write-wins can silently discard one of two concurrent writes that were both acknowledged to their clients.
options: True
False
hld:key-value-store.explanation: LWW keeps the version with the higher timestamp and drops the other, even though neither write saw the other. That is why merge-friendly data such as a cart union needs vector clocks plus an application merge.

hld:key-value-store.prompt: Which mechanisms help bring a stale replica back in sync? Select all that apply.
options: Merkle-tree anti-entropy between replicas
Replaying hinted handoff writes once the owner returns
Gossip of membership state
Read repair on a read that sees mismatched replicas
hld:key-value-store.explanation: Read repair, Merkle-tree comparison and hint replay all move missing data to a lagging replica. Gossip only spreads who is alive and who owns which tokens; it carries no key-value data.

hld:key-value-store.prompt: Which are real benefits of giving each physical node many virtual nodes on the ring? Select all that apply.
options: Bigger machines can take more tokens than smaller ones
A failed node's load is shared among many peers
R + W > N is no longer needed for consistency
Load spreads more evenly across nodes
hld:key-value-store.explanation: Many small ranges smooth out hot spots, let capacity-weighted token counts, and spread both failure load and rebalancing across many neighbours. Virtual nodes affect placement only; quorum overlap is still needed.

hld:key-value-store.prompt: A store holds 10 TB of data at RF=3 on nodes with 300 GB disks, and you keep disks at most 50% full to leave room for compaction. How many nodes do you need?
options: 100 nodes
150 nodes
200 nodes
300 nodes
hld:key-value-store.explanation: Raw data: 10 TB x 3 = 30 TB. Usable per node: 300 GB x 50% = 150 GB. 30 TB / 150 GB = 200 nodes. 100 nodes assumes disks can run 100% full, which leaves no space for compaction to rewrite SSTables.

hld:key-value-store.prompt: A node is down for 2 hours. While it is down, stand-in nodes take 1,000 writes/s of 1 KB each meant for it, stored as hints. About how much hinted data builds up?
options: About 720 MB
About 720 GB
About 7.2 GB
About 72 GB
hld:key-value-store.explanation: 2 h = 7,200 s; 7,200 x 1,000 = 7.2M writes; 7.2M x 1 KB = 7.2 GB. This is why hint storage has a time window: a long outage makes hints too big, and repair has to take over.

hld:key-value-store.prompt: With N=3, which setting gives the fastest acknowledged writes while still guaranteeing that read and write quorums overlap?
hld:key-value-store.explanation: Overlap needs R + W > N. W=1 acks after one replica (fastest write), so reads must contact all 3 (1 + 3 = 4 > 3). W=1, R=1 and W=2, R=1 sum to 2 and 3, which don't exceed N.

hld:key-value-store.prompt: Interviewer follow-up: "What does R + W > N guarantee, exactly?" Which answer is most precise?
options: Every operation is linearizable, including concurrent writes from different clients to the same key
Every replica applies writes to a key in the same order
With strict quorums, any read set shares a replica with the latest acknowledged write set
No acknowledged write is lost even if all W replicas that acked it fail
hld:key-value-store.explanation: The guarantee is only set overlap: some replica in the read quorum saw the latest acked write, so the read can return it (using versions). It doesn't order concurrent writes, give linearizability, or survive losing every replica that holds the write.

hld:key-value-store.prompt: A shopping cart has concurrent siblings {A, B} and {A, C}, and the app merges by set union into {A, B, C}. Which anomaly does the Dynamo paper report for this approach?
options: Merged carts grow without limit because union never removes duplicates
The vector clock stops being able to detect later conflicts
Items the user deleted can reappear in the cart
Items added on one replica can vanish after the merge
hld:key-value-store.explanation: Union keeps any item present in either sibling, so a delete on one branch is undone if the other branch still holds the item. Adds are never lost under union; that safety for adds is why Amazon accepted the reappearing-delete anomaly.

hld:key-value-store.prompt: In the LSM storage engine, a get for a key that doesn't exist could have to check every SSTable. What usually avoids reading each SSTable from disk?
options: Writing deletes in place so missing keys are never searched
Keeping every SSTable fully in RAM
A Bloom filter per SSTable that rules out files without the key
A global B-tree index over all SSTables that is rebuilt on each flush
hld:key-value-store.explanation: A Bloom filter can say "definitely not here" with no false negatives, so most SSTables are skipped without disk I/O. Keeping all SSTables in RAM defeats the point of a disk-backed store.

hld:key-value-store.prompt: Each node appends every write to a commit log before acknowledging it, even though the write also goes into the memtable. Why?
options: Gossip ships the commit log to other nodes to replicate the data
The log keeps the memtable sorted so flushes are sequential
The memtable is in memory, so the log lets the node replay writes after a crash
The commit log is what reads are served from until the memtable is flushed and compacted
hld:key-value-store.explanation: The memtable is lost on a crash; replaying the sequential commit log rebuilds it, so an acked write survives. Reads are served from the memtable and SSTables, and replication is done by the coordinator, not gossip.

hld:key-value-store.prompt: In Cassandra, deletes write tombstones that are only purged by compaction after gc_grace_seconds. What goes wrong if tombstones are purged before a replica that missed the delete is repaired?
options: Compaction fails and the node stops accepting writes
The deleted value can return, as repair copies it back from the stale replica
Reads at QUORUM start returning errors instead of values
Vector clocks on the key overflow and every later write to it becomes a sibling
hld:key-value-store.explanation: With no tombstone left to win, repair treats the stale replica's old value as live data and spreads it back: the classic "zombie" resurrection. That's why repairs must run more often than gc_grace_seconds.

hld:key-value-store.prompt: One key (a viral counter) receives 50k ops/s and its replicas are overloaded. Adding more nodes to the cluster doesn't help. Why, and what does?
options: Virtual nodes spread one key over many nodes, so add more vnodes per node
The key still maps to the same N replicas; split it into sub-keys or cache it
New nodes only receive data after compaction, so trigger a major compaction on all nodes
Gossip slows as the ring grows; reduce the node count instead
hld:key-value-store.explanation: Consistent hashing maps a single key to one token, so its load always lands on the same N replicas however big the cluster is. Spreading it over key#0..key#k sub-keys (summed on read) or caching it spreads the load. Vnodes split ranges, not a single key.

hld:key-value-store.prompt: When does hinted handoff fail to bring a recovered replica up to date on its own? Select all that apply.
options: The target recovers within the hint window and the stand-in stays healthy
The stand-in node holding the hints dies before handing them off
The target stays down longer than the hint window, so new hints stop being kept
The client wrote at consistency QUORUM rather than ONE
hld:key-value-store.explanation: Hints live only on the stand-in and only for a bounded window; losing the stand-in or exceeding the window leaves gaps that read repair or Merkle-tree anti-entropy must close. The consistency level doesn't stop hints for down replicas.

hld:key-value-store.prompt: Which statements about LSM-tree compaction are true? Select all that apply.
options: It merges SSTables and drops overwritten values and purgeable tombstones
It causes write amplification because data is rewritten several times
It turns incoming writes into random in-place disk updates
It removes the need for per-SSTable Bloom filters
It competes for disk I/O and can cause read latency spikes
hld:key-value-store.explanation: Compaction keeps read cost bounded by merging files, at the price of rewriting data and using background I/O. Incoming writes stay sequential (log + memtable), and there are still several SSTables per key range, so Bloom filters remain useful.

hld:key-value-store.prompt: The store is "always writable" (AP). A network partition splits a key's replicas into two sides. Which can happen? Select all that apply.
options: Vector clocks block the second side from accepting conflicting writes
With sloppy quorum, the minority side can still ack writes via stand-in nodes
A strict QUORUM write succeeds on the side holding only one of three replicas
A read at consistency ONE returns a stale value
Both sides accept writes to the same key, creating siblings
hld:key-value-store.explanation: Accepting writes during partitions means divergence (siblings) and stale reads; sloppy quorum uses stand-ins to keep acking. Vector clocks only detect conflicts after the fact, and a strict quorum of 2 can't be met with one real replica.

hld:key-value-store.prompt: In Cassandra, any node can act as the coordinator for a request on any key, forwarding it to that key's replicas.
options: True
False
hld:key-value-store.explanation: True. The node the client contacts becomes the coordinator, uses ring metadata to find the replicas, and gathers acks according to the consistency level. Token-aware drivers simply pick a replica as coordinator to save a hop.

hld:key-value-store.prompt: Giving each physical node more virtual nodes reduces the total amount of data the cluster has to store.
options: True
False
hld:key-value-store.explanation: False. Vnodes change how token ranges are spread across machines (better balance, smoother rebalancing), not how much data exists. Total storage is still data size x replication factor.

hld:rate-limiter.prompt: A gateway fleet keeps limiter state for 5M active clients at roughly 120 B each in Redis. About how much memory is that?
options: 6 GB
600 MB
60 MB
12 GB
hld:rate-limiter.explanation: 5M x 120 B = 600 MB, comfortably one Redis instance. 60 MB drops a zero; 6 GB adds one. Memory is rarely the limit here; operations per second and latency matter more.

hld:rate-limiter.prompt: A fixed-window limiter allows 100 requests per minute. A client sends 100 requests at 12:00:59 and another 100 at 12:01:00. How many requests are admitted in those two seconds?
hld:rate-limiter.explanation: Each burst lands in a different window, so both are admitted: 200 requests in about 2 seconds, twice the intended rate. Sliding-window log and counter approaches exist to close this edge gap.

hld:rate-limiter.prompt: A token bucket has capacity 20 and refills 5 tokens per second, starting full. A client sends 50 requests at t=0 and another 50 at t=2s (ignore refill within an instant). How many requests are admitted in total?
hld:rate-limiter.explanation: At t=0 the full bucket admits 20. By t=2s it has refilled 2 x 5 = 10 tokens, so 10 of the second 50 pass: 30 total. Capacity bounds the burst and the refill rate bounds the long-run average.

hld:rate-limiter.prompt: Two gateways both read a counter of 99 against a limit of 100, both allow the request, and both write 100. What is the right fix?
options: Read the counter first and write it back with a short TTL
Take a local in-process lock in each gateway before the read and write
Add a Redis replica and read the count from the replica
Do the check and decrement as one atomic step in Redis, such as a Lua script or INCR
hld:rate-limiter.explanation: The race is across processes, so the read-modify-write must be atomic where the state lives. A per-gateway lock cannot see other gateways, a replica read adds staleness, and a short TTL does not make read-then-write atomic.

hld:rate-limiter.prompt: The limiter's Redis store becomes unreachable. Which default policy fits a public product-search API versus a login/OTP verification endpoint?
options: Both fail closed so nothing goes unprotected
Both fail open so users are never blocked
Search fails open and login fails closed
Search fails closed and login fails open
hld:rate-limiter.explanation: Search should keep serving (availability beats a short loss of throttling), whereas allowing unlimited login or OTP attempts invites brute force. A single global policy gets one of the two wrong.

hld:rate-limiter.prompt: A limiter allows 1,000 requests per minute per key across 1M busy keys. Which statement about a sliding-window log versus a sliding-window counter is correct?
options: The log is exact but stores up to 1,000 timestamps per key, while the counter keeps two bucket counts and approximates
The log uses less memory because a timestamp is smaller than a counter
Both are exact and differ only in speed
The counter is exact and the log approximates because timestamps are rounded
hld:rate-limiter.explanation: The log keeps one entry per admitted request, so memory grows with the limit. The counter weights the previous and current window counts, giving small constant memory and a small approximation error.

hld:rate-limiter.prompt: To avoid a network hop on a very hot path, gateways keep local token buckets that sync with Redis periodically. What is the accepted cost?
options: Tokens are never refilled because Redis is only read
Rules can no longer change without redeploying gateways
Every request still waits on a Redis round trip
A key can briefly exceed its global limit while gateways act on stale state
hld:rate-limiter.explanation: Between syncs each gateway admits traffic against its own view, so total admission can overshoot a little. Teams accept this approximation in exchange for removing the network hop from the request path.

hld:rate-limiter.prompt: A request is rejected by the limiter. Select everything a well-behaved response should include.
options: Information about remaining quota, such as a remaining-requests header
A Retry-After value telling the client when to try again
Status 429 Too Many Requests
A 500 status so clients retry immediately
hld:rate-limiter.explanation: 429 is the standard signal, and Retry-After plus quota headers let clients back off instead of hammering. A 500 mislabels a deliberate policy decision as a server fault and invites instant retries.

hld:rate-limiter.prompt: Which statements about a token bucket (capacity b, refill rate r) are true? Select all that apply.
options: Over a long period the average rate is bounded by r
A full bucket permits a burst of up to b requests
Per-client state can be just a token count and a last-refill time
It must store a timestamp for every request to be correct
hld:rate-limiter.explanation: The bucket stores a count and the last refill instant and computes refills lazily on each call. Storing every timestamp is the sliding-window log, a different algorithm.

hld:rate-limiter.prompt: Requirements: 100 requests/min per API key, 1,000 requests/min per IP, and 5 logins/min per IP. How should the limiter evaluate a login request?
options: Merge all rules into one counter keyed by IP and use the smallest limit
Apply only the first matching rule and ignore the others
Check each applicable rule against its own counter keyed by (rule, client) and reject if any denies
Sum the limits and enforce the total across all clients
hld:rate-limiter.explanation: Each dimension has its own limit and identity, so each gets its own key and a request must pass all of them. One merged counter cannot express different limits and windows, and skipping rules leaves gaps.

hld:rate-limiter.prompt: A leaky bucket lets a client burst up to the bucket capacity and then throttles to the refill rate, while a token bucket forces output to a constant rate.
options: True
False
hld:rate-limiter.explanation: The two are swapped. A token bucket permits bursts up to its capacity; a leaky bucket drains at a fixed rate and smooths output.

hld:rate-limiter.prompt: If a limiter keys only on client IP, many users behind one corporate NAT share a single quota.
options: True
False
hld:rate-limiter.explanation: They all appear as one address, so one noisy user can exhaust the allowance for everyone. Keying on API key or user id, possibly with an IP rule as a backstop, avoids that.

hld:rate-limiter.prompt: Gateways take 50k req/s and each request checks 3 rules (per key, per IP, per endpoint), one Redis op per rule. If one Redis shard comfortably handles 100k ops/s and you want 2x headroom, how many shards do you need?
options: 2 shards
3 shards
6 shards
1 shard
hld:rate-limiter.explanation: 50k x 3 = 150k ops/s; with 2x headroom that's 300k ops/s; 300k / 100k = 3 shards. Two shards would cover only the raw 150k load with no headroom.

hld:rate-limiter.prompt: A sliding-window log stores an 8-byte timestamp per request. The limit is 1,000 requests per minute and 10,000 keys sit at their limit. About how much memory do their logs use, ignoring overhead?
options: About 800 MB
About 8 GB
About 80 MB
About 8 MB
hld:rate-limiter.explanation: 1,000 timestamps x 8 B = 8 KB per key; 8 KB x 10,000 = 80 MB. Memory grows with the limit, which is why a sliding-window counter (two numbers per key) is preferred at scale.

hld:rate-limiter.prompt: A sliding-window counter enforces 100 requests/min. The previous minute had 80 requests, the current minute has 30 so far, and we are 25% into the current minute. What is the estimate, and is the next request allowed?
options: 90, so the request is allowed
30, so the request is allowed
50, so the request is allowed
110, so the request is rejected
hld:rate-limiter.explanation: Estimate = current + previous x (fraction of the previous window still inside the sliding window) = 30 + 80 x 0.75 = 90, so request 91 is under 100. 110 wrongly counts the whole previous minute.

hld:rate-limiter.prompt: A team proposes enforcing limits only in the client SDK, so requests over quota are never sent. Why isn't that enough?
options: SDKs can't read Retry-After headers from the server
SDK timers drift across devices, so the per-minute windows become too inaccurate
Clients can be modified or bypassed, so limits must be enforced server-side
Client-side limits make 429 responses impossible to return
hld:rate-limiter.explanation: Anyone can call the API without the SDK or patch it, so only a server-side check (gateway or service) actually protects the backend. Client-side limiting is still useful to avoid wasted calls, but it is a courtesy, not enforcement.

hld:rate-limiter.prompt: A fixed-window limiter runs INCR key, then EXPIRE key 60 as two separate commands from the gateway. What failure can this cause?
options: INCR on a missing key throws an error, so the first request always fails
EXPIRE resets the counter to zero, so the limit is never enforced
A crash between the commands leaves the key without a TTL, so the client stays blocked
The two commands double-count every request when several gateways run them concurrently
hld:rate-limiter.explanation: If the gateway dies after INCR but before EXPIRE, the counter never expires and keeps climbing past the limit for good. A Lua script (or setting the TTL atomically on first increment) makes it one atomic step. INCR on a missing key starts at 1; it doesn't error.

hld:rate-limiter.prompt: On Redis Cluster, one Lua script updates both the per-API-key counter and the per-IP counter for a request, and it fails with a CROSSSLOT error. Why?
options: Scripts can't call INCR on keys that already have a TTL
Lua scripts are disabled on Redis Cluster because they could block other shards
All keys a script touches must hash to one slot, and these two don't
The script took longer than the cluster's replication timeout
hld:rate-limiter.explanation: Redis Cluster runs a script on one node, so all its keys must be in the same hash slot. Use a shared hash tag such as {client42} in both key names, or run the checks as separate calls. Scripting works on Cluster; the slot rule is the constraint.

hld:rate-limiter.prompt: Each limiter key in Redis (rule + client) is written with a TTL. What is the main purpose?
options: To make the take-a-token operation atomic
To make Redis replicate the key to every shard
To let state for inactive clients expire, so memory tracks active keys only
To force each client to re-authenticate with the gateway at the start of every window
hld:rate-limiter.explanation: With a TTL, idle clients' buckets disappear on their own, so memory stays near active keys x ~100 B. Atomicity comes from Lua or single commands, not from TTLs.

hld:rate-limiter.prompt: Gateways run in two regions, but the single Redis limiter cluster is in one of them, 40 ms away from the other. The budget is < 2 ms per request. What is the usual design?
options: Raise the latency budget, because global accuracy outweighs the 2 ms target
Make the far region's gateways call Redis asynchronously and allow while waiting
Keep one global Redis and add a read replica in the far region for token checks
Run a Redis per region with per-region limits, accepting an approximate global limit
hld:rate-limiter.explanation: A cross-region hop alone breaks the 2 ms budget, so each region enforces locally (often limit / regions, or periodically synced counts) and accepts a few percent error. Taking tokens from a read replica can't work because it's a write.

hld:rate-limiter.prompt: A token bucket stores tokens + last refill time and refills lazily on each request. Capacity is 10, refill rate 5 tokens/s, and 2 tokens were left at the last refill 3 seconds ago. How many tokens are available before this request takes one?
hld:rate-limiter.explanation: Refill = 3 s x 5/s = 15, so 2 + 15 = 17, capped at capacity 10. Forgetting the cap (17) would let a client build up bursts larger than the bucket allows.

hld:rate-limiter.prompt: A client gets a 429 from the API. Which client behaviours are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Retry with exponential backoff plus jitter if no header is given
Retry immediately in a tight loop until a request succeeds
Treat the 429 as a permanent error and never retry the request
Wait at least as long as the Retry-After header says
hld:rate-limiter.explanation: 429 is temporary: honour Retry-After, otherwise back off with jitter so many clients don't retry in sync. A tight loop just burns more quota, and giving up for good throws away a request that would succeed later.

hld:rate-limiter.prompt: The limiter fails open when Redis is unreachable. Which safeguards make failing open safer? Select all that apply.
options: Retrying the Redis call five times before every request
Short timeouts and a circuit breaker so requests don't wait on a dead Redis
Coarse local in-memory buckets on each gateway as a fallback
Alerting whenever gateways are running in fail-open mode
hld:rate-limiter.explanation: Local buckets keep some protection, circuit breakers keep latency within budget, and alerts make the degraded mode visible. Retrying a dead Redis five times per request adds latency and load exactly when things are already failing.

hld:rate-limiter.prompt: Which algorithms keep per-client memory constant, no matter how many requests the client sends? Select all that apply.
options: Fixed-window counter
Sliding-window counter
Token bucket
Sliding-window log
hld:rate-limiter.explanation: Token bucket (tokens + timestamp), fixed window (one counter) and sliding-window counter (two counters) are O(1) per client. A sliding-window log keeps one timestamp per request in the window, so memory grows with the limit.

hld:rate-limiter.prompt: A token bucket with capacity 1 and refill rate r admits at most one request every 1/r seconds and allows no bursts.
options: True
False
hld:rate-limiter.explanation: True. Only one token can ever be stored, and the next takes 1/r seconds to refill, so requests are spaced at least 1/r apart. Capacity b is exactly the burst allowance.

hld:rate-limiter.prompt: HTTP standards require every 429 response to include X-RateLimit-Limit and X-RateLimit-Remaining headers.
options: True
False
hld:rate-limiter.explanation: False. X-RateLimit-* headers are a widely used convention (GitHub documents its own set); they are not mandated. Retry-After is standard but optional. Returning them is still good API design.

hld:unique-id-generator.prompt: A Snowflake variant gives the timestamp 40 bits of milliseconds instead of 41. About how long until the timestamp field overflows?
options: 139 years
35 years
69 years
17 years
hld:unique-id-generator.explanation: 2^41 ms is about 69 years, so 2^40 ms is half of that, about 35 years. Each bit doubles or halves the lifetime, which is why the epoch is custom and recent.

hld:unique-id-generator.prompt: A variant uses 8 sequence bits per millisecond with the other fields unchanged. What is the maximum number of IDs one worker can issue per second?
hld:unique-id-generator.explanation: 2^8 = 256 IDs per millisecond x 1,000 ms = 256,000 per second. The original 12-bit layout gives 4,096 per millisecond. 256 forgets the millisecond-to-second factor.

hld:unique-id-generator.prompt: A worker last issued an ID at timestamp 1000 ms and now sees its clock stepped back to 990 ms by NTP. What should it do?
options: Reset the sequence to 0 and continue with 990 ms
Continue with 990 ms, since the sequence keeps IDs distinct
Wait or refuse until the clock passes the last issued timestamp
Add the clock offset into the machine id bits
hld:unique-id-generator.explanation: IDs for 990 ms may already have been issued by this same worker, so reusing that timestamp can reproduce an earlier timestamp, worker and sequence combination. Waiting or failing fast preserves uniqueness.

hld:unique-id-generator.prompt: Why is plain UUIDv4 a poor primary key for a large B-tree indexed table?
options: It cannot be generated across data centres
Its values are random and 128-bit, so inserts scatter across index pages and the index grows larger
It needs a ZooKeeper lease before each use
It collides often at 10k IDs per second
hld:unique-id-generator.explanation: Random keys land anywhere in the index, hurting locality, causing page splits and cache misses, and 128 bits cost more space than 64. Collisions are astronomically unlikely and no coordination is needed.

hld:unique-id-generator.prompt: A worker receives 5,000 ID requests inside one millisecond with a 12-bit sequence. What happens if it simply lets the sequence wrap to 0 and keeps the same timestamp?
options: IDs stay unique but lose time ordering
The worker id bits increment automatically to compensate
Nothing, because the sequence is unsigned and wraps safely
It issues duplicate IDs, because timestamp, worker and sequence repeat
hld:unique-id-generator.explanation: Only 4,096 sequence values exist per millisecond, so wrapping reproduces earlier values within the same millisecond. The generator should spin until the next millisecond instead.

hld:unique-id-generator.prompt: How should the 10-bit worker ids of a Snowflake fleet be assigned safely?
options: Take the last byte of the host's IP address
Pick a random 10-bit number at startup
Use the process id modulo 1,024
Lease them from a coordination service like ZooKeeper or etcd and reclaim them when leases expire
hld:unique-id-generator.explanation: Two live workers sharing an id can issue identical IDs, so assignment must be unique. Random picks collide quickly by the birthday effect, and IP bytes or pids repeat across subnets and hosts.

hld:unique-id-generator.prompt: Flickr-style ticket servers use two databases handing out odd and even IDs. What does that solve, and what does it still lack?
options: It removes the one-database failure point, but IDs still cost a round trip and are not time-sorted
It removes the network call per ID, and it keeps IDs strictly time-ordered
It hides creation volume from outsiders, but the two servers can issue clashing IDs
It makes IDs unguessable to outsiders, but it halves the throughput of one server
hld:unique-id-generator.explanation: Two servers with different parity avoid collisions and survive one failing, but each ID still needs a round trip and ordering is only roughly interleaved. IDs also still reveal volume.

hld:unique-id-generator.prompt: Which are properties of Snowflake-style IDs? Select all that apply.
options: A worker can issue them without a network call per ID
They fit in a signed 64-bit integer
They reveal nothing about creation time
They are strictly increasing across all workers
They sort roughly by creation time
hld:unique-id-generator.explanation: The layout is 64 bits with a timestamp prefix and each worker generates locally. Ordering across workers is only approximate because clocks differ, and the timestamp bits plainly leak creation time.

hld:unique-id-generator.prompt: Compared with UUIDv4, which statements about UUIDv7 and ULID are true? Select all that apply.
options: They fit in a 64-bit integer column
They are still 128-bit values
Nodes can generate them without coordinating
A time prefix makes new inserts cluster near the end of an index
hld:unique-id-generator.explanation: The time-ordered prefix improves B-tree locality, and no coordination is required like UUIDv4. They remain 128 bits, so a 64-bit column does not hold them; that is Snowflake's niche.

hld:unique-id-generator.prompt: Snowflake IDs from two different workers are guaranteed to be strictly ordered by their real creation time.
options: True
False
hld:unique-id-generator.explanation: Each worker stamps IDs using its own clock, and clocks differ by skew. IDs are roughly time-ordered, but two IDs created close together on different workers can sort the wrong way.

hld:unique-id-generator.prompt: Using a database auto-increment ID as a public identifier can leak business volume, such as how many orders were created.
options: True
False
hld:unique-id-generator.explanation: Sequential values let an observer compare two IDs over time and compute the rate of creation. Snowflake IDs also leak creation time, so this trade-off applies to time-prefixed schemes as well.

hld:unique-id-generator.prompt: In practice each ID worker is CPU-limited to about 200k IDs/s, and the fleet needs 50M IDs/s at peak. How many workers are needed, and does that fit the 10-bit worker space?
options: 250 workers; fits within 1,024
12 workers, since 4,096 IDs/ms per worker is the real limit
2,500 workers; exceeds 1,024
25 workers; fits easily
hld:unique-id-generator.explanation: 50M / 200k = 250 workers, well under 2^10 = 1,024. The 4,096 IDs/ms bit limit (~4M/s) is a ceiling, not achievable throughput when CPU caps a worker at 200k/s.

hld:unique-id-generator.prompt: A Snowflake generator uses a custom epoch of 2020-01-01 and 41 bits of milliseconds. Roughly when does the timestamp field run out?
options: Around 2038
Around 2156
Around 2089
Around 2059
hld:unique-id-generator.explanation: 2^41 ms = ~2.2e12 ms = ~69.7 years, so 2020 + 69.7 = ~2089. 2038 is the 32-bit Unix seconds overflow, a different limit.

hld:unique-id-generator.prompt: Why does Snowflake count milliseconds from a custom epoch instead of the Unix epoch (1970)?
options: Counting from 1970 would waste over 50 years of the ~69-year range
The Unix epoch is not the same across time zones
A custom epoch makes IDs impossible for outsiders to decode into timestamps
Unix time is in seconds, so it can't express milliseconds
hld:unique-id-generator.explanation: 41 bits give ~69 years from the epoch; starting at 1970 would mean that window ends around 2039. A custom epoch near launch uses the full range. IDs can still be decoded by anyone who knows the epoch.

hld:unique-id-generator.prompt: A Node.js API returns Snowflake IDs as JSON numbers, and browser clients see IDs whose last digits are wrong. Why, and what's the standard fix?
options: IDs above 2^53 - 1 lose precision as JS doubles; send them as strings
Snowflake IDs are signed, so the sign bit flips; mask it off first
Browsers parse JSON numbers in base 10 but the IDs are base 16; send them as hex strings
JSON.stringify truncates integers over 32 bits; switch to BigInt64Array
hld:unique-id-generator.explanation: JS numbers are IEEE-754 doubles with 53 bits of integer precision, and 64-bit IDs with recent timestamps exceed that, so parsing rounds them. Send IDs as strings (Twitter added id_str for this) and use BigInt server-side.

hld:unique-id-generator.prompt: Layout: 1 sign | 41 timestamp | 5 DC | 5 worker | 12 sequence. Given an ID as a JavaScript BigInt, which expression yields milliseconds since the custom epoch?
options: id >> 12n
id & 0xFFFn
id >> 22n
id >> 41n
hld:unique-id-generator.explanation: Below the timestamp are 5 + 5 + 12 = 22 bits, so shift right by 22. >> 12n only removes the sequence and leaves the DC and worker bits mixed in; & 0xFFFn extracts the sequence.

hld:unique-id-generator.prompt: A worker's etcd lease on worker id 17 expires during a long GC pause, and id 17 is leased to a new worker. The old worker resumes and keeps issuing IDs. What's the risk and the fix?
options: None, since the two workers' clocks differ slightly and IDs won't match
Duplicate IDs; a worker must stop issuing once its lease may have lapsed
The timestamp overflows early; restart the worker with a new epoch
Gaps in the sequence; the new worker should start its sequence at 4,096 to stay clear
hld:unique-id-generator.explanation: Two live workers with the same DC + worker id in the same millisecond produce identical IDs. Workers must check the lease before issuing (stopping when unsure), and the coordinator should wait a safety margin before reusing an id. Clock differences don't stop collisions.

hld:unique-id-generator.prompt: Order IDs are Snowflake IDs and appear in public URLs. What can an outsider learn from them?
options: Each order's creation time to the millisecond, and which DC and worker issued it
The customer's account id, because Snowflake encodes it in the low sequence bits of each ID
Nothing, since Snowflake IDs are cryptographically random
The exact running total of orders, like an auto-increment counter
hld:unique-id-generator.explanation: The timestamp, DC and worker fields decode directly, so creation time leaks (and request rates can be roughly inferred). Unlike auto-increment, they don't give an exact global count, and they are not random.

hld:unique-id-generator.prompt: A team wants IDs that need no coordination at all and sort roughly by time, and 128 bits is acceptable. Which choice fits best?
options: Snowflake with leased worker ids
UUIDv4
A database sequence
UUIDv7
hld:unique-id-generator.explanation: UUIDv7 (RFC 9562) starts with a Unix millisecond timestamp followed by random bits: time-ordered and needs no worker ids. UUIDv4 is random, so not ordered; Snowflake needs worker-id coordination.

hld:unique-id-generator.prompt: Rows are sharded by id % 1024. Most workers are low-traffic and issue about one ID per millisecond, so the sequence is usually 0. What goes wrong?
options: The shard map overflows because Snowflake IDs exceed 2^63
Most IDs have zero low bits, so a few shards get most of the rows
Nothing, since the timestamp bits make id % 1024 uniform
IDs collide across shards because the modulus discards the timestamp
hld:unique-id-generator.explanation: The lowest 12 bits are the sequence, which resets every millisecond; at low rates it's mostly 0, so id % 1024 is mostly 0 and one shard gets hot. Hash the ID (or shard on other bits) instead. Timestamp bits sit above bit 22, so they don't affect % 1024.

hld:unique-id-generator.prompt: Which measures reduce the risk of duplicate IDs when a worker's clock moves backwards? Select all that apply.
options: Run NTP in slewing mode so corrections speed up or slow the clock instead of stepping it
Refuse to issue and raise an alert when the backward jump is large
Remember the last issued timestamp and wait until the clock passes it
Switch the worker to local time instead of UTC
Reset the sequence to 0 and keep issuing with the older timestamp
hld:unique-id-generator.explanation: Waiting avoids reissuing past timestamps, slewing avoids jumps, and refusing on big jumps fails safely. Reusing an older timestamp with a reset sequence can duplicate IDs already issued; time zones are irrelevant to epoch milliseconds.

hld:unique-id-generator.prompt: Compare running Snowflake as an in-process library versus a small network service. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
options: The network service makes IDs strictly ordered across the whole fleet
A central service keeps worker-id management to a few known hosts
The library needs a unique worker id per process, using up the 1,024 ids faster
The library removes a network hop and the service as a failure point
hld:unique-id-generator.explanation: In-process is fastest and has no extra dependency, but every process needs its own worker id. A service keeps ids to a few hosts but adds a hop. Neither gives strict global ordering, since multiple workers still issue IDs in parallel.

hld:unique-id-generator.prompt: Which ID schemes keep B-tree index inserts mostly at the right-hand edge instead of scattering them? Select all that apply.
options: ULID
UUIDv4
SHA-256 of the row content
Snowflake IDs
UUIDv7
hld:unique-id-generator.explanation: Snowflake, UUIDv7 and ULID start with a timestamp, so new keys sort after recent ones and pages stay hot in cache. UUIDv4 and content hashes are effectively random, causing page splits and random I/O across the index.

hld:unique-id-generator.prompt: With 5 data-centre bits and 5 worker bits, the layout supports up to 32 data centres with up to 32 workers each.
options: True
False
hld:unique-id-generator.explanation: True. 2^5 = 32 for each field, 1,024 combinations in total. Some deployments merge the two into a single 10-bit worker id to use the space more flexibly.

hld:unique-id-generator.prompt: If two workers are accidentally given the same worker id, the 12-bit sequence still keeps their IDs unique.
options: True
False
hld:unique-id-generator.explanation: False. Each worker keeps its own sequence, so both start at 0 each millisecond and can produce exactly the same ID. Uniqueness depends on distinct worker ids; that's why they're leased carefully.

hld:notification-system.prompt: A campaign must push to 50M users within 20 minutes. What sustained send rate is required?
options: About 2.5 million per second
About 42,000 per second
About 420,000 per second
About 4,200 per second
hld:notification-system.explanation: 20 minutes = 1,200 s; 50M / 1,200 is about 41,700 per second. That is far above the 200 per second average, which is why bursts are buffered in queues and workers scale out.

hld:notification-system.prompt: A campaign burst arrives at 50k messages per second for 60 seconds, while workers can send 10k per second. How large is the queue backlog at the end of the burst?
options: 2.4 million
3 million
hld:notification-system.explanation: The queue grows by (50k - 10k) = 40k per second for 60 s = 2.4 million. 3 million forgets that workers drain during the burst; 600,000 counts only what was drained. The backlog then drains at 10k per second.

hld:notification-system.prompt: Push, SMS and email share one queue and one worker pool. The SMS provider goes down and each SMS attempt hangs. What goes wrong?
options: Messages are acknowledged and lost without retry
Stuck SMS attempts and retries occupy workers, delaying push and email too
Push and email messages are rerouted to SMS
Nothing, because retries are asynchronous
hld:notification-system.explanation: With shared capacity, a slow or failing provider consumes workers and grows a common backlog. A queue per channel isolates the failure and lets each pool scale independently.

hld:notification-system.prompt: 1,000 workers all retry a failed provider call after exactly 2s, then 4s, then 8s, and the provider keeps struggling. What is missing from the retry policy?
options: A longer first delay of 10 minutes
Jitter, so retries from different workers do not hit in synchronized waves
Retrying on a different channel for every attempt
A fixed retry interval instead of exponential backoff
hld:notification-system.explanation: Backoff alone keeps clients in lockstep, so each wave lands together and prolongs the outage. Random jitter spreads retries out. A DLQ after N attempts then bounds the work.

hld:notification-system.prompt: A worker sends a push, then crashes before acknowledging its queue message, so the queue redelivers it. How do you prevent a visible duplicate?
options: Acknowledge before sending so it can never be redelivered
Use a queue advertised as exactly-once
Disable retries after a crash
Have the next worker check the delivery log for the idempotency key before sending
hld:notification-system.explanation: At-least-once delivery means redelivery happens, so the sender must dedup using an idempotency key and a log. Acking first becomes at-most-once and loses messages when a crash comes after the ack. A small send-then-record window remains.

hld:notification-system.prompt: A bug in an upstream service loops and calls the API 500 times in a minute for the same user, each call with a different idempotency key. Which control limits the damage?
options: The idempotency key check
A per-user frequency cap before enqueueing
A dead-letter queue
Retry with exponential backoff
hld:notification-system.explanation: Distinct keys look like distinct requests, so dedup passes them all. A per-user frequency cap stops excessive volume regardless of caller bugs. Backoff and a DLQ handle delivery failures, not excess demand.

hld:notification-system.prompt: How should a 50M-user campaign be sent?
options: A loop in the API server thread that calls the provider for each user
A campaign job reads the segment in pages and enqueues per-user messages at a controlled rate into the channel queues
One synchronous API call that carries all 50M user ids
Fan out all 50M messages instantly so workers autoscale to absorb them
hld:notification-system.explanation: Paging through the segment and enqueueing at a controlled rate keeps memory bounded, lets queues buffer, and respects provider limits. A single giant request or inline loop fails or ties up the API, and an instant flood can overwhelm queues and providers.

hld:notification-system.prompt: APNs is down for an hour. What is the sensible behaviour for queued iOS push messages?
options: Move them to the SMS queue so users still get a message
Reroute them through FCM, which bypasses APNs
Drop them, since push is best-effort
Keep them in the push queue, retry with backoff and jitter, and expire stale ones by TTL
hld:notification-system.explanation: APNs is the delivery gateway to iOS, and FCM reaches iOS through APNs anyway, so rerouting does not help. Waiting with backoff and a TTL works, and SMS and email queues keep flowing independently. Dropping loses important messages.

hld:notification-system.prompt: Choosing a message broker with exactly-once semantics is enough to guarantee a user's device receives a notification exactly once, end to end.
options: True
False
hld:notification-system.explanation: Exactly-once inside the broker does not cover the provider call or the device. A crash after the provider accepts but before the ack leads to a retry, so systems use at-least-once plus idempotent dedup.

hld:notification-system.prompt: Quiet hours should be evaluated in the user's time zone, not the server's.
options: True
False
hld:notification-system.explanation: A user's 10 pm to 7 am window is local to them. Evaluating in server time would wake users abroad. Store the time zone with the preference and compare against it.

hld:notification-system.prompt: After N failed delivery attempts a notification is parked. Select all practices that apply.
options: Move it to a dead-letter queue
Keep it so it can be inspected and replayed after a fix
Drop it silently to protect queue health
Alert when the DLQ depth grows
hld:notification-system.explanation: A DLQ keeps poison or unlucky messages from blocking retries while preserving them. Alerting on its depth surfaces provider or payload problems, and silent drops lose messages.

hld:notification-system.prompt: Which signals best show that the SMS pipeline is falling behind? Select all that apply.
options: Error rate from the SMS provider
Growth of the SMS dead-letter queue
Average template length
Age of the oldest message in the SMS queue
hld:notification-system.explanation: Queue age, provider errors and DLQ growth all directly reflect delivery trouble. Template length is a static content property and says nothing about throughput or health.

hld:notification-system.prompt: The system sends 16M notifications a day, and each delivery-log row is about 200 B. Rows are kept for 90 days. About how much log storage is that, before replication?
options: About 288 GB
About 2.9 TB
About 3.2 GB
About 29 GB
hld:notification-system.explanation: 16M x 200 B = 3.2 GB/day; x 90 days = 288 GB. 3.2 GB is one day's worth. A TTL or time-partitioned table makes the 90-day cleanup cheap.

hld:notification-system.prompt: Each push worker can send about 500 messages/s to APNs/FCM. To keep up with a 50k msgs/s campaign burst without a growing backlog, how many push workers are needed?
options: 100 workers
1,000 workers
50 workers
10 workers
hld:notification-system.explanation: 50,000 / 500 = 100 workers. Fewer workers is fine if a backlog that drains later is acceptable, but keeping pace with the burst needs about 100.

hld:notification-system.prompt: A 50M-user marketing push is draining through the push queue when users start reporting that password-reset and OTP pushes arrive 15 minutes late. What's the best fix?
options: Separate queues for transactional and bulk traffic, serving transactional first
Cap campaigns at 1M users so they never fill the queue
Add more push workers so the campaign drains faster and the OTPs reach the front sooner
Send OTPs by email instead whenever a campaign is running
hld:notification-system.explanation: A FIFO queue puts OTPs behind millions of marketing messages. Separate priority lanes protect the < 5 s transactional SLO no matter how big a campaign gets. More workers only shortens the delay; it doesn't remove head-of-line blocking.

hld:notification-system.prompt: APNs answers a push with 410 Unregistered (FCM: UNREGISTERED) for a device token. What should the worker do?
options: Send the message by SMS instead, without checking preferences
Mark the token inactive in devices and stop sending to it
Move the message to the dead-letter queue for manual review
Retry with exponential backoff, since the device may be offline
hld:notification-system.explanation: That response means the app was uninstalled or the token rotated; retrying will never succeed and repeated sends to bad tokens can get you throttled. Remove or deactivate the token. Offline devices are queued by APNs/FCM, not rejected like this.

hld:notification-system.prompt: A product service's POST /v1/notifications times out, and it retries with the same idempotencyKey. The first request had actually succeeded. What should the API do?
options: Return the original result without enqueuing the notification again
Reject the retry with 409 so the caller knows it was a duplicate
Enqueue it again, since workers will dedup by user id
Enqueue it again but lower its priority
hld:notification-system.explanation: The idempotency key (stored with a TTL) maps to the first outcome, so a retry replays that response and causes no second send. A 409 forces every caller to special-case retries; deduping by user id would block legitimate different notifications.

hld:notification-system.prompt: Preferences are checked when a campaign is enqueued. A user opts out of marketing while their message has been sitting in the queue for two hours. What should the design do?
options: Recheck opt-outs (cached) in the worker just before sending
Purge every queued message whenever any preference changes
Nothing; the check at enqueue time is binding for that campaign
Send it anyway and apologise in the next campaign
hld:notification-system.explanation: Checking at enqueue filters early, but long queues mean preferences can change before send; a cheap cached recheck in the worker respects the opt-out (often a legal requirement). Purging queues on every change is far too expensive at this scale.

hld:notification-system.prompt: Email goes to a primary provider with failover to a second. A request to the primary times out, and the worker fails over immediately. What risk does this create?
options: The primary may have delivered anyway, so the user can get the email twice
The delivery log ends up with two rows and fails its unique constraint
The second provider rejects messages already seen by the primary
None, because a timeout means the primary didn't send it
hld:notification-system.explanation: A timeout is an unknown outcome, not a failure, so failing over can duplicate. For transactional mail a rare duplicate is usually accepted; otherwise wait for the provider's status callback before failing over. Providers don't share dedup state.

hld:notification-system.prompt: A campaign must reach each user "at 10:00 their local time" worldwide. How should it be scheduled?
options: Have each device poll every minute and show the message at 10:00
Group users by time zone and release each group's batch at its local 10:00
Send everything at 10:00 server time, since most users are in one region
Send at 10:00 UTC and let quiet hours drop the rest
hld:notification-system.explanation: Bucketing users by time zone and scheduling one batch per zone delivers at the right local time and naturally spreads the load over ~24 hours. Relying on quiet hours would silently drop users rather than reschedule them.

hld:notification-system.prompt: The email provider starts returning 429 Too Many Requests during a large send. What should the email workers do?
options: Switch every email to SMS until the provider recovers
Throttle to the provider's rate with a shared limiter and retry the 429s with backoff
Scale out the email workers so that more parallel requests get through the provider's limit
Mark those messages as failed and move them to the DLQ immediately
hld:notification-system.explanation: 429 means slow down: a shared token bucket matching the provider's quota, plus backoff on rejected sends, gets everything delivered. More workers make the throttling worse, and 429s are retryable, not permanent failures.

hld:notification-system.prompt: Which provider responses should a worker retry with backoff? Select all that apply.
options: 503 Service Unavailable from the provider
Network timeout while calling the provider
429 Too Many Requests
400 Bad Request because the template payload is invalid
Device token reported as unregistered
hld:notification-system.explanation: 503s, timeouts and 429s are transient and may succeed later. An unregistered token or a malformed payload will fail every time; retrying only wastes capacity, so deactivate the token or send to the DLQ and fix the bug.

hld:notification-system.prompt: Which controls stop the system from spamming users? Select all that apply.
options: Collapsing or digesting near-identical notifications within a time window
A per-user frequency cap per channel
A kill switch that halts a campaign mid-send
Relying on APNs/FCM to drop repeated messages
hld:notification-system.explanation: Caps, collapsing/digests and a campaign kill switch are all owned by your system. Push providers deliver what you send (collapse keys only replace undelivered messages you explicitly tag), so they are no protection against your own bugs.

hld:notification-system.prompt: Which delivery facts can the system learn reliably from providers? Select all that apply.
options: The user actually saw the push, inferred from APNs returning 200
The provider accepted the message for delivery
An email hard-bounced, via the provider's webhook
An SMS delivery receipt, where the carrier supports it
hld:notification-system.explanation: Acceptance, bounces and SMS delivery receipts are reported by providers. An APNs 200 only means Apple accepted the push; whether it reached or was seen on the device needs an in-app open/receipt event.

hld:notification-system.prompt: Exponential backoff with "full jitter" waits a random time between 0 and the current exponential cap before each retry.
options: True
False
hld:notification-system.explanation: True. Full jitter picks uniformly in [0, min(cap, base x 2^attempt)], spreading retries out so clients don't hit the provider in synchronized waves. Plain exponential backoff without jitter keeps them in lockstep.

hld:notification-system.prompt: Writing the idempotency key to the delivery log only after the provider call succeeds fully prevents duplicates if a worker crashes mid-send.
options: True
False
hld:notification-system.explanation: False. If the worker crashes after the provider sends but before the log write, the redelivered message finds no record and sends again. Record a 'sending' state first (and check it on retry), or pass a provider-side idempotency key, to narrow that window.

hld:news-feed.prompt: A news feed uses pure fan-out on write: every new post id is pushed into each follower's cached timeline. An account with 100 million followers posts once. What is the core problem, and what is the usual remedy?
options: Post ids are no longer unique at that scale; move to UUIDs generated per follower
Reads become O(n) in the number of followees; switch the whole system to pull on read
One post triggers about 100 million cache inserts; keep pushing for normal users but merge that account's recent posts in at read time
The follow graph cannot be read for an account that large; cap followers at a fixed limit
hld:news-feed.explanation: Push makes write cost proportional to follower count, so a celebrity post becomes a huge burst of inserts. The hybrid keeps cheap O(1) reads for ordinary authors and pulls only the few celebrity authors a user follows at read time. Switching everything to pull would make every read slow to fix a problem that only a few accounts cause.

hld:news-feed.prompt: A feed service has 300M daily active users, each loading the timeline 5 times a day. Spread evenly over 86,400 seconds, roughly how many timeline reads per second is that on average?
options: About 17k per second
About 1.7k per second
About 1.7M per second
About 170k per second
hld:news-feed.explanation: 300M x 5 = 1.5 billion reads per day. Divided by roughly 86,400 seconds, that is about 17,400 reads per second on average. Peak traffic is a multiple of this, which is why the case budgets about 50k per second for peak. The other options are off by a factor of ten in one direction or the other.

hld:news-feed.prompt: Posts arrive at 50 million per day, which is about 580 per second. Under fan-out on write, the average author has 400 followers instead of 200. Roughly how many timeline-cache inserts per second does that imply?
options: About 58k per second
About 231k per second
About 460k per second
About 116k per second
hld:news-feed.explanation: 580 posts/s x 400 followers is about 231k inserts per second. The 116k option is the figure for 200 followers, so it ignores the change, and doubling write amplification doubles inserts. This is the write amplification trade-off: reads stay O(1) but write load scales with the follower count.

hld:news-feed.prompt: The timeline cache stores only post ids (a capped Redis list per user) and hydrates bodies from a post cache. Which benefits does this give? Select all that apply.
options: The timeline service no longer needs any read from the post cache or posts DB
Each cached entry is small, so many more timelines fit in memory
A deleted or edited post is reflected at hydration time without rewriting every follower's list
Capping list length bounds the memory used per user
hld:news-feed.explanation: Ids are tiny, and bodies live in one place, so edits and deletes show up at hydration and the cap bounds per-user memory. The id-only design does not remove the post lookup: that hydration step is exactly where the bodies come from, so claiming no post reads are needed is wrong.

hld:news-feed.prompt: In a hybrid feed design, a user sees a celebrity's new post because the fan-out workers insert it into that user's cached timeline just like any other post.
options: True
False
hld:news-feed.explanation: False. The point of the hybrid is that celebrity posts are not fanned out; the timeline service fetches those authors' recent posts at read time and merges them with the pre-built cache. Fanning them out would reintroduce the 100M-insert burst the hybrid exists to avoid.

hld:news-feed.prompt: A ranked feed is paged with ?page=2&limit=20, and the service re-scores and re-sorts candidates on every request. Users report seeing the same post on consecutive pages. What is the best fix?
options: Re-run ranking and drop any post the user has ever seen from the whole history
Use OFFSET pagination but sort by author id to make results deterministic
Return a cursor tied to a stable snapshot of the ranked candidate ids, and continue from it
Give each page a larger limit so users rarely reach page two
hld:news-feed.explanation: With re-ranking, scores and new posts shift positions between requests, so an offset lands on items already shown. A cursor into a fixed ranked candidate list (or one that carries the last position plus an exclusion of ids already served) keeps pages consistent. Sorting by author id would destroy the ranking.

hld:news-feed.prompt: Many accounts are inactive: they have not opened the app in weeks. Which policy best balances freshness against cost?
options: Keep fanning out to every follower's timeline so it is always fresh
Move their timelines to the posts DB and read them synchronously on every load
Delete inactive users' follow edges so fan-out has fewer targets
Skip fan-out for long-inactive users and rebuild their timeline on demand when they return
hld:news-feed.explanation: Pushing into timelines nobody reads wastes writes and cache memory. Rebuilding on demand at next login trades a slower first load for a large saving. Deleting follow edges loses user data, and the DB-only variant just moves cost to every read.

hld:news-feed.prompt: A fan-out worker consumes 'new post' events and must find all followers of the author. The follows table is only indexed by follower_id. What is the problem?
options: Followers of an author cannot be looked up efficiently, so the data also needs an index or copy keyed by followee_id
Followers must be stored inside the post row instead
A relational database cannot store a many-to-many relationship
The table needs a unique constraint on follower_id to be queryable
hld:news-feed.explanation: Fan-out asks 'who follows X', while timeline reads ask 'whom does Y follow'. Both directions are needed, which is why the data model stores the relation both ways. An index keyed only by follower_id would force a full scan for every post.

hld:news-feed.prompt: A user deletes a post that already sits in many followers' cached timelines (id lists). Which approaches are sound? Select all that apply.
options: Block the delete request until the id is removed from every follower's list
Mark the post deleted in the post store and drop ids whose post is missing or deleted when hydrating
Publish a delete event so workers remove the id from cached timelines asynchronously
