Rely only on timeline TTL expiry, accepting that the post may stay visible for days
hld:news-feed.explanation: Hydration filtering gives immediate correctness, and an async delete event cleans up the lists eventually. Blocking the author on millions of list edits does not scale and is unnecessary. Relying on TTL alone leaves a deleted post visible to followers, which is a correctness and privacy failure.

hld:news-feed.prompt: Fan-out on read keeps write cost low because posting only stores one row, but timeline latency grows with the number of accounts a user follows.
options: True
False
hld:news-feed.explanation: True. Pull builds the timeline by merging recent posts from every followee at request time, so read cost scales with followee count and is hard to keep under a 200 ms target for heavy followers. That is the mirror image of push, whose reads are O(1) but writes explode.

hld:news-feed.prompt: Each of 300M users has a cached timeline of up to 800 post ids at 8 bytes each. About how much memory do the id lists need, before Redis overhead and replication?
options: About 192 GB
About 1.9 TB
About 19 TB
About 19 GB
hld:news-feed.explanation: 800 x 8 B = 6.4 KB per user; 6.4 KB x 300M = 1.92 TB. That's why inactive users' timelines are often not kept and are rebuilt on demand instead.

hld:news-feed.prompt: At a peak of 50k timeline loads/s, each load hydrates 20 posts with one batched multi-get to the post cache. What load does the post cache see?
options: About 50k post lookups/s in 2,500 batches
About 20k post lookups/s in 1k batches
About 1M post lookups/s in 50k batches
About 100k post lookups/s in 50k batches
hld:news-feed.explanation: 50k x 20 = 1M post lookups/s, grouped into 50k multi-get calls. Batching cuts round trips, not keys, so the cache must still be sized for ~1M key reads/s.

hld:news-feed.prompt: In the hybrid fan-out design, how is "celebrity" usually decided?
options: Accounts that post more than 10 times a day are treated as celebrities
Accounts manually verified by staff skip fan-out and the timeline cache entirely
Any account with a profile photo and over 1,000 likes
Accounts above a follower-count threshold are excluded from fan-out on write
hld:news-feed.explanation: Fan-out cost scales with follower count, so a threshold on followers (often tuned around tens of thousands or more) decides who is pulled at read time. Posting frequency matters less than how many timelines each post touches.

hld:news-feed.prompt: After a big live event the fan-out queue lags by two minutes. Users post and then don't see their own post in their home timeline. What's the best fix?
options: Merge the user's own recent posts into their timeline at read time
Make the post request wait until fan-out to all followers has finished
Tell users to refresh after two minutes
Shorten the timeline cache TTL to a few seconds
hld:news-feed.explanation: Read-your-own-writes only needs the author's view fixed: merge their latest posts (from the posts DB or a small per-user cache) at read time, or insert them client-side. Blocking the post on fan-out would make posting take minutes.

hld:news-feed.prompt: A chronological timeline is served with GET /v1/timeline?cursor=…&limit=20. What makes a good cursor?
options: The id of the last post shown, so the next page fetches ids below it
A random token mapped to a server-side session
The timestamp of the client's last request
The page number, multiplied by limit to compute an OFFSET into the timeline
hld:news-feed.explanation: Snowflake post ids sort by time, so "ids < cursor" is stable even when new posts arrive at the top. Offsets shift when new posts are inserted, causing duplicates or skipped posts.

hld:news-feed.prompt: A user follows a new account, but the new followee's posts only appear after that account posts again. How do you fix this?
options: Disable the timeline cache for users who followed someone today
Asynchronously backfill the followee's recent posts into the cached timeline
Wait for the nightly batch job to fold in new follows
Rebuild the user's whole timeline from scratch, synchronously, on every follow
hld:news-feed.explanation: A follow event triggers a small job that merges the followee's last N posts into the cached id list by id. A full rebuild is far more work than needed, and a nightly job breaks the expectation that follows show up immediately.

hld:news-feed.prompt: Fan-out workers do LPUSH timeline:{user} postId followed by LTRIM timeline:{user} 0 799. What is the LTRIM for?
options: It removes duplicate post ids from the list
It caps each list at 800 ids so cache memory stays bounded
It makes the preceding LPUSH atomic across all of the Redis replicas
It sorts the list by post id after the push
hld:news-feed.explanation: Without trimming, every list grows forever; capping at ~800 ids bounds memory, and older pages fall back to the posts DB. LTRIM doesn't deduplicate or sort.

hld:news-feed.prompt: Posts are sharded by author_id. A celebrity with 80M followers posts, and millions of readers pull that post at read time. The celebrity's shard is overloaded. What helps most?
options: Keep celebrities' recent posts in a replicated in-memory cache
Switch the celebrity back to fan-out on write for this post
Re-shard posts by post_id so the celebrity's posts spread across shards
Rate-limit how often followers can open their timeline
hld:news-feed.explanation: Reads concentrate on a handful of hot posts, so caching celebrities' latest posts (replicated across cache nodes) absorbs the load. Re-sharding by post_id breaks "recent posts by author" queries, and fan-out on write for 80M followers is what the hybrid avoids.

hld:news-feed.prompt: The ranked feed fetches a candidate set of a few hundred post ids and scores only those. Why not score every recent post from all followees?
options: Ranking models can only take a fixed input of a few hundred rows
Older posts can't be scored because their engagement data is deleted
Scoring everything would surface posts from accounts the user doesn't even follow
Scoring thousands of posts per request would blow the latency and compute budget
hld:news-feed.explanation: Two-stage ranking (cheap candidate generation, then an expensive model on a few hundred items) keeps latency and cost bounded. Models can score more rows; it's simply too slow and costly per request.

hld:news-feed.prompt: Which statements about fan-out on write are true? Select all that apply.
options: Write work grows with the author's follower count
New followers automatically see the author's older posts
Timeline reads are cheap because the id list is precomputed
Deleting a post needs no extra handling
Work is wasted on followers who never open the app
hld:news-feed.explanation: Push precomputes timelines, so reads are fast but writes scale with followers, including inactive ones. Deletes must be removed or filtered from many lists, and new follows need a backfill to show older posts.

hld:news-feed.prompt: In a chronological feed, which events should change a user's cached timeline? Select all that apply.
options: Someone likes a post that is already in their timeline
They unfollow an account (remove or filter its posts)
They block an account they were following
A non-celebrity account they follow publishes a post
They follow a new account (backfill recent posts)
hld:news-feed.explanation: Posts, follows, unfollows and blocks all change which ids belong in the list. A like changes a post's engagement, which matters for ranking, not for the membership or order of a chronological id list.

hld:news-feed.prompt: New-post events go to Kafka partitioned by author_id and fan-out workers consume them. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
options: Kafka delivers each event exactly once, so timeline inserts never repeat
Storing timelines as sorted sets keyed by post id makes reprocessing idempotent
One author's posts are processed in order within their partition
Fan-out capacity scales by adding partitions and consumers
hld:news-feed.explanation: Keying by author preserves per-author order, and partitions are the unit of parallelism. Consumer crashes can replay events, so a plain LPUSH could insert twice; ZADD with the post id as member and score makes repeats harmless.

hld:news-feed.prompt: Storing follows in both directions is unnecessary, because a single index on follower_id serves "who follows X?" just as efficiently.
options: True
False
hld:news-feed.explanation: False. An index on follower_id answers "whom does X follow?". Fan-out needs "who follows X?", which would mean scanning every partition. Keeping both directions makes each a single-partition read.

hld:news-feed.prompt: With Snowflake post ids, sorting a timeline by post id gives roughly chronological order without storing created_at in the cache.
options: True
False
hld:news-feed.explanation: True. Snowflake ids start with a millisecond timestamp, so id order roughly follows creation time (within clock skew between workers). That's why the cache can store bare ids and still paginate by time.

hld:chat.prompt: A chat service has 100M daily users sending 40 messages a day each at about 100 bytes per message (400 GB/day). Roughly how much raw message data accumulates per year, before replication?
options: About 1.46 PB
About 146 TB
About 14.6 TB
About 14.6 PB
hld:chat.explanation: 400 GB/day x 365 is roughly 146,000 GB, or about 146 TB. With replication (commonly 3x) and multiple years, history reaches the petabyte scale, which is why the case partitions by chat in a wide-column store. The other options are off by factors of ten.

hld:chat.prompt: Each WebSocket gateway can hold about 500k connections. At a future peak of 250 million concurrent connections, what is the minimum number of gateways, ignoring headroom?
hld:chat.explanation: 250M / 500k = 500 gateways. In practice you add headroom for failures and spikes, so the real fleet is larger. The 250 option divides by 1M instead, and 50 and 2,500 are order-of-magnitude slips.

hld:chat.prompt: Why does the design assign a sequence number per chat rather than one global total order across all messages?
options: A global order would reveal the number of users on the platform
Global ordering is impossible because clocks differ between phones
Per-chat numbers use fewer bits, which is what allows partitioning in Cassandra
Users only need messages ordered within a conversation, and a global sequencer would be a bottleneck and single point of failure
hld:chat.explanation: Ordering only matters inside one chat, so each chat can be sequenced independently and spread across shards. A single global counter would limit throughput and availability. Clock differences matter for timestamps, but a server-assigned sequence does not depend on client clocks anyway.

hld:chat.prompt: A sender's phone sends a message, the server persists it, but the ack is lost on a flaky network. The client retries the same send. How should the server behave?
options: Store it again with a new sequence number, since the retry is a new request
Reject the retry with an error so the client gives up
Compare timestamps and keep the earlier copy only if it is under a second old
Recognise the clientMsgId as already stored and return the original msgId and seq
hld:chat.explanation: The client-generated clientMsgId makes the send idempotent: the server looks it up and returns the earlier result, so there is no duplicate and the sender learns the seq. Assigning a new seq would show the message twice. Timestamp matching is fragile and unnecessary.

hld:chat.prompt: A WS gateway crashes while handling messages. Which practices help guarantee that no accepted message is lost? Select all that apply.
options: Rely on the push notification provider to guarantee delivery
Keep messages only in gateway memory until the recipient acknowledges them
Persist the message and assign its seq before acknowledging the sender
On reconnect the client fetches any messages after its last seen seq
The client retries unacknowledged sends with the same clientMsgId
hld:chat.explanation: Durable write before ack plus idempotent client retries plus gap-fetch on reconnect cover the failure windows. Gateway memory is lost with the crash, and push providers are best effort and carry little data, so neither can be the source of truth.

hld:chat.prompt: A phone was offline for a week. What is the most sensible way for it to catch up?
options: The client sends its last seen seq per chat and pages through newer messages from the messages store
Push notifications replay each missed message to the device
The server queues every WebSocket push for a week and replays them on connect
The client re-downloads its entire history for every chat
hld:chat.explanation: Because messages are durable and ordered by seq per chat, sync is a pull: ask for everything after last-seen seq, page by page. Server-side replay buffers would be huge and push notifications are lossy. Re-downloading all history wastes bandwidth.

hld:chat.prompt: Messages are stored with chat_id as the partition key and seq as the clustering key. If the table were instead partitioned by sender_id, what would be the main consequence for loading a chat?
options: Messages would become unordered within each partition
Group chats would no longer be possible
Nothing, as long as an index on seq exists
A chat's messages would be scattered across many partitions, so reading history becomes a multi-partition scatter-gather
hld:chat.explanation: The access pattern is 'give me the recent messages of this chat'. Partitioning by chat and clustering by seq makes that one sequential read; partitioning by sender spreads it across every participant's partitions and forces merging. Order within a partition is still sorted by its clustering key.

hld:chat.prompt: At hundreds of millions of connections, long polling is generally the better choice than WebSockets because it holds less state per connected client.
options: True
False
hld:chat.explanation: False. Long polling creates repeated HTTP request/response cycles with headers and re-connection overhead for every message window, which costs more at scale. WebSockets keep one lightweight persistent connection per client, giving lower latency and less per-message overhead.

hld:chat.prompt: Presence uses a heartbeat roughly every 30 seconds that refreshes a TTL key. Why not simply mark a user offline when their connection closes?
options: Crashes, dead batteries and network loss often close nothing cleanly, so only expiry of the TTL reveals the user is gone
WebSockets cannot report disconnects at all
Presence must be eventually consistent, so explicit events are forbidden
Closing a connection is too slow to detect
hld:chat.explanation: Clean disconnect events are not guaranteed: a phone that loses signal never says goodbye. A TTL key expires on its own when heartbeats stop, so stale 'online' states self-heal. Explicit close events can still be used as an optimisation.

hld:chat.prompt: The service stores messages on the server so it can sync devices. If the product moved to end-to-end encryption, which server-side features would be limited? Select all that apply.
options: Showing message text in push notification previews generated by the server
Assigning a per-chat sequence number to each message
Server-side full-text search over message bodies
Routing a message to the recipient's gateway through the connection registry
Storing an encrypted blob so an offline device can fetch it later
hld:chat.explanation: Search and body-based previews need plaintext on the server. Sequencing, routing and storing opaque ciphertext need only metadata, so they keep working, which is why E2E chat can still do ordering and offline sync.

hld:chat.prompt: The registry says the recipient is on gateway 7, but gateway 7 has just crashed. The message was already persisted. What should happen?
options: Broadcast the message to every gateway in case the user has moved
Treat the forward failure like an offline recipient: send a push notification and let the client sync from the store on reconnect
Delete the message and tell the sender the send failed
Retry forwarding until gateway 7 is back so ordering is preserved
hld:chat.explanation: Since the message is durable, delivery is just an optimisation over the sync path. A failed forward degrades to the offline case, and the client picks it up by seq on reconnect. Blocking on a dead gateway stalls the chat and broadcasting wastes capacity.

hld:chat.prompt: Chat averages 46k messages/s, peak is 3x average, and each message is delivered to an average of 5 online recipients. Roughly how many deliveries per second must gateways push at peak?
options: About 2.3M/s
About 140k/s
About 230k/s
About 690k/s
hld:chat.explanation: Peak sends: 46k x 3 = 138k/s; x 5 recipients = 690k deliveries/s. 230k/s applies the fan-out to the average rate and ignores the peak.

hld:chat.prompt: 200M concurrent clients send a presence heartbeat every 30 s, each refreshing a TTL key. About how many presence writes per second is that?
options: About 200M/s
About 67M/s
About 6.7M/s
About 670k/s
hld:chat.explanation: 200M / 30 s = ~6.7M writes/s, which is large for a central store. Designs keep presence in gateway memory, batch updates, or lengthen intervals instead of writing every heartbeat to a database.

hld:chat.prompt: A group has 500 members. How should a group message be stored?
options: Once in the chat's partition; delivery is fanned out to members
Only in the sender's partition, keyed by sender_id
Once per member in a per-user inbox table
Once per online member; offline members fetch from the sender's device
hld:chat.explanation: Writing once per chat (chat_id partition, seq clustering) costs one write; each member's device then syncs from its last seq. Per-member copies multiply storage and writes by up to 500x.

hld:chat.prompt: Read receipts in groups of up to 500: storing a row per message per member explodes storage. What's the common approach?
options: Keep each member's last-read seq per chat, and derive "read by" from it
Batch the per-message receipts in memory and write them all once an hour
Store receipts only in the clients and never on the server
Drop read receipts for any group with over 10 members
hld:chat.explanation: Since messages are ordered by seq, a per-member (per-device) last-read watermark implies every earlier message is read: one small row per member instead of one per message. Hourly batching keeps the same row count and makes receipts stale.

hld:chat.prompt: A user is online on a phone and a laptop at the same time. How does multi-device delivery work?
options: The registry lists every live connection; each device tracks its own last seq
The phone forwards each message to the laptop over the local network
Only the most recently connected device gets messages; the other syncs at logout
The server keeps one shared read pointer for the user across all devices
hld:chat.explanation: The connection registry holds one entry per device connection, so the chat service pushes to all of them, and per-device last-read seqs let each catch up on its own. A single shared pointer would make one device skip messages the other has seen.

hld:chat.prompt: A deploy restarts a gateway holding 500k WebSockets, and all its clients reconnect within the same second, overloading the remaining gateways and the registry. What's the fix?
options: Drain connections gradually and have clients reconnect with jittered backoff
Move clients to long polling during deploys
Raise each gateway's limit to 1M connections
Give each user a fixed gateway so that reconnects always return to the same host
hld:chat.explanation: This is a thundering herd: closing connections in waves and adding random delay to client reconnects spreads the load. Pinning users to one gateway fails exactly when that host is the one restarting.

hld:chat.prompt: Several chat-service instances handle sends for the same busy group. How can each message still get a strictly increasing per-chat seq?
options: Use each instance's wall-clock milliseconds as the seq
Let the client assign seq from its own message count
Route a chat's writes to one owner, or use an atomic per-chat counter
Assign random seqs and have clients sort messages by server timestamp on read
hld:chat.explanation: Monotonic seqs need one serialization point per chat: a partition owner, or an atomic increment (e.g. Redis INCR or a conditional write). Clocks on different instances skew, and clients can't coordinate seqs with other senders.

hld:chat.prompt: A client receives messages with seq 101, 102 and then 105 for a chat. What should it do?
options: Fetch 103-104 from the history API, then render in seq order
Display 105 and assume 103 and 104 were deleted
Renumber the messages locally to 101, 102, 103
Drop 105 and wait for the server to notice and resend everything from 103
hld:chat.explanation: A gap means some messages haven't arrived yet; the client fetches them via GET /v1/chats/{id}/messages and renders by seq. Dropping 105 throws away a valid message, and assuming deletion loses data.

hld:chat.prompt: Discord's messages were partitioned by channel_id alone, and very busy channels produced huge partitions. What did it change?
options: It capped each channel's history at one million messages
It partitioned by message_id so every message landed on a random node
It partitioned by (channel_id, time bucket), bounding each partition's size
It moved its largest channels into a sharded relational database instead
hld:chat.explanation: Adding a time bucket (Discord used roughly 10-day windows) to the partition key bounds partition size while keeping recent history a few sequential reads. Partitioning by message_id would scatter a channel's history across the cluster.

hld:chat.prompt: Which statements about WebSockets are true? Select all that apply.
options: Every message carries full HTTP headers, like a REST call
The connection starts as an HTTP request with an Upgrade handshake
Once open, either side can send messages at any time over one TCP connection
The server can only send data in response to a client message
Load balancers must allow long-lived connections and idle timeouts above the heartbeat interval
hld:chat.explanation: RFC 6455 starts with an HTTP Upgrade, then switches to lightweight frames in both directions, which is why proxies must tolerate long idle connections. Frames have a few bytes of overhead, not HTTP headers, and the server can push at will.

hld:chat.prompt: Which descriptions of sent / delivered / read receipts are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Delivered: the server handed a push notification to APNs/FCM
Delivered: a recipient device acknowledged receiving it
Read: the recipient opened the chat past that message
Sent: the server has persisted the message and acked the sender
Read receipts in groups must be stored per message per member
hld:chat.explanation: Each tick is backed by an ack from the next hop: server persist, device receipt, then a read watermark. Handing a push to APNs doesn't mean the device got it, and group read state is usually a last-read seq per member, not per-message rows.

hld:chat.prompt: Which techniques keep presence affordable in large groups? Select all that apply.
options: Batch and debounce presence changes instead of sending each flicker
Fetch presence lazily when a user opens a chat or member list
Broadcast every heartbeat to all members of every group
Fan presence changes out only to contacts who are online
hld:chat.explanation: Presence is high-churn and low-value per update, so limit who receives it, collapse rapid changes, and fetch on demand. Broadcasting each heartbeat to 500-member groups multiplies millions of writes per second by hundreds.

hld:chat.prompt: When a gateway crashes, its clients must reconnect, possibly to a different gateway, and the connection registry must be updated so new messages reach them.
options: True
False
hld:chat.explanation: True. Registry entries for the dead gateway are stale; on reconnect the client registers its new gateway (stale entries expire by TTL), then syncs missed messages from its last seq.

hld:chat.prompt: Ordering a chat's messages by the sender devices' timestamps is safe, because phones keep their clocks synced with NTP.
options: True
False
hld:chat.explanation: False. Device clocks drift, can be set manually, and two senders' clocks never agree exactly, so messages would show out of order. The server-assigned per-chat seq is the source of order.

hld:video-streaming.prompt: 500 hours of video are uploaded every minute, and one hour takes about 1.5 GB across all renditions. About how much new storage is that per day?
options: About 1.08 EB
About 108 TB
About 1.08 PB
About 10.8 PB
hld:video-streaming.explanation: 500 x 60 x 24 = 720,000 hours per day. 720,000 x 1.5 GB = 1,080,000 GB, which is about 1.08 PB. This matches the case's estimate of roughly 1 PB per day and explains why object storage is required.

hld:video-streaming.prompt: The platform serves 1 billion views per day. Spread evenly, about how many view events per second is that, and what does it suggest for counting?
options: About 1.2k/s, so a single DB row per video is fine
About 11.6k/s, and viral videos concentrate it onto few keys, so batch and aggregate asynchronously
About 1.2M/s, so a streaming job cannot keep up
About 116k/s, so views must be sharded across a hundred nodes
hld:video-streaming.explanation: 1B / 86,400 is about 11.6k per second on average, and a viral video concentrates a large share on one counter. Client-side batching plus an async aggregation job avoids a hot row and keeps the DB off the hot path. The other figures are off by 10x or more.

hld:video-streaming.prompt: Why is the uploaded video split into chunks before transcoding?
options: Chunks transcode in parallel across workers, so processing time stops scaling with video length and a failed chunk can be retried alone
CDNs cannot cache files larger than one chunk
HLS and DASH refuse to play unchunked files
Chunking reduces the final file size of each rendition
hld:video-streaming.explanation: Parallel chunk transcoding shortens time to publish to minutes and limits the blast radius of a failed worker. Segment packaging is a separate step for streaming. Chunking itself does not shrink output or relate to CDN size limits.

hld:video-streaming.prompt: A team increases segment length from 2 s to 10 s. Which outcome is most likely?
options: No change, since segment length only affects the manifest
Faster bitrate switching but higher CDN egress
Lower start-up time and fewer rebuffers on mobile
Better compression and fewer requests, but slower reaction to bandwidth changes
hld:video-streaming.explanation: Longer segments amortise keyframes and request overhead, improving efficiency, but the player can only change rendition at a segment boundary, so it reacts more slowly to drops. Short segments are the opposite trade-off.

hld:video-streaming.prompt: Which signals does an adaptive-bitrate player typically use to choose the next segment's rendition? Select all that apply.
options: A per-segment decision returned by the playback API
The video's total view count
Current buffer occupancy
Measured download throughput of recent segments
hld:video-streaming.explanation: With HLS and DASH the decision is made in the client from measured throughput and buffer level, picking from the ladder in the manifest. The server does not decide per segment, and popularity of a title is not a network signal.

hld:video-streaming.prompt: A major series launches tomorrow at 09:00 and will be watched by millions immediately. Which CDN strategy fits best?
options: Cache only the manifest and fetch segments from object storage
Pre-position the segments to edge or ISP caches beforehand during off-peak hours
Serve it from the origin and scale the origin horizontally
Pull-through caching only, since the CDN fills itself on first request
hld:video-streaming.explanation: For predictable hot content, pre-positioning moves bytes during quiet hours so launch traffic never hits the origin. Pull-through suits the long tail, but a cold start for millions would stampede the origin.

hld:video-streaming.prompt: Every view does UPDATE videos SET view_count = view_count + 1 against one row. What goes wrong for a viral video?
options: Row lock contention on a hot key serialises the writes and slows or times out the DB
Reads of that video stop working
The counter can never exceed a 32-bit value
The CDN cache is invalidated on every update
hld:video-streaming.explanation: Thousands of increments per second on one row queue behind each other on its lock. Client-side batching and an asynchronous aggregation job turn those into occasional bulk updates. Overflow is a separate matter and the CDN is not involved.

hld:video-streaming.prompt: Because egress dominates cost, maximising the CDN cache hit ratio is more important than saving transcoding compute.
options: True
False
hld:video-streaming.explanation: True. Bytes delivered to viewers dwarf the one-off cost of encoding, so each point of CDN offload cuts the dominant bill and also improves start-up latency. That is why ISP-embedded caches are worth the effort.

hld:video-streaming.prompt: Uploads use a pre-signed multipart URL to object storage instead of POSTing the file to the API servers. What is the main advantage?
options: The video is automatically transcoded by object storage
It guarantees the file is a valid video
The large upload bypasses the application tier and can be resumed part by part
It removes the need to authenticate the uploader
hld:video-streaming.explanation: The client streams bytes straight to storage, so API servers are not bandwidth bottlenecks and a failed part can be retried alone. The URL is issued after authentication, and validation and transcoding still happen later in the pipeline.

hld:video-streaming.prompt: A transcode worker crashes halfway through chunk 37 of 120. Which statements hold in a well-designed pipeline? Select all that apply.
options: The chunk's task returns to the queue and another worker retries it
The manifest is published only after all required chunks and renditions are done
Outputs are keyed by video, chunk and rendition so a re-run overwrites safely
The raw upload is deleted immediately to avoid duplicates
The whole video is re-transcoded from chunk 1
hld:video-streaming.explanation: Queues give at-least-once retries, so tasks must be idempotent. Publishing the manifest last avoids exposing a partial video. Restarting everything wastes work, and deleting the raw file would destroy the input needed for the retry.

hld:video-streaming.prompt: In this design the player fetches segments from the CDN, while the playback API only returns the manifest and metadata.
options: True
False
hld:video-streaming.explanation: True. The playback API reads video metadata and issues the manifest, and every segment request goes to the CDN edge. Proxying bytes through the API would remove the offload that makes the economics work.

hld:video-streaming.prompt: 1B views per day each stream an average of 30 minutes at 3 Mbps. Roughly how much egress is that per day?
options: About 6.75 PB
About 675 PB
About 6.75 EB
About 67.5 PB
hld:video-streaming.explanation: Per view: 1,800 s x 3 Mb/s = 5,400 Mb = 675 MB. x 1B views = 675 PB/day. At that volume serving from origin is unthinkable; CDN and ISP caches carry nearly all of it.

hld:video-streaming.prompt: At peak, 10M viewers watch at the same time at an average of 5 Mbps. What aggregate bandwidth must the CDN deliver?
options: About 500 Gbps
About 50 Tbps
About 500 Tbps
About 5 Tbps
hld:video-streaming.explanation: 10M x 5 Mb/s = 50M Mb/s = 50 Tb/s. Numbers like this are why big services place caches inside ISP networks instead of relying on a few central origins.

hld:video-streaming.prompt: A bitrate ladder has 6 renditions whose bitrates add up to 12 Mbps. How much storage does one hour of video take across all renditions?
options: About 540 MB
About 1.5 GB
About 43 GB
About 5.4 GB
hld:video-streaming.explanation: 12 Mb/s x 3,600 s = 43,200 Mb; / 8 = 5,400 MB = 5.4 GB. 43 GB forgets to convert bits to bytes.

hld:video-streaming.prompt: An upload finished but transcoding hasn't, and a viewer requests the video. What should the playback API return?
options: The video's "processing" status from metadata, with no manifest yet
A manifest pointing at the raw upload file
A 404, as if the video didn't exist
A manifest listing every planned rendition, even unfinished ones
hld:video-streaming.explanation: videos.status tracks the pipeline; the manifest is published only once renditions are ready, so players never ask for segments that don't exist. Serving the raw file skips ABR and may use a codec the device can't play.

hld:video-streaming.prompt: Creators complain that new uploads take too long to become watchable. Which change shortens time to first playback most?
options: Wait until all renditions are finished, but move to faster dedicated transcode machines
Skip chunking and transcode each video on one large machine
Transcode the lowest renditions first, publish the manifest, then add higher ones
Use 20-second segments so there are fewer files to produce
hld:video-streaming.explanation: Publishing a playable ladder early (e.g. 360p/720p) and appending 1080p/4K later lets viewers start in minutes. Not chunking removes parallelism and makes processing slower.

hld:video-streaming.prompt: Encoding in AV1 instead of H.264 is being considered. What is the main trade-off?
options: AV1 removes the need for multiple renditions in the ladder
AV1 files are larger, but every phone, TV and browser can decode them in hardware
AV1 can't be packaged into HLS or DASH segments
AV1 needs fewer bits for the same quality but is far costlier to encode
hld:video-streaming.explanation: AV1 saves substantial bandwidth at equal quality, but encoding is much more compute-heavy and older devices lack hardware decoders. So services typically encode AV1 for popular titles (where egress savings pay off) and keep H.264 as a fallback.

hld:video-streaming.prompt: Which change most directly helps meet "playback starts in < 2 s"?
options: Serve the first segment from the origin to guarantee freshness
Start with a lower-bitrate rendition and short first segments, then step up
Always start at the highest rendition so the picture is never visibly low quality
Download the whole video before starting playback
hld:video-streaming.explanation: A small first segment at a modest bitrate arrives fast from the edge; ABR then climbs as the buffer fills. Starting at the top rendition makes the first download big and slow, and going to origin adds latency.

hld:video-streaming.prompt: How should CDN cache lifetimes differ between media segments and playlists (.m3u8)?
options: Cache immutable segments long; give live playlists short TTLs
Segments get short TTLs because they're large; playlists get long ones
Neither should be cached, because ABR needs per-viewer responses
Both should use very short TTLs so viewers always get fresh video
hld:video-streaming.explanation: A published segment never changes, so long TTLs maximise hit ratio. Live playlists are updated every few seconds with new segments, so they need short TTLs. Responses are the same for all viewers, so they cache well.

hld:video-streaming.prompt: A creator uploads a 20 GB file over a flaky connection using a pre-signed multipart upload. What happens when the connection drops halfway?
options: The whole upload must restart from byte zero
Object storage stitches together whatever arrived and transcodes it
Only the failed parts are re-sent, and the upload completes once all parts are in
The API server buffers the remaining bytes and finishes the upload to storage itself
hld:video-streaming.explanation: Multipart upload stores parts independently, so the client retries only missing parts and then calls complete. The API servers never touch the bytes, and an incomplete upload isn't published.

hld:video-streaming.prompt: Which statements about HLS are true? Select all that apply.
options: Each variant playlist lists the URLs of its media segments
It sends media only over UDP to avoid TCP retransmits
It runs over plain HTTP, so ordinary CDNs can cache it
It needs a persistent WebSocket between player and server
A master playlist lists the variant streams with their bandwidths
hld:video-streaming.explanation: HLS is playlists plus segment files fetched with HTTP GET, which is exactly why CDNs can serve it. There is no WebSocket or UDP transport; the player just downloads files.

hld:video-streaming.prompt: Egress dominates cost. Which measures reduce it? Select all that apply.
options: Using more efficient codecs for popular titles
Adding more renditions to every bitrate ladder
Halving segment length everywhere
Placing caches inside ISP networks (e.g. Netflix Open Connect)
Per-title encoding that lowers bitrates for easy-to-compress content
hld:video-streaming.explanation: ISP-embedded caches cut transit, and better codecs or per-title ladders send fewer bits at the same quality. More renditions add storage and compute without reducing bytes watched, and shorter segments slightly reduce compression efficiency.

hld:video-streaming.prompt: How should view counts be collected without hammering a database? Select all that apply.
options: A stream job aggregates views per video per minute and writes totals
Clients batch view events and send them periodically
Views are filtered for bots and duplicates before they're counted
Each segment request increments the counter in the metadata DB
hld:video-streaming.explanation: Batching, stream aggregation and validation turn billions of events into a few writes per video per minute. Counting per segment both overcounts (many segments per view) and puts a write on every CDN request.

hld:video-streaming.prompt: When a pull-through CDN edge serves a rarely watched video for the first time, it has to fetch the segments from origin or a parent cache, so that first viewer sees higher latency.
options: True
False
hld:video-streaming.explanation: True. A cold cache miss goes upstream; later viewers in that region get the cached copy. That's why popular titles are pre-positioned and only the long tail is pulled on demand.

hld:video-streaming.prompt: With adaptive bitrate streaming, the server measures each viewer's bandwidth and pushes the right rendition to them.
options: True
False
hld:video-streaming.explanation: False. ABR in HLS/DASH is client-driven: the player measures throughput and buffer and picks which rendition's next segment to request. The server and CDN just serve files.

hld:ride-hailing.prompt: 5M drivers each send a location update every 4 s, which is 1.25M writes/s. If the interval were cut to 2 s, how many updates per second would the location service need to ingest?
options: About 1.25M per second
About 625k per second
About 2.5M per second
About 10M per second
hld:ride-hailing.explanation: 5M / 2 s = 2.5M updates per second: halving the interval doubles the rate. This is why the location path is in-memory and sharded by region rather than backed by a durable database.

hld:ride-hailing.prompt: At peak the system sees about 100k ride requests per minute, and 1.25M location updates per second. About how many times larger is the location rate than the request rate?
options: About the same
About 750 times
About 75 times
About 7,500 times
hld:ride-hailing.explanation: 100k per minute is about 1,667 per second. 1.25M / 1,667 is about 750. Location ingest dominates traffic by orders of magnitude, so it gets its own in-memory design while the lower-rate, high-value trip writes go to a strongly consistent DB.

hld:ride-hailing.prompt: A shard of the in-memory location index restarts and loses its contents. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
options: Trips in progress lose their assigned driver
Driver positions repopulate within seconds as drivers send their next updates
Matching for that region is impossible until a database backup is restored
Trip state is unaffected because it lives in the trips DB
hld:ride-hailing.explanation: Locations are ephemeral and refreshed every few seconds, so the index heals itself. Trip assignments and states are persisted separately in the consistent store. That split is why in-memory speed is acceptable for locations but not for trips.

hld:ride-hailing.prompt: A rider stands near the edge of an H3 cell. If matching only searches that one cell, what is the risk?
options: It will always find the geometrically nearest driver
Drivers just across the boundary in a neighbouring cell are missed, so search the cell plus its k-ring neighbours
The query will return duplicate drivers
H3 cannot index a point on an edge
hld:ride-hailing.explanation: Cell boundaries are arbitrary relative to the rider, so close drivers can sit in an adjacent cell. Searching the rider's cell plus its neighbours covers the radius, and candidates are then ranked by ETA.

hld:ride-hailing.prompt: Two candidate drivers: one is 300 m away across a river with the nearest bridge 8 km off; another is 1.2 km away on the same road. How should the matcher rank them?
options: By the order their location updates arrived
By estimated time of arrival along the road network
By straight-line distance, since it is the cheapest to compute
By driver rating alone
hld:ride-hailing.explanation: Pickup time is what the rider experiences, so rank by ETA using road routing rather than as-the-crow-flies distance. The straight-line shortlist is a fine first filter, but not the final ordering.

hld:ride-hailing.prompt: Two ride services try to claim the same driver at once. Which implementation prevents double-booking?
options: A conditional update that atomically sets state to reserved only if it is currently available
Read the driver state, check it is available, then write reserved in a separate call
Use a per-instance in-memory lock inside each ride service
Offer the driver to both riders and let the driver pick one
hld:ride-hailing.explanation: Compare-and-set in the store that owns the driver state is atomic, so exactly one claim wins. The read-then-write has a race, and per-instance locks do not coordinate across multiple instances.

hld:ride-hailing.prompt: Matching each rider greedily to the nearest free driver at request time always minimises total pickup time across all riders.
options: True
False
hld:ride-hailing.explanation: False. Greedy choices can steal a driver that would be a much better fit for the next rider, leaving a poor global result. Batching requests over a short window and solving an assignment problem can lower total wait, at the cost of a little added latency.

hld:ride-hailing.prompt: A driver is reserved for an offer, then closes the app and never responds. If reserved had no expiry, what would happen?
options: The location index would delete the driver
The rider would be charged
Nothing, because reserved automatically reverts
The driver would stay unavailable and the rider would never be offered another driver
hld:ride-hailing.explanation: A reservation without a timeout becomes a stuck lock: the driver is invisible to matching and the rider waits. Offers have a short timeout after which the driver returns to available and the next candidate is tried.

hld:ride-hailing.prompt: A rider cancels at the same instant the driver accepts. What is the safest way for the trips DB to resolve it?
options: Queue both and process them in a random order
Accept the cancel always because it is cheaper
Use a state-conditional update so only one transition from the current state succeeds, and report the loser's failure
Apply both and let the later timestamp win
hld:ride-hailing.explanation: Trip transitions should be compare-and-set on the current state (or a version), so concurrent events cannot both apply. The loser gets a clear failure and the trip stays in a valid state. Timestamp-wins is vulnerable to clock skew.

hld:ride-hailing.prompt: Which statements compare geohash and H3 correctly? Select all that apply.
options: Geohash cells have identical area at every latitude
H3 removes the need to search neighbouring cells
Neighbouring geohash cells can have very different prefixes, so a prefix match can miss nearby points
All six neighbours of an H3 hexagon have centres at the same distance
Geohash prefix length can be shortened to search a coarser area
hld:ride-hailing.explanation: Hexagons give uniform neighbour distances, geohash prefixes give simple hierarchical lookups but suffer boundary cases. Both need neighbour searches near edges, and geohash cells narrow towards the poles so their area is not constant.

hld:ride-hailing.prompt: Dropping an occasional driver location update over UDP is acceptable because the next update, a few seconds later, supersedes it.
options: True
False
hld:ride-hailing.explanation: True. Location pings are ephemeral and only the latest one matters, so loss is tolerable and cheaper than reliable delivery. The same logic would be wrong for trip state changes, which must never be lost.

hld:ride-hailing.prompt: Each driver location update is about 100 bytes and the fleet sends 1.25M updates per second. Roughly what inbound bandwidth must the ingest tier absorb?
options: 125 MB/s
hld:ride-hailing.explanation: 1.25M x 100 B = 125,000,000 B/s, about 125 MB/s (roughly 1 Gbit/s). 1.25 GB/s treats each update as 1 KB; 12.5 MB/s drops a factor of ten. It is spread across many gateway nodes, so it is very manageable.

hld:ride-hailing.prompt: The location index keeps only the latest position per driver: driver id, lat, lng, timestamp and status, about 64 bytes with overhead. For 5M active drivers, how much memory does that take?
options: 32 MB
32 GB
3.2 GB
320 MB
hld:ride-hailing.explanation: 5M x 64 B = 320M bytes, about 320 MB. That fits comfortably in RAM even before sharding, which is why the latest-position view lives in memory. 3.2 GB assumes 640 B per driver; the hard part is the write rate, not the size.

hld:ride-hailing.prompt: The trips DB receives a 'complete trip' call for a trip whose state is still 'driver_assigned' (the ride never started). What should the service do?
options: Accept it now and repair the trip state later in a nightly batch reconciliation job
Delete the trip row, because an invalid transition sequence means the data is corrupt
Reject it with a conditional update that requires the expected prior state
Set the state to completed, since the driver app is the source of truth for trips
hld:ride-hailing.explanation: A trip is a state machine (requested, assigned, arriving, in_progress, completed or cancelled). Applying each transition as UPDATE ... WHERE state = expected rejects illegal jumps and races. Trusting the driver app blindly lets bugs or tampering bill a ride that never happened.

hld:ride-hailing.prompt: Surge pricing is computed from the ratio of open requests to available drivers. Why compute it per small geo cell over a short window rather than once per city?
options: City-wide values cannot be cached at the edge, but small per-cell values can be
Regulators in most markets require surge to be calculated on a hexagonal grid
Supply and demand vary block by block; a city average hides local shortages
Per-cell values are cheaper to store and refresh than a single city-wide number
hld:ride-hailing.explanation: Demand spikes are local (a stadium emptying, rain in one district). A per-cell ratio over the last few minutes raises prices only where drivers are scarce and draws drivers there. A city-wide average would barely move. Cost and caching aren't the reason.

hld:ride-hailing.prompt: At peak there are 1M trips in progress. If each rider app polls GET /v1/rides/{id} every 2 seconds for the driver's position, about how many requests per second does that create?
options: 5k/s
50k/s
2M/s
hld:ride-hailing.explanation: 1M riders / 2 s = 500k requests per second, almost all returning a slightly moved dot. That is why the API offers WebSocket updates: the server pushes the driver's position to the one subscribed rider instead of being polled. 2M/s would be polling every 0.5 s.

hld:ride-hailing.prompt: A team shards the in-memory location index by hash(driverId) instead of by region or cell. What happens to the 'find drivers near this rider' query?
options: It fails for drivers who move to a different cell while the query is running
It gets faster, because location writes and reads are spread evenly over all shards
It must scatter to every shard and merge, since nearby drivers can live anywhere
It is unaffected, because H3 cell ids already encode which shard holds the driver
hld:ride-hailing.explanation: The hot query is spatial, so data for one area should live together (shard by city or cell range). Hashing by driver id balances writes but forces every nearby-driver search to hit all shards. The cell id tells you where to look only if the shard key is the cell.

hld:ride-hailing.prompt: Uber's Ringpop provides application-layer sharding for services like dispatch. What is its core mechanism?
options: Gossip-based membership plus a consistent-hash ring; nodes forward non-owned keys
Every node holds a full copy of all data, and reads go to the least-loaded replica
A central coordinator owns the key map, and clients ask it on every single lookup
A relational database partitions tables by key range, and the app simply connects
hld:ride-hailing.explanation: Ringpop uses SWIM-style gossip so every node learns the membership, places nodes on a consistent-hash ring, and forwards a request to the node that owns the key. No central coordinator sits on the request path, and keys move minimally when nodes join or leave.

hld:ride-hailing.prompt: The location index is sharded by region. A rider stands 100 m from the boundary between two region shards. How should the search for nearby drivers work?
options: Keep widening the search radius until the rider's own shard returns enough drivers
Query every shard that owns any cell in the rider's k-ring, then merge
Move the rider into whichever neighbouring shard currently has more free drivers
Query only the rider's own shard, since boundary cases are rare enough to ignore
hld:ride-hailing.explanation: The search area is the rider's cell plus neighbours, and those cells can belong to different shards. Mapping each cell to its owning shard and querying all of them (then merging and ranking by ETA) finds the closest driver. Querying one shard misses drivers just across the line.

hld:ride-hailing.prompt: On a flaky network a rider taps 'Request ride' and the app retries POST /v1/rides after a timeout. The rider ends up with two matched drivers. What is the best fix?
options: Let both rides proceed and auto-cancel whichever matched driver arrives second
Send a client request id and allow one active ride per rider
Add a 5-second delay before the server processes any new ride request it receives
Disable client retries for ride requests so a request is only ever sent once
hld:ride-hailing.explanation: Retries are necessary on mobile, so make the create idempotent: the server stores the client's request id (or a unique 'one active ride per rider' constraint) and returns the existing ride on a retry. Disabling retries just turns lost responses into failed requests.

hld:ride-hailing.prompt: Which of these must be written to the strongly consistent trips store rather than only kept in memory? Select all that apply.
options: Trip state transitions such as assigned and completed
The ETA currently shown to the rider
The final fare and the payment reference for the trip
Every 4-second GPS ping from every driver
hld:ride-hailing.explanation: Trip state and money must never be lost or double-assigned, so they go to a durable, strongly consistent DB. Pings are ephemeral (the latest one supersedes the last) and go to memory plus Kafka for analytics; ETAs are recomputed constantly.

hld:ride-hailing.prompt: Instead of matching each request immediately, the dispatcher collects requests for 2 seconds and solves an assignment over the batch. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
options: It can lower total pickup time across riders compared with greedy matching
It removes the need for a conditional claim on the chosen driver
It guarantees every rider gets their individually nearest driver
It adds a short wait before any single rider is matched
hld:ride-hailing.explanation: Batching sees several riders and drivers at once, so it can avoid one greedy choice stealing the only good driver for another rider, at the cost of a small delay. Drivers can still go offline or be claimed elsewhere, so the atomic claim stays. Optimising the total sometimes gives a rider a farther driver.

hld:ride-hailing.prompt: A driver's phone loses connectivity for 30 seconds in the middle of the city. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Matching should skip drivers whose last update is older than that threshold
Its last position should age out of the available set after a staleness threshold
The server should keep offering it rides at its last known position until it reconnects
Its in-progress trip state is lost, because the location index is in memory
hld:ride-hailing.explanation: Locations carry timestamps, so a TTL removes stale drivers and matching ignores them; offering rides to an unreachable driver just burns offer timeouts. Trip state lives in the durable trips DB, not the in-memory location index, so it survives.

hld:ride-hailing.prompt: For an ordinary hexagonal H3 cell, a k-ring search with k = 1 covers 7 cells: the rider's cell plus its 6 neighbours.
options: True
False
hld:ride-hailing.explanation: Hexagons have 6 edge-sharing neighbours at equal centre distance, so k = 1 gives 1 + 6 = 7 cells (k = 2 gives 19). Only the 12 pentagon cells per resolution have 5 neighbours. Geohash squares, by contrast, have 8 neighbours at two different distances.

hld:ride-hailing.prompt: Since driver locations already live in a sharded in-memory store, it is equally safe to keep trip records there too.
options: True
False
hld:ride-hailing.explanation: Losing a location is harmless because the next ping replaces it within seconds. Losing a trip means lost billing, disputes and possibly a driver assigned twice. Trips need a durable, strongly consistent DB; locations trade durability for speed.

hld:payment-system.prompt: 1M payments a day are processed (about 12 per second). Each payment posts 4 ledger entries. About how many ledger entry rows per second is that on average?
options: About 460
About 4,600
About 46
About 4.6
hld:payment-system.explanation: 1M x 4 = 4M rows per day, divided by 86,400 seconds gives roughly 46 per second. That is easily handled by one SQL primary with replicas, which is why the hard part is correctness rather than throughput.

hld:payment-system.prompt: A client sends POST /v1/payments and the connection times out with no response. What should it do?
options: Retry with a fresh Idempotency-Key to avoid a conflict
Show a failure and ask the customer to try again
Retry with the same Idempotency-Key so the service returns the original result or finishes the same payment
Look up the order and create a payment only if none exists
hld:payment-system.explanation: The key lets the server tell a retry from a new payment: it returns the stored outcome rather than charging twice. A new key would risk a second charge, and telling the customer to retry manually invites double payment.

hld:payment-system.prompt: A request arrives with an Idempotency-Key that was used earlier, but the amount in the body differs. What should the service do?
options: Reject it as a key reuse with a different request, since the stored request hash does not match
Process it as a new payment with the new amount
Return the first response silently, ignoring the new amount
Overwrite the stored request and charge the difference
hld:payment-system.explanation: A matching key with a different request fingerprint indicates a client bug. Silently returning the old result hides it and process-as-new can double charge. Rejecting with an error is the safe, explicit behaviour.

hld:payment-system.prompt: Which statements about a double-entry ledger are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Keeping the account's balance as a single mutable column is enough for audit
A refund should edit the original entry in place to keep the table small
The entries of one transaction may be committed in separate DB transactions
Each transaction's debits and credits must balance, so its entries sum to zero
Balances are derived from entries, and corrections are new reversing entries
hld:payment-system.explanation: Balanced entries make errors detectable, and append-only entries with reversals preserve history. In-place edits and single mutable balances destroy the audit trail, and splitting a transaction's entries across commits can leave the books unbalanced after a crash.

hld:payment-system.prompt: The provider's webhook for a charge arrives before your API call to the provider returns. What design handles this correctly?
options: Delay processing webhooks by a fixed 30 seconds
Always trust the API response over the webhook
Make state transitions idempotent and forward-only, so whichever of the webhook or API response arrives first is applied and the second is a no-op
Reject the webhook until the API response has been stored
hld:payment-system.explanation: The payment state machine accepts either source, matches on provider_ref, and ignores stale or duplicate events, so ordering does not matter. Dropping the webhook risks losing the only notification, and fixed delays are guesswork.

hld:payment-system.prompt: The service commits the payment to the database and then publishes 'payment captured' to Kafka in a separate step. What is the flaw?
options: Kafka cannot store payment data
A crash between the commit and the publish loses the event, so downstream systems never learn of the capture
Publishing is too slow after a commit
The database transaction will not roll back
hld:payment-system.explanation: This is a dual write: two systems cannot be updated atomically. With a transactional outbox, the event is written in the same DB transaction and a relay publishes it, so the event exists if and only if the commit does.

hld:payment-system.prompt: Every ledger transaction sums to zero, yet the daily provider settlement file totals 1 rupee more than your records. Where do you look first?
options: Inside the ledger, to find the entry that does not balance
Re-run the day's webhooks
Check the database indexes
Match payments with the settlement file by provider reference and compare amount and status for each one
hld:payment-system.explanation: The ledger's internal consistency is already guaranteed, so the gap is between your records and the provider's. Reconciliation line by line on provider_ref finds missing, extra or differing items. Replaying webhooks may add duplicates.

hld:payment-system.prompt: It is safe to skip verifying a webhook's signature if the endpoint URL is long and kept secret.
options: True
False
hld:payment-system.explanation: False. URLs leak through logs and proxies, and anyone who learns it could forge 'payment captured' events. The signature proves the provider sent the payload, so it must be verified, ideally with a timestamp check against replay.

hld:payment-system.prompt: Which storage choice best fits the ledger and payments tables, given 12 payments per second but zero tolerance for lost or doubled money?
options: A document store with last-write-wins
An in-memory cache with periodic snapshots
An eventually consistent key-value store that favours availability
A relational database with ACID transactions, accepting reduced availability in a partition
hld:payment-system.explanation: The workload is small, so scale is no issue; what matters is atomic multi-row ledger writes and UNIQUE constraints for idempotency. An SQL database provides both. Eventual consistency and last-write-wins can lose or duplicate money.

hld:payment-system.prompt: The provider call times out after 10 s with an unknown outcome. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Retry later with the same provider idempotency key, or query the provider for status
Mark the payment pending or unknown instead of failed
Mark it failed and let the customer retry with a new key
Immediately issue a refund in case it was charged
hld:payment-system.explanation: The charge may have succeeded, so the outcome must stay unresolved until the provider confirms it via status query, webhook or a safe retry with the same key. Failing it early invites a second charge, and an immediate refund may refund money never taken.

hld:payment-system.prompt: A payment was captured for 100. Two refund requests for 60 each arrive simultaneously, and each reads 'refunded so far = 0' before writing. What can happen, and what fixes it?
options: Only the first succeeds because SQL serialises everything by default
Both succeed, refunding 120; lock the payment row or use a conditional update on the refunded total inside the transaction
Both fail, so nothing is refunded; add a retry
The ledger will reject one because it always balances
hld:payment-system.explanation: This is a classic check-then-act race: both pass the validation. A row lock (SELECT FOR UPDATE) or a conditional update such as refunded_total + 60 <= amount makes the check atomic. A balanced ledger does not prevent over-refunding, since both entries balance.

hld:payment-system.prompt: Two concurrent requests with the same Idempotency-Key are safe because the UNIQUE constraint lets only one insert succeed, so the other can wait for or return the first result.
options: True
False
hld:payment-system.explanation: True. The unique key constraint is enforced by the database even under concurrency, so one request wins the insert and the other sees a conflict and returns or waits for the stored result. A check-then-insert in application code would not give this guarantee.

hld:payment-system.prompt: The system averages 12 payments per second; assume peak is 10x that. What does this imply for the ledger database?
options: It must be sharded across many nodes from day one
It needs an in-memory cache in front of every ledger write
It should be an eventually consistent NoSQL store to handle the write rate
A single well-run relational primary with replicas easily handles it
hld:payment-system.explanation: 120 payments/s, even at 4 ledger rows each, is about 480 inserts/s: trivial for one PostgreSQL primary. The hard part is correctness (transactions, constraints, audit), so a strongly consistent SQL DB fits and sharding would add complexity for nothing.

hld:payment-system.prompt: Your service calls the provider's charge API and retries on timeouts. What idempotency key should it send to the provider?
options: A fresh random UUID on every attempt, so that each request is clearly unique
A key derived from the payment id, reused on every retry of it
No key at all, since the provider deduplicates identical amounts automatically
The customer's id, so that a customer can never be charged twice on the same day
hld:payment-system.explanation: The key must identify the logical operation, so every retry of payment X carries the same key and the provider returns the original result. A new UUID per attempt defeats dedup. A customer-level key would wrongly block a second legitimate purchase.

hld:payment-system.prompt: An online store authorises the card at checkout but captures only when the order ships. What is the main benefit of separating the two steps?
options: Capturing later lowers the provider's per-transaction processing fee to zero
Funds are held without moving money, and can be voided on cancellation
Authorisations never expire, so the store can capture whenever it likes later
It removes the need to send idempotency keys on the later capture call
hld:payment-system.explanation: An authorisation places a hold on the customer's funds; capture actually moves the money. Voiding an uncaptured auth is cleaner than a refund. Authorisations do expire (often around a week for cards), and capture calls still need idempotency.

hld:payment-system.prompt: A captured payment is refunded in full. How should the double-entry ledger record this?
options: Delete the original capture entries so the balance goes back to zero
Edit the original entries' amounts to zero and keep the rows
Post a new balanced transaction that moves the money back
Update the merchant's balance column directly and skip ledger entries
hld:payment-system.explanation: Ledgers are append-only: corrections and reversals are new balanced transactions, so history stays auditable and balances are derived by summing entries. Editing or deleting entries destroys the audit trail that makes errors detectable.

hld:payment-system.prompt: Weeks after a sale, the customer disputes the charge with their bank and the provider sends a chargeback webhook. How should the system model it?
options: Issue a normal refund through the provider's refund API to settle the dispute
Mark it disputed and post a ledger move out of the merchant balance
Delete the payment row entirely, since the original sale is being reversed
Ignore it until the dispute is resolved, then record only the final outcome
hld:payment-system.explanation: The bank pulls the money when the dispute opens, so the ledger must reflect it now (merchant balance down, disputes account up) and the payment gets a 'disputed' state. If the merchant wins, another transaction reverses it. Calling the refund API would return the money twice.

hld:payment-system.prompt: The provider delivers webhooks at least once, and you receive the same 'charge.succeeded' event twice. How should the handler cope?
options: Turn off webhook retries in the provider dashboard so duplicates never arrive
Return HTTP 500 on the second copy so that the provider stops sending it
Store the provider's event id uniquely and skip ones already processed
Process both copies, since a second delivery means a second charge happened
hld:payment-system.explanation: At-least-once delivery means duplicates are normal. Store the event id (and keep state transitions idempotent) so a repeat becomes a no-op that still returns 2xx. Returning 500 makes the provider retry even more; the same event id is the same charge, not a new one.

hld:payment-system.prompt: Because of retries, a 'payment.captured' webhook is processed after the 'payment.refunded' webhook for the same payment. What should the state machine do?
options: Set the status back to captured, since the most recently processed message wins
Apply only forward transitions; ignore the stale backwards one
Raise an error and leave the payment stuck in its current state for manual review
Reverse the refund at the provider so that the two states arrive in proper order
hld:payment-system.explanation: Webhooks can arrive out of order, so transitions must be monotonic: created, authorised, captured, refunded. A stale event that would move state backwards is acknowledged and ignored (the ledger already reflects capture before refund). Last-message-wins would show a refunded payment as captured.

hld:payment-system.prompt: The outbox relay reads a 'payment captured' row, publishes it to Kafka, then crashes before marking the row as sent. What happens, and what must consumers do?
options: Kafka rejects the duplicate automatically, so consumers need no changes at all
The event is lost, so consumers must also poll the payments table as a backup
It is published again on restart; consumers dedupe by event id
The DB transaction rolls back the capture, so the customer was never charged
hld:payment-system.explanation: The outbox guarantees at-least-once publication: the unmarked row is re-sent on restart. Consumers must be idempotent (track processed event ids). The capture was already committed, and a plain Kafka producer retry setting doesn't dedupe across a relay restart.

hld:payment-system.prompt: Your API timed out calling the provider and wrongly marked a payment 'failed'. The next day the settlement file shows that charge as captured. What is the right response?
options: Trust the provider for that charge: fix state and ledger, then fulfil or refund
Delete that line from the settlement import so that the daily totals match up
Keep your record as failed, since the internal database is the source of truth
Charge the customer again so that the payment finally shows as successful
hld:payment-system.explanation: Reconciliation exists to catch exactly this. Money moved at the provider, so fix the payment state, post the ledger entries and either fulfil the order or refund. Also fix the bug: a timeout means 'unknown', not 'failed'. Charging again would double-charge.

hld:payment-system.prompt: Which measures make POST /v1/payments safe for clients to retry? Select all that apply.
options: Store each Idempotency-Key with the request hash and the response
Treat two requests with the same amount and customer within a minute as duplicates
Enforce a UNIQUE constraint on the idempotency key column
Ask clients to generate a new key whenever they retry
hld:payment-system.explanation: A stored key plus response lets retries replay the original result, and the unique constraint makes concurrent duplicates collide in the DB. Matching on amount and customer blocks legitimate identical purchases; a new key per retry defeats idempotency.

hld:payment-system.prompt: Compare synchronous capture (wait for the provider in the request) with async capture (return 'pending', finish via webhook). Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
options: Async lets the API respond quickly and ride out provider slowness
Async means the client and UI must handle a pending state
Sync capture removes the need to handle webhooks at all
With sync capture, a slow provider holds up the user's request
hld:payment-system.explanation: Async decouples the user from provider latency but adds a visible pending state; sync is simpler for the client but ties request latency to the provider. Even with sync capture you still need webhooks for disputes, refunds, async payment methods and timeouts with unknown outcomes.

hld:payment-system.prompt: Which practices shrink your PCI DSS compliance scope when accepting cards? Select all that apply.
options: Collect card details in the provider's hosted fields so raw card numbers never reach your servers
Store only the provider's token for the card, not the card number
Log full request bodies at the API gateway for debugging
Store full card numbers yourself, encrypted at rest
hld:payment-system.explanation: Scope follows where card data flows. Hosted fields and tokens keep card numbers off your systems, which greatly reduces scope. Encrypted card numbers you store are still in scope, and logging request bodies can leak card data into logs.

hld:payment-system.prompt: Retrying a timed-out provider charge with the same idempotency key is safe even if the original call actually succeeded.
options: True
False
hld:payment-system.explanation: That is the purpose of the key: the provider recognises it and returns the original result instead of charging again. It is only unsafe if the key changes between attempts or the request parameters differ.

hld:payment-system.prompt: A correct double-entry ledger guarantees that your records match the payment provider's records.
options: True
False
hld:payment-system.explanation: Double entry guarantees internal consistency (every transaction sums to zero). It can't detect a charge you never recorded or a fee the provider deducted. Matching the outside world needs reconciliation against settlement files.

hld:ticket-booking.prompt: Two buyers click the same available seat at the same instant. The booking API runs an atomic conditional UPDATE (set status to held WHERE seat is still available). What happens?
options: Both UPDATEs run, the later one overwrites the earlier, and both buyers see success
Whichever request reached the load balancer first wins, as enforced by the API tier
The database raises a deadlock error to both buyers and neither of them gets the seat
Only one UPDATE changes the row; the other affects zero rows and that buyer is told the seat is taken
hld:ticket-booking.explanation: The database serialises writes to the same row, so the second UPDATE re-evaluates its WHERE clause, sees status is no longer available and changes nothing. The service reads the affected-row count to decide the winner. Arrival order at the load balancer does not decide it, and there is no deadlock because only one row is touched.

hld:ticket-booking.prompt: A popular on-sale has 10 million users trying to buy and only 50,000 seats. If every user makes exactly one hold attempt, what is the maximum share of attempts that can succeed?
hld:ticket-booking.explanation: 50,000 / 10,000,000 = 0.005 = 0.5%. At least 99.5% of attempts must fail, which is why the system should absorb most of that traffic in front of the database (waiting room, CDN, fast rejects) instead of letting every request reach the inventory table.

hld:ticket-booking.prompt: A virtual waiting room admits users to the booking API at 2,000 users per second. Roughly how long until the first 50,000 users (the number of seats) have been admitted?
options: About 42 minutes
About 2.5 seconds
About 4 minutes
About 25 seconds
hld:ticket-booking.explanation: 50,000 / 2,000 = 25 seconds. The admission rate is set by what the backend can handle, and queue position gives fairness. In practice more than 50,000 are admitted because some buyers abandon, but the arithmetic shows how a controlled rate turns a 10M-user spike into a manageable stream.

hld:ticket-booking.prompt: A buyer's card payment succeeds, but by the time the order is confirmed their 10-minute hold has already expired and another buyer may have taken the seat. What is the correct handling?
options: Confirm anyway and flip the seat to sold, since the buyer has already paid
Flip held to sold only if the hold is still valid for this buyer; otherwise refund or void the payment
Ignore the payment event and let the buyer retry the whole purchase from scratch
Extend the expired hold silently so the paid order can proceed
hld:ticket-booking.explanation: Confirmation must be a conditional write: it succeeds only if the seat is still held by this hold and not expired. If the seat was resold, forcing it would double-sell. The payment must then be refunded or voided. Ignoring it leaves the customer charged with no ticket.

hld:ticket-booking.prompt: Why does the design reserve seats with one atomic conditional write in the inventory database instead of acquiring a distributed lock per seat for the whole checkout?
options: A lease-based lock can expire while its holder is paused or delayed and still believes it owns the seat, whereas the conditional write is checked by the database that holds the truth
A lock cannot be created for a seat that is not yet in the database
Locks cannot expire, so an abandoned checkout would block the seat forever
Distributed locks are always at least ten times slower than SQL updates
hld:ticket-booking.explanation: Lease-based locks have the classic problem that the holder can stall (GC pause, network delay), the lease expires, and a stale writer proceeds. A check-and-set inside the source of truth has no such window. Locks can expire, so the third option is wrong, and the other two claims are not true in general.

hld:ticket-booking.prompt: A teammate proposes this seat-hold logic. What is wrong with it under concurrent traffic?
options: Two requests can both read available before either updates, so both get OK and one hold silently overwrites the other
Each statement is atomic, so the code is safe and only slightly slower than a single UPDATE
The SELECT should use a larger isolation level only for reads, which makes the later UPDATE safe
The seat row needs a TTL column, and adding one removes the race
hld:ticket-booking.explanation: This is a check-then-act race: the check and the write are separate steps, so both requests can pass the check. The fix is to put the condition in the UPDATE itself (WHERE status = 'available') and inspect the affected-row count. Per-statement atomicity does not make the pair of statements atomic.

hld:ticket-booking.prompt: A user asks to hold three adjacent seats in one request. The conditional UPDATE over those three seat ids reports only 2 rows changed. Given that the group must stay together, what should the service do?
options: Mark the two held seats as sold to avoid leaving gaps in the seat map
Roll back the two changes (or run it in one transaction) and report a conflict so the request is all-or-nothing
Retry the same UPDATE in a loop until all three rows change
Keep the two seats held and tell the user to pick a third one later
hld:ticket-booking.explanation: A multi-seat hold succeeds only if all rows changed, so a partial result must be undone. Keeping two seats locks inventory for a request that cannot complete, looping may spin forever on a seat someone else is paying for, and marking seats sold without payment is plainly wrong.

hld:ticket-booking.prompt: Which of these measures protect the database at on-sale time? Select all that apply.
options: Rejecting excess requests early with a quick overload response instead of queueing them inside the API
Raising the hold time to 60 minutes so fewer hold requests are made
Having clients retry failed requests immediately and without backoff
Serving the static seat-map layout from a CDN
A waiting room that admits users at the rate the backend can handle
hld:ticket-booking.explanation: Admission control, edge caching of static content and early load shedding all keep traffic away from the inventory DB. A longer hold mostly locks seats up and does not reduce attempts much, and immediate retries without backoff multiply load during exactly the moment the system is saturated.

hld:ticket-booking.prompt: Holds expire after about 10 minutes. Which approaches correctly make an expired hold's seat available again? Select all that apply.
options: Treating a held seat with an expired hold time as available inside the conditional write or the read path
Relying on the buyer's browser to call a release endpoint when the tab is closed
A background worker that periodically releases holds whose expiry time has passed
Relying on database row locks timing out, which frees the seat automatically
hld:ticket-booking.explanation: Server-side expiry, either by a sweeper or by a lazy check of hold_expires_at, is reliable. Browsers crash, lose connectivity or never fire the call, so client-driven release cannot be trusted. Row locks last for a transaction and say nothing about the application-level hold state stored in a column.

hld:ticket-booking.prompt: Making the seat hold duration much longer always increases sales, because buyers get more time to finish paying.
options: True
False
hld:ticket-booking.explanation: A longer hold improves conversion for slow payers but keeps seats unavailable to others, so abandoned checkouts lock up inventory that could have sold. It is a trade-off between conversion and locked-up stock, not a free win.

hld:ticket-booking.prompt: Someone argues that once the waiting room limits admissions to 2,000 users per second, the conditional UPDATE is no longer necessary. What is wrong with that argument?
