hld:message-queue.explanation: Each partition adds files, metadata, failover work and producer batches, so oversizing costs throughput and recovery time. Ordering within a partition is unchanged by partition count; only the key-to-partition mapping changes.

hld:message-queue.prompt: Select all correct statements about how a partition is stored on disk.
options: A sparse offset index lets the broker binary-search to a nearby position and scan forward to the requested offset
Time-based retention deletes whole closed segments rather than individual records
Only the newest (active) segment is appended to; older segments are immutable
A single message in the middle of a segment of a non-compacted topic can be deleted in place through the produce API
hld:message-queue.explanation: Segments are append-only, indexed sparsely, and retired whole, which keeps IO sequential and deletion cheap. There is no in-place deletion of a single record in a delete-policy topic.

hld:message-queue.prompt: Raising the producer's linger.ms usually increases throughput but adds per-message latency, because records wait longer to fill larger batches.
options: True
False
hld:message-queue.explanation: True. Larger batches amortise per-request overhead and compress better, at the cost of records waiting up to linger.ms before being sent.

hld:message-queue.prompt: Setting acks=0 still gives at-least-once delivery, because the broker retries any write that failed on its side.
options: True
False
hld:message-queue.explanation: False. With acks=0 the producer does not wait for any response, so it cannot know a write failed and never retries it; this is at-most-once.

hld:metrics-monitoring.prompt: A fleet exposes 60 million active time series, and every series is scraped once every 15 seconds. What sustained ingest rate, in samples per second, must the pipeline handle?
options: About 4 million
About 900 thousand
About 15 million
About 60 million
hld:metrics-monitoring.explanation: Each series yields one sample per scrape, so the rate is 60M / 15 s = 4M samples/s. Quoting 60M confuses the number of series with the sample rate, and 15M multiplies by the interval instead of dividing by it.

hld:metrics-monitoring.prompt: Ingest is 5 million samples per second. A raw sample is 16 B (8 B timestamp + 8 B value); with Gorilla-style delta-of-delta and XOR compression assume 1.5 B per sample. About how much storage does one day of compressed data need?
options: About 650 GB
About 69 TB
About 6.9 TB
About 65 GB
hld:metrics-monitoring.explanation: 5M x 1.5 B = 7.5 MB/s, times 86,400 s is about 648 GB per day. The 6.9 TB figure is what you get without compression (5M x 16 B x 86,400 s), which is the tempting wrong answer; 65 GB drops a factor of ten.

hld:metrics-monitoring.prompt: A developer adds a user_id label (about 2 million distinct values) to a request counter that already carries service and status labels. What is the most likely consequence, and the best remedy?
options: The Kafka topic runs out of partitions; add partitions by series hash
Each sample gets larger on disk; tune compression and extend retention
Series count and memory multiply; drop user_id and keep per-user detail in logs or traces
Queries return wrong values because labels get re-sorted; rewrite the dashboards
hld:metrics-monitoring.explanation: Every unique label combination is a new series, so the series count and head-block and index memory grow multiplicatively, slowing ingestion and queries. Compression and extra partitions do not fix that; unbounded identifiers belong in logs or traces, or behind quotas.

hld:metrics-monitoring.prompt: A team keeps only the average per 5-minute window in its long-term rollups. Why can they not, in general, compute a correct 1-hour average from the twelve stored averages?
options: Rollups discard timestamps, so the twelve windows cannot be located
Windows can contain different numbers of samples, so the plain mean of means is skewed; sum and count fix it
An average is undefined unless min and max are stored next to it
Averages overflow floating-point storage; they should store integers
hld:metrics-monitoring.explanation: A window with 5 samples and one with 30 must be weighted differently. Storing sum and count lets you add them and divide at query time, which stays correct for any window size. Min and max are kept for spike visibility, not to make averages valid.

hld:metrics-monitoring.prompt: Each of 1,000 hosts exports its own latency p99 every minute. How do you get a correct fleet-wide p99 for the service?
options: Average the per-host p99 values, weighted by each host's request count
Take the median of the per-host p99 values
Export histogram bucket counts, sum them across hosts, then estimate the quantile from the merged buckets
Take the maximum of the per-host p99 values and report that as the fleet p99
hld:metrics-monitoring.explanation: Quantiles cannot be combined by averaging or taking a max or median of per-host quantiles; each of those gives a different number from the true p99. Histogram bucket counts are additive, so merging buckets and then computing the quantile is the correct approach.

hld:metrics-monitoring.prompt: The metrics pipeline and its alert evaluator run in the same cluster as the services they watch, and the whole cluster loses power. Which design still gets someone paged?
options: Show a red banner on the dashboards so on-call notices on their next visit
An always-firing heartbeat alert sent to an external service that pages when it stops arriving
Alert on a cluster_up metric evaluated by the existing evaluator
Add another evaluator replica inside the same cluster so one can take over
hld:metrics-monitoring.explanation: The alerting path must not depend on what it monitors. A dead-man's-switch heartbeat checked by an independent external service turns silence into a page. Anything evaluated inside the failed cluster goes down with it, and a dashboard only helps if someone is looking.

hld:metrics-monitoring.prompt: A nightly batch job runs for about 5 seconds, while the collector scrapes targets every 15 seconds. How should its metrics reach the system?
options: Keep the job process alive for an hour after it finishes so it can be scraped
Have the job push its final values to an intermediary (a push gateway) that the collector scrapes
Lower the global scrape interval to 1 second so the job is always caught
Skip metrics for batch jobs and rely on logs only
hld:metrics-monitoring.explanation: Pull cannot reliably see short-lived jobs, so they push to an intermediary that stays up and is scraped normally. A 1 second global interval multiplies ingest for every target; keeping a process alive just to be scraped is a hack that wastes resources.

hld:metrics-monitoring.prompt: One database host dies and 50 dependent alerts start to fire. Which alert manager features reduce the page storm? Select all that apply.
options: Shortening the 'for' duration so every alert fires sooner
Inhibition rules that suppress dependent alerts while the node-down alert is firing
Running more evaluator replicas and sending each replica's copy as its own notification
Grouping related alerts into a single notification
hld:metrics-monitoring.explanation: Grouping merges related alerts into one message and inhibition mutes symptoms while the root cause is firing. A shorter 'for' makes alerts fire faster, which adds noise, and unduplicated replica copies multiply it; replicated evaluators need deduplication, not separate pages.

hld:metrics-monitoring.prompt: Select all statements that are true about placing a Kafka topic between collectors and TSDB writers in a metrics pipeline.
options: It absorbs ingestion spikes so writers can lag briefly without samples being lost
Partitioning by series hash keeps each series' samples ordered on one partition and one writer
It lowers end-to-end latency compared with collectors writing straight to the TSDB
It removes the need for per-tenant series quotas
hld:metrics-monitoring.explanation: The buffer decouples collectors from storage and absorbs bursts, and keying by series hash preserves per-series order. It adds a hop, so latency goes up rather than down, and it does nothing about cardinality: a flood of new series still lands in the TSDB.

hld:metrics-monitoring.prompt: Because the TSDB writes immutable, time-partitioned blocks, retention can be enforced by deleting whole expired blocks rather than deleting rows one by one.
options: True
False
hld:metrics-monitoring.explanation: Each block covers a fixed time range, so expiring old data is a cheap file delete, and queries can also skip blocks outside the requested range. Row-by-row deletes would be expensive in a write-heavy, compressed layout.

hld:metrics-monitoring.prompt: An alert rule has a 'for' duration of 5 minutes, so the rule's expression is only evaluated once every 5 minutes.
options: True
False
hld:metrics-monitoring.explanation: The rule is still evaluated at the normal evaluation interval (for example every 30 to 60 s). The 'for' duration only requires the condition to stay true across those evaluations for 5 minutes before the alert fires, which filters out blips.

hld:metrics-monitoring.prompt: You keep one year of 5-minute rollups for 100M series, storing 4 aggregates (min, max, sum, count) per point at about 2 B each after compression. Roughly how much storage is that?
options: About 840 TB
About 8.4 TB
About 84 TB
About 2.5 TB
hld:metrics-monitoring.explanation: One year has 365 x 288 = 105,120 five-minute points per series. 100M x 105,120 x 8 B is about 8.4 x 10^13 B, about 84 TB. 8.4 TB drops a factor of ten in the series count.

hld:metrics-monitoring.prompt: The alert evaluator runs 120,000 rules, each every 30 seconds. About how many rule queries per second hit recent data?
options: About 400
About 3.6 million
About 2,000
About 4,000
hld:metrics-monitoring.explanation: 120,000 / 30 s = 4,000 queries per second. 2,000 would be the rate for a 60-second interval.

hld:metrics-monitoring.prompt: A metric has labels service (50 values), endpoint (200), status (10) and instance (100). In the worst case, how many series can it create?
options: About 1 million
About 100,000
About 10 million
About 360
hld:metrics-monitoring.explanation: Series count multiplies across labels: 50 x 200 x 10 x 100 = 10,000,000. Adding the counts (360) is the common mistake; every unique combination is its own series.

hld:metrics-monitoring.prompt: Why do services export a monotonically increasing request counter and compute rate() at query time, rather than exporting 'requests in the last interval' as a gauge?
options: rate() is defined only for counters that never reset, which makes the query simpler
Gauges cannot be stored with XOR compression, so they cost far more disk in the TSDB
A missed scrape loses nothing; the next increase covers the gap, and drops mean resets
Counters take less memory than gauges on the target, so exporting them is cheaper
hld:metrics-monitoring.explanation: Cumulative counters are robust to lost or delayed samples: the delta between any two samples is still right, and rate() treats a decrease as a counter reset. A per-interval gauge silently loses the requests of any missed scrape.

hld:metrics-monitoring.prompt: In pull mode, a target process crashes and emits nothing at all. How does the system notice?
options: The target pushes a final 'goodbye' metric to the collector as part of crashing
It cannot notice, because absent data looks the same as a healthy but idle service
The TSDB deletes the target's series right away, and the deletion triggers an alert
The failed scrape records up = 0, and an alert fires on up == 0 for a 'for' duration
hld:metrics-monitoring.explanation: One advantage of pull is that the collector knows what should exist (via service discovery), so a failed scrape is itself a signal recorded as up = 0. A crashed process cannot reliably send a goodbye.

hld:metrics-monitoring.prompt: An alert on 'error rate > 5%' with for: 0s pages on-call 30 times a night on 20-second spikes that are never actionable. What is the best fix?
options: Require the condition for several minutes, or better, alert on SLO burn rate
Scrape the targets less often so short spikes are averaged away and less visible
Route the alert to email instead of the pager so that it no longer wakes anyone
Raise the threshold to 50% so that only very large incidents ever page anyone
hld:metrics-monitoring.explanation: A 'for' window suppresses blips, and burn-rate alerts page on sustained user impact rather than noise. A 50% threshold would miss real incidents that hurt users at 10% errors.

hld:metrics-monitoring.prompt: How does the TSDB find the series matching {service='api', status='500'} without scanning every series?
options: It range-scans all series names alphabetically and filters out non-matching ones
It reads every block's chunks and filters the decoded samples by their labels
It hashes the whole label matcher to a single series id and looks that series up
It intersects the postings lists (series ids) of each label pair in an inverted index
hld:metrics-monitoring.explanation: The inverted index maps each label=value pair to a sorted list of series ids, so a multi-label matcher is a fast intersection. Reading every chunk would be a full scan of the data.

hld:metrics-monitoring.prompt: Kubernetes pods are redeployed about 20 times a day, and every metric carries a pod label. Head-block memory and the index keep growing even though the live pod count is flat. What is happening, and what is the best remedy?
options: Series churn from new pod names; aggregate away the pod label for long-term data
The scrape interval is too short; raise it to 60 s so fewer samples reach the head block
There are too many alert rules; delete unused ones so the evaluator holds less state
A memory leak in the TSDB process; schedule a restart every night to reclaim the memory
hld:metrics-monitoring.explanation: Every redeploy creates a new label value and so new series, while the old ones linger in the head block and index until they age out. Dropping or aggregating the churning label caps the series count; a nightly restart only hides the growth.

hld:metrics-monitoring.prompt: Samples arrive at timestamps 1000, 1010, 1020, 1030, 1041. Gorilla-style encoding stores the first timestamp and the first delta. Which delta-of-delta values are stored for the remaining three timestamps?
hld:metrics-monitoring.explanation: Deltas are 10, 10, 10, 11, so the deltas of deltas for the third, fourth and fifth timestamps are 0, 0, 1. Zeros encode in a single bit, which is why regular scrapes compress so well. '10, 10, 11' are plain deltas, not deltas of deltas.

hld:metrics-monitoring.prompt: Rollups keep min, max, sum and count per 5-minute window. Select all statements that are correct.
options: Keeping histogram bucket counters in the rollups allows approximate percentiles later
An exact p99 can be computed from the stored min, max and average
The exact 1-hour maximum is the largest of the twelve 5-minute maxima
The exact 1-hour average is sum of sums divided by sum of counts
hld:metrics-monitoring.explanation: Sum and count combine exactly into averages, and max of maxes is exact. Percentiles need distribution data such as histogram buckets; min, max and mean cannot reconstruct a p99.

hld:metrics-monitoring.prompt: Push ingestion is open to many teams. Select all protections against a misbehaving client flooding the pipeline.
options: Per-tenant rate limits on samples per second
Disable the write-ahead log during bursts to keep up
Reject over-limit requests with 429 so well-behaved clients back off and retry
Per-tenant active-series quotas
hld:metrics-monitoring.explanation: Rate limits, series quotas and explicit 429 backpressure contain one bad client. Disabling the WAL protects nobody from the client and risks losing in-memory data on a crash.

hld:metrics-monitoring.prompt: Select all sound choices for making the TSDB horizontally scalable and multi-tenant.
options: Have the query layer fan out to the relevant shards and merge the results
Shard by time only, so all current writes go to the node owning the current hour
Replicate each series to 2 or 3 ingesters so one failure loses no recent data
Shard incoming series by a hash of tenant plus series labels across ingesters
hld:metrics-monitoring.explanation: Hashing by series spreads write load, replication covers failures, and query fan-out merges results. Time-only sharding sends every current write to one hot node.

hld:metrics-monitoring.prompt: The write-ahead log next to the in-memory head block lets the TSDB recover recent samples that had not yet been flushed into an immutable block when it crashed.
options: True
False
hld:metrics-monitoring.explanation: True. Samples are appended to the WAL before being acknowledged, so after a crash the head block is rebuilt by replaying it.

hld:metrics-monitoring.prompt: Total HTTP requests served should be exported as a gauge, because rate() only works on gauges.
options: True
False
hld:metrics-monitoring.explanation: False. Totals are counters, and rate() is designed for counters (it handles resets). Gauges are for values that go up and down, such as memory in use or queue depth.

hld:email-service.prompt: An SMTP edge server replies '250 OK' as soon as it holds the DATA in memory, and writes the message to the inbound queue a moment later in the background. What is the flaw?
options: SMTP forbids writing to a queue after the final reply
If the server crashes in between, the sender believes delivery succeeded but the message is gone
The reply to the end of DATA must be 354 rather than 250
The sender will retry immediately and cause a duplicate on every single message
hld:email-service.explanation: Once we say 250, responsibility for the message transfers to us, so it must already be durable. Replying early opens a window where an acknowledged message can vanish. If we cannot persist it, we should answer with a temporary 4xx so the sender keeps it and retries.

hld:email-service.prompt: While delivering outbound mail, a remote server answers one recipient with a 451 temporary error and another with a 550 'mailbox does not exist'. What should the sender workers do?
options: Retry the 550 recipient from another IP and drop the 451 one
Retry both with backoff for several days, since any error may clear
Reschedule the 451 recipient with exponential backoff; stop on the 550 and send a non-delivery report to the sender
Bounce both immediately so the queue does not grow
hld:email-service.explanation: 4xx replies are transient, so the row is rescheduled with increasing delays up to a few days. 5xx is a permanent failure: retrying wastes effort and hurts IP reputation, so we stop and generate a DSN. Dropping a 4xx would lose mail that would have been delivered.

hld:email-service.prompt: Assume 60 million users each receive 30 messages a day. Roughly what is the average inbound rate in messages per second?
options: About 210 thousand
About 2 thousand
About 1.8 million
About 21 thousand
hld:email-service.explanation: 60M x 30 = 1.8 billion messages a day; divided by 86,400 s that is about 21 thousand per second. The 1.8 million figure is the daily total mistaken for a per-second rate; peaks would be a few times higher than this average.

hld:email-service.prompt: Assume 1.8 billion messages a day arrive with an average size of 60 KB including attachments. About how much raw data per day goes to storage, before compression, dedup and replication?
options: About 10.8 TB
About 108 TB
About 1.08 PB
About 18 TB
hld:email-service.explanation: 1.8 x 10^9 x 60 KB = 108 x 10^12 B, about 108 TB per day, or roughly 40 PB per year. That is why bodies and attachments go to a blob store and only about 1 KB of metadata per message stays in the hot store.

hld:email-service.prompt: Mail metadata is partitioned by user_id, and one user's mailbox grows to tens of millions of messages, creating an oversized partition. Which change keeps newest-first folder listing cheap?
options: Re-partition all messages by message_id so load spreads evenly
Move that user's messages into a global table sorted by time
Bucket the partition key as (user_id, month), clustering by folder and time inside each bucket
Partition by received date so each day is one partition
hld:email-service.explanation: Time-bucketing within the user keeps partitions bounded while the newest page of a folder still lives in the latest bucket or two. Partitioning by message_id scatters a listing across the cluster, and partitioning by date creates hot, cross-user partitions.

hld:email-service.prompt: A remote server timed out waiting for our reply after we had already stored its message, so it retries the same message. How do we avoid a duplicate in the recipient's mailbox?
options: Reject any second connection from the same sending IP within an hour
Reply 550 to every retry so senders give up
Accept it and let users delete duplicates themselves
Check the Message-ID, with a content hash, against messages already delivered to that mailbox and drop the repeat
hld:email-service.explanation: Mail transfer is at-least-once, so the receiver makes delivery idempotent by recognising a message it already stored for that user. Blocking by IP rejects legitimate mail, and a 550 would bounce a message that was in fact delivered once.

hld:email-service.prompt: A new reply arrives whose In-Reply-To header matches the Message-ID of a message already stored in the user's mailbox, but the subject line was edited completely. Which thread should it join?
options: The existing thread, because header references take priority over subject matching
The thread with the most similar subject inside a time window
Whichever thread was updated most recently
A new thread, because the subject differs
hld:email-service.explanation: Threading uses In-Reply-To and References first, since they identify the parent explicitly. Normalised subject matching within a time window is only a fallback when no header matches, and recency has nothing to do with conversation membership.

hld:email-service.prompt: Select all statements that correctly describe inbound sender authentication.
options: DMARC checks that the From domain aligns with an SPF or DKIM pass and applies the domain's requested policy
SPF verifies that the message body was not altered in transit
DKIM verifies a signature over headers and body using a public key published in DNS
DKIM checks the connecting IP against a list of authorized senders in DNS
SPF checks whether the connecting IP is allowed to send for the MAIL FROM domain
hld:email-service.explanation: SPF is about which IPs may send for a domain; DKIM is a cryptographic signature that detects tampering; DMARC ties the visible From domain to a passing SPF or DKIM result and says what to do on failure. The two wrong options swap SPF's and DKIM's jobs.

hld:email-service.prompt: The outbound queue is partitioned by recipient domain. Select all benefits of that choice.
options: A slow or throttling destination domain delays only its own queued rows
Sender IP reputation no longer needs monitoring, because each domain is isolated
Per-domain concurrency caps and rate limits are simple to apply
All recipients of one message are delivered atomically or not at all
hld:email-service.explanation: One row per recipient domain isolates head-of-line blocking and makes throttling per destination natural. It gives no atomicity across recipients (each domain succeeds or fails on its own), and reputation is still shared across the IPs we send from.

hld:email-service.prompt: When a user deletes a message, the content-addressed blob for an attachment that was deduplicated across many users should be removed from the blob store immediately.
options: True
False
hld:email-service.explanation: Deduplicated blobs are shared and carry a reference count. Deleting one user's message only drops its reference; the blob is removed when the count reaches zero. Removing it immediately would break every other recipient's copy.

hld:email-service.prompt: If we accept a message, later decide it is spam, and send a bounce to its MAIL FROM address, we may be mailing an innocent person whose address was forged.
options: True
False
hld:email-service.explanation: Spam senders usually forge the envelope sender, so a post-acceptance bounce lands on a third party (backscatter) and damages our reputation. Rejecting during the SMTP dialogue, before the 250, leaves the bounce to the sending server instead.

hld:email-service.prompt: Assume 200M users each send 15 messages a day. Roughly what is the average outbound rate in messages per second?
options: About 35,000
About 3,500
About 350,000
About 12,000
hld:email-service.explanation: 200M x 15 = 3B messages/day; 3B / 86,400 s is about 34,700/s. 3,500 is off by a factor of ten.

hld:email-service.prompt: 2B messages arrive per day with about 1 KB of metadata each, kept for 5 years with replication factor 3. Roughly how much metadata storage is that?
options: About 3.7 PB
About 11 PB
About 110 TB
About 1.1 PB
hld:email-service.explanation: 2 TB/day x 365 x 5 is about 3,650 TB (3.65 PB); x3 replicas is about 11 PB. 3.7 PB forgets replication.

hld:email-service.prompt: A company newsletter with a 2 MB attachment is sent to 1M mailboxes on our service. Attachments are content-addressed by SHA-256. Roughly how much attachment storage does deduplication save?
options: About 200 GB
About 2 TB
About 2 GB
Nothing, since each mailbox needs its own copy
hld:email-service.explanation: Without dedup: 1M x 2 MB = 2 TB. With content addressing, one 2 MB blob plus 1M references is stored, saving about 2 TB. Mailboxes only need a pointer and a reference count, not a private copy.

hld:email-service.prompt: A simple forwarding service relays a message from bank.com to our users without modifying it. Which authentication result typically survives the forward?
options: SPF, because the forwarder copies the original sender's IP into the forwarded headers
Neither, because any forwarding hop always invalidates both SPF and DKIM checks
Both of them, as long as the forwarder delivers the message to us over TLS
DKIM, because the signature over the unchanged headers and body still verifies
hld:email-service.explanation: SPF checks the connecting IP, which is now the forwarder's and is not in bank.com's SPF record, so SPF fails. DKIM signs the content, so an unmodified message still verifies and DMARC can pass through DKIM alignment.

hld:email-service.prompt: Millions of IMAP clients keep IDLE connections open waiting for new mail. Which design scales?
options: Each IMAP server keeps the full mailboxes of all its connected users in memory
Each IMAP server polls the metadata store for every connected user once per second
Clients drop IDLE and reconnect every 10 seconds to check for new messages instead
Event-driven servers subscribe to per-user change notifications and push on new mail
hld:email-service.explanation: Idle connections are cheap on event-driven servers; the work should happen only when mail arrives, through a per-user notification channel. Polling every user every second would turn millions of idle clients into millions of reads per second.

hld:email-service.prompt: A newsletter goes to 5 million external subscribers. How should the pipeline treat it differently from a normal message?
options: Send it from a fresh, unused IP so the main pool's sending reputation is not affected
Send it synchronously inside the API request so the sender gets one combined result
Put all 5 million addresses into the RCPT TO list of a single SMTP transaction per domain
Expand recipients into queued batches, rate-limited per domain, with VERP and List-Unsubscribe
hld:email-service.explanation: Bulk mail must be spread over time and domains to avoid throttling, track bounces per recipient and give recipients an unsubscribe path, which protects reputation. A cold, unwarmed IP sending 5 million messages is quickly throttled or blocklisted.

hld:email-service.prompt: Bounce rates from one outbound IP suddenly spike, and replies cite a public blocklist. What is the right response?
options: Disable DKIM signing for mail from that IP until the listing expires on its own
Keep sending from the same IP so the receivers learn over time that it is legitimate
Retry every rejected message immediately from the same IP until the receivers accept it
Shift traffic to other warmed IPs, suspend the abusive sender, then request delisting
hld:email-service.explanation: The immediate fix is to stop using the blocked IP, the root cause is usually one abusive sender, and delisting comes after the cause is gone. Immediate retries from the same IP only deepen the reputation damage.

hld:email-service.prompt: Opening a message costs two hops (metadata row, then blob store), and p99 open latency suffers. Most messages are under 4 KB of text. What is the best change?
options: Inline bodies under a size threshold in the metadata row; keep pointers for the rest
Move every body, including large attachments, into the metadata rows themselves
Drop the blob store and keep message bodies on the SMTP edge servers that received them
Add a third cache tier in front of the blob store that holds every stored message
hld:email-service.explanation: Inlining small bodies removes a hop for the common case while large blobs stay out of the hot store. Inlining everything bloats the metadata partitions and the hot set, which hurts list queries.

hld:email-service.prompt: IMAP requires UIDs that strictly increase within a folder. Why does the design keep each folder's writes on a single partition owner?
options: So that each user's search index stays small enough to fit on a single node
Because SMTP requires exactly one server to be responsible for each recipient
Because wide-column stores cannot hold more than one folder per node at a time
So the owner can hand out the next UID from a local counter, with no coordination
hld:email-service.explanation: Monotonic UIDs need a single sequencer per folder; one owner makes allocation a cheap local increment. If several nodes wrote to a folder, they would need a distributed counter or locks on every delivery.

hld:email-service.prompt: A user's mailbox must move to a different shard without downtime. Select all steps of a sound migration.
options: Copy a snapshot of the mailbox to the new shard
Briefly pause writes for that user, apply the final changes, then flip the routing entry to the new shard
Tail and apply changes made after the snapshot until the copy catches up
Delete the source data before copying so the two cannot diverge
hld:email-service.explanation: Snapshot, catch up, then a short per-user cutover is the standard live migration. Deleting first risks losing the mailbox if the copy fails.

hld:email-service.prompt: Select all sound practices for spam filtering in the inbound pipeline.
options: File likely spam into a Spam folder rather than deleting it, so false positives can be recovered
Run cheap checks (rate limits, IP reputation, recipient exists) before expensive content scanning
Send a bounce to the MAIL FROM address for every message found to be spam after acceptance
Reject clear spam with a 5xx during the SMTP dialogue rather than bouncing it after acceptance
hld:email-service.explanation: Cheap checks first save compute, in-dialogue rejection avoids backscatter, and a Spam folder limits the cost of false positives. Bouncing accepted spam mails forged, innocent addresses.

hld:email-service.prompt: Select all correct statements about mailbox search in this design.
options: A lost index shard can be rebuilt from the event log or the stored messages
Each user's index lives on one shard, so a query touches a single shard
A single global index over all users makes per-user search cheaper than per-user shards
The indexer consumes delivery events, so search may lag delivery by a few seconds
hld:email-service.explanation: Per-user co-location avoids scatter-gather, asynchronous indexing means slight lag, and the index is derived data that can be rebuilt. A global index makes every user query filter a huge shared index.

hld:email-service.prompt: In SMTP, a 4xx reply tells the sending server to try again later, while a 5xx reply signals a permanent failure.
options: True
False
hld:email-service.explanation: True. 4xx codes (such as 451) are transient and trigger retries with backoff; 5xx codes (such as 550) are permanent and produce a bounce.

hld:email-service.prompt: For a message to pass DMARC, both SPF and DKIM must pass and both must align with the From domain.
options: True
False
hld:email-service.explanation: False. DMARC passes if either SPF or DKIM passes with alignment to the From domain. That is why DKIM alone can carry a forwarded message through DMARC.

hld:object-storage.prompt: A cluster stores 60 PB of usable data. How much raw capacity does a 10+4 erasure code need?
options: 90 PB
180 PB
84 PB
72 PB
hld:object-storage.explanation: Raw = usable x (data + parity) / data = 60 x 14 / 10 = 84 PB, a 40 percent overhead. 180 PB is what 3x replication needs; 90 PB would be a 1.5x ratio (like 8+4), and 72 PB uses the wrong ratio.

hld:object-storage.prompt: In an 8+4 erasure-coded cluster a 16 TB drive fails. Each lost fragment is rebuilt from 8 surviving fragments of its stripe. Roughly how much data is read across the cluster to restore the drive, compared with 3x replication?
options: About 128 TB with erasure coding versus about 16 TB with replication
About 192 TB with erasure coding versus about 32 TB with replication
About 64 TB with erasure coding versus about 16 TB with replication
About 16 TB with either scheme, since only the lost bytes are rebuilt
hld:object-storage.explanation: Each rebuilt fragment needs 8 fragments read, so 16 TB x 8 = 128 TB. Replication copies one surviving replica, reading 16 TB. This 8x repair amplification is the price paid for the lower storage overhead.

hld:object-storage.prompt: A system holds 200 PB of usable data with an average object size of 4 MB, and keeps about 300 B of metadata per object. About how large is the metadata?
options: About 15 PB
About 1.5 TB
About 150 TB
About 15 TB
hld:object-storage.explanation: 200 PB / 4 MB = 50 billion objects; 50 x 10^9 x 300 B = 15 TB. That is too large for a single database node and needs strong consistency and ordered scans, so the metadata store is sharded and kept separate from the data plane.

hld:object-storage.prompt: A PUT streams the bytes to data nodes first and commits the metadata row afterwards. The data is written, but the metadata commit fails. What is the outcome?
options: The object is visible but may serve partial bytes
Other objects stored in the same append-only file lose durability
A metadata row points at missing data, so GETs fail until repaired
An orphan blob that nothing references, which the garbage collector later reclaims
hld:object-storage.explanation: Because the metadata row is committed only after the bytes are durable, a failure in between leaves unreferenced bytes: wasted space but no wrong answer for any client, and GC cleans it up. The reverse order would produce rows pointing at nothing.

hld:object-storage.prompt: Data nodes pack many small objects into large append-only files. After millions of deletes, how is the disk space actually reclaimed?
options: The next PUT of similar size overwrites the deleted bytes in place
After a safety delay, GC compacts files by copying live objects into new files and removing the old ones
The metadata store deleting its rows frees the disk blocks immediately
Space is reclaimed only when the whole disk is retired
hld:object-storage.explanation: Append-only files are never edited in place, and deleting metadata does not touch data files. A garbage collector waits a safety delay (to protect against races and bugs), then compacts by rewriting live objects. This is the cost of packing small objects.

hld:object-storage.prompt: Versioning is enabled on a bucket. A client sends DELETE /bucket/report.csv with no versionId. What happens?
options: A delete marker becomes the latest version; older versions remain and can be fetched by versionId
Every version is permanently removed and the space is freed after GC
Only the latest version is removed and the previous one becomes current
The request is rejected until each version is deleted individually
hld:object-storage.explanation: On a versioned bucket a plain DELETE just inserts a delete marker, so a normal GET returns not found while all versions survive. Bytes are freed only when a specific version is deleted or a lifecycle rule expires it.

hld:object-storage.prompt: Object metadata is hash-partitioned by key instead of range-partitioned. Why does listing a bucket by prefix and delimiter become expensive?
options: Keys are stored in random order inside each partition, so no partition can answer a prefix query
Keys sharing a prefix are spread over all partitions, so a listing must query every partition and merge the results
Listing must read the data nodes rather than the metadata store
Hash partitions cannot be replicated with consensus
hld:object-storage.explanation: Range partitioning keeps adjacent keys together, so a prefix becomes a range scan that can skip whole common prefixes. With hashing, neighbours land on different partitions and the lister must scatter-gather and merge sort. The gain is even load and no hot prefix.

hld:object-storage.prompt: Which mechanisms help detect silent data corruption in an object store? Select all that apply.
options: Verifying a fragment's checksum whenever it is read
A higher replication factor with no verification of any copy
A client-supplied Content-MD5 or SHA-256 checked on PUT
Heartbeats between data nodes and the placement manager
A background scrubber that slowly reads every disk and verifies checksums
hld:object-storage.explanation: Read-time checks, periodic scrubbing (catching bit rot before several fragments are bad) and end-to-end client checksums (catching corruption on the network path) each detect corruption. Heartbeats only reveal dead nodes, and more unverified copies just store the same bad bytes more times.

hld:object-storage.prompt: Select all statements that are true of an 8+4 erasure code placed on 12 separate failure domains.
options: The object survives 4 simultaneous fragment losses
Any 8 of the 12 fragments are enough to reconstruct the object
Rebuilding one lost fragment needs to read only 4 surviving fragments
Storage overhead is 100 percent of the usable data
hld:object-storage.explanation: Any 8 fragments reconstruct the object, so up to 4 can be lost at once. Repair reads 8 fragments, not 4, and the overhead is 4/8 = 50 percent (1.5x raw), versus 200 percent for 3x replication.

hld:object-storage.prompt: In this design, completing a multipart upload first copies all the parts into one new contiguous data object before the object becomes visible.
options: True
False
hld:object-storage.explanation: Each part is already stored as its own data object. Complete atomically writes a single metadata row whose data pointer is the ordered part list, so no bytes are copied, which keeps completion fast even for multi-TB objects.

hld:object-storage.prompt: Compared with 8+4, a 20+4 erasure code lowers storage overhead to 20 percent, but rebuilding one lost fragment reads 20 fragments and the code needs 24 failure domains per stripe.
options: True
False
hld:object-storage.explanation: Overhead is parity / data = 4/20 = 20 percent versus 50 percent, but repair read amplification grows from 8x to 20x, degraded reads touch more nodes, and 24 distinct failure domains must be available. That is why very wide codes are used sparingly.

hld:object-storage.prompt: A cluster stores 90 PB of usable data with a 6+3 erasure code on 20 TB drives kept at most 75% full. About how many drives are needed?
options: About 9,000
About 4,500
About 13,500
About 6,000
hld:object-storage.explanation: 6+3 stores 9/6 = 1.5x, so 135 PB raw. Each drive holds 20 TB x 0.75 = 15 TB usable; 135,000 TB / 15 TB = 9,000 drives. 6,000 forgets the parity overhead.

hld:object-storage.prompt: A cluster has 10,000 drives with an assumed 2% annual failure rate. Roughly how many drive failures should the repair system expect?
options: About 2 per day
About 20 per year
About 4 per week
About 2 per year
hld:object-storage.explanation: 10,000 x 0.02 = 200 failures a year, about 4 per week. At this scale repair is routine background work, not an exceptional event.

hld:object-storage.prompt: At peak there are 30,000 PUT/s of 4 MB objects, stored with an 8+4 erasure code. About how much data per second is written to data nodes, including parity?
options: About 120 GB/s
About 360 GB/s
About 180 GB/s
About 60 GB/s
hld:object-storage.explanation: Ingest is 30,000 x 4 MB = 120 GB/s. 8+4 writes 12/8 = 1.5x that, so about 180 GB/s reach the data nodes. 120 GB/s ignores the parity fragments.

hld:object-storage.prompt: Most objects in a bucket are 4 KB. Why is erasure coding each one separately with 8+4 a poor fit?
options: An 8+4 code stores four extra full copies of each small object instead of parity
Each becomes 12 fragments of about 512 B, so metadata and IOPS overhead dwarf the data
Erasure codes cannot mathematically encode objects that are smaller than 1 MB in size
Small objects are almost always hot, and erasure-coded data cannot be cached at all
hld:object-storage.explanation: Splitting a tiny object into 12 pieces multiplies index entries and disk operations for very little data. Packing small objects into large files before coding (or replicating them) keeps the overhead reasonable. The code itself works at any size; it is just inefficient.

hld:object-storage.prompt: One customer writes millions of keys under the single prefix logs/2024-06-01/, and the metadata range partition holding it is overloaded. What is the primary fix in the storage system?
options: Put a CDN in front of the bucket so that the PUT requests are absorbed there
Automatically split the hot key range into more partitions based on load
Reject or heavily throttle further writes from that customer's account
Switch the whole metadata store from range partitioning to hash partitioning
hld:object-storage.explanation: Range-partitioned stores split hot ranges dynamically, keeping ordered listing while spreading load. Hash partitioning would fix the hotspot but make every prefix listing a scatter-gather across all partitions.

hld:object-storage.prompt: A GET arrives for an 8+4 object while the node holding one of its data fragments is down. What happens?
options: The object is unavailable until the node holding that data fragment comes back
It reads any 8 of the 11 surviving fragments and decodes, at higher latency
It returns the 7 available data fragments to the client as a partial object
It sends all 11 surviving fragments to the client, which decodes them itself
hld:object-storage.explanation: Any 8 of 12 fragments reconstruct the object, so the read succeeds as a degraded read with extra decode work and IO. Decoding happens server-side; clients receive normal object bytes.

hld:object-storage.prompt: Why does each metadata shard replicate its writes through a consensus protocol such as Raft or Paxos?
options: To let DELETE requests return immediately and be applied asynchronously later
To compress metadata rows by sharing common key prefixes across the replicas
To decide how object bytes are spread across the data nodes and racks
So a LIST right after a PUT sees the new key, and acked writes survive a failure
hld:object-storage.explanation: Consensus gives each shard one linearisable order of writes, which delivers strong read-after-write for objects and listings and durability for acknowledged writes. Data placement is the data plane's job, separate from metadata replication.

hld:object-storage.prompt: Why does the garbage collector wait for a safety delay before deleting a blob that has no metadata row?
options: Customers are billed for a minimum storage period, so blobs are kept until it ends
Erasure coding requires every fragment to exist for a day before it can be removed
Disks need idle time between writes and deletes, so the GC spaces out its work
An in-flight PUT has written data but not yet metadata, so a quick delete could lose it
hld:object-storage.explanation: Data is written before the metadata commit, so 'no metadata row' can mean 'in flight', not 'orphan'. The delay also guards against GC bugs. Billing rules are a pricing policy and do not explain the delay.

hld:object-storage.prompt: A client starts many multipart uploads and never completes or aborts them. What happens to the uploaded parts?
options: They are merged into a partial object automatically after 24 hours of inactivity
They use storage until aborted, usually by a lifecycle rule for stale uploads
They are deleted automatically as soon as the client's connection is closed
They become visible in listings as separate objects named after part numbers
hld:object-storage.explanation: Parts are stored as real data objects tied to the upload, so they consume space until an abort, usually via a lifecycle rule. Parts are never visible as user objects before Complete.

hld:object-storage.prompt: Objects use 8+4 erasure coding with each stripe spread over 12 racks, and one whole rack goes down. Select all that hold.
options: All writes must stop until the rack returns, since stripes need 12 racks
Repair rebuilds the lost fragments onto other healthy racks, starting with stripes that have lost the most fragments
Reads continue as degraded reads, since each stripe still has 11 fragments
Repair traffic is throttled so it does not starve foreground requests
hld:object-storage.explanation: One lost fragment per stripe still leaves 3 more failures of tolerance; repair restores redundancy, prioritised and throttled. New writes can be placed on stripes across the remaining healthy failure domains, so there is no need to stop writes.

hld:object-storage.prompt: A client issues GET with Range: bytes=0-1048575 for a large object stored with a systematic 8+4 code, and all fragments are healthy. Select all statements that are true.
options: Only the data fragments covering that byte range need to be read
The response is 206 Partial Content
The parity fragments must also be read and verified on every request
No decoding is needed, since data fragments contain the original bytes
hld:object-storage.explanation: With a systematic code, data fragments hold the plain bytes, so a healthy range read touches only the relevant fragments and returns 206. Parity is used only when data fragments are missing or corrupt, and checksums cover integrity.

hld:object-storage.prompt: Select all statements that are correct about asynchronous cross-region replication.
options: It removes the need for erasure coding or replication within each region
It can be driven by a change stream of committed metadata writes
It protects against a region-wide outage that in-region erasure coding cannot
The destination region may lag, so its recovery point is not zero
hld:object-storage.explanation: Replaying committed changes to another region adds disaster protection with some lag. Each region still needs local redundancy for routine disk and rack failures; otherwise every drive failure would need a cross-region copy.

hld:object-storage.prompt: The 11 nines advertised for S3 Standard describe durability (the chance of losing an object), not availability (the chance of a request succeeding).
options: True
False
hld:object-storage.explanation: True. Durability of 99.999999999% is a data-loss design target; availability is a separate, much lower figure, because a temporarily unreachable object is not a lost one.

hld:object-storage.prompt: Storing each object as its own file on the data nodes scales well to billions of 1 KB objects, because modern filesystems have no practical inode or metadata limits.
options: True
False
hld:object-storage.explanation: False. Billions of tiny files strain inode tables and directory metadata and cause random IO; that is why data nodes pack many objects into large append-only files with their own index.

hld:digital-wallet.prompt: Assume 400 million transfers a day, a peak rate of 10x the daily average, and about 1,000 transfers per second sustained by one database shard. What is the minimum number of shards needed at peak?
hld:digital-wallet.explanation: Average = 400M / 86,400 = about 4,630/s, so the peak is about 46,300/s. At 1,000/s per shard that needs 47 shards, before adding replicas and headroom. Using the average rate gives 5, which fails at peak.

hld:digital-wallet.prompt: Each transfer writes about 0.7 KB (a transfer row, two ledger entries and an idempotency row). At 2 billion transfers a day, roughly how much is written per year before replication and indexes?
options: About 5.1 PB
About 51 TB
About 511 TB
About 1.4 PB
hld:digital-wallet.explanation: 2 x 10^9 x 0.7 KB = 1.4 TB a day, and x 365 gives about 511 TB a year. The 1.4 PB option is a per-year figure with a slip in the daily volume; the 51 TB option drops a factor of ten.

hld:digital-wallet.prompt: A merchant wallet receives 5,000 credits per second, and a single wallet row can absorb about 1,000 updates per second. If each credit goes to a randomly chosen sub-balance row, what is the minimum number of sub-balances, ignoring headroom?
hld:digital-wallet.explanation: 5,000 / 1,000 = 5 sub-rows, assuming perfectly even spread. Random selection is not perfectly even, so a real design adds headroom. Giving every credit its own row would make the logical balance (the sum) expensive to read.

hld:digital-wallet.prompt: A client retries POST /v1/transfers with the same Idempotency-Key it used before, but this time the amount is different. How should the server respond?
options: Execute it as a new transfer, since the amount is different
Return the stored result of the first request as if nothing changed
Reject it with an error because the key was already used with a different request hash
Apply only the difference between the two amounts
hld:digital-wallet.explanation: The key identifies one logical request. Storing a hash of the request lets the server detect misuse: the same key with different content is a client bug, so it is rejected (for example with a 422). Silently replaying or merging could hide the bug and move the wrong amount.

hld:digital-wallet.prompt: Two concurrent transfers of 80 each hit a wallet holding 100. Which implementation reliably prevents an overdraft?
hld:digital-wallet.code:
UPDATE wallets
SET balance = balance - :amt
WHERE wallet_id = :from AND balance >= :amt;
-- proceed only if rows affected = 1
options: Hold a mutex in each application instance around the check and the update
Check the balance in a cache first, then run an unconditional decrement
Run the conditional UPDATE shown and treat zero rows affected as insufficient funds
Read the balance in the application, check it is at least 80, then write back the computed new balance
hld:digital-wallet.explanation: The check and the decrement happen atomically inside the database under the row lock, so the second transfer sees 20 and updates zero rows. Read-then-write races (both read 100), a cache check, or a per-process mutex (useless with several instances) can all let both through.

hld:digital-wallet.prompt: In a cross-shard transfer built as a saga, the source wallet was debited and then the service crashed before the destination was credited. What happens?
options: Persisted saga state lets a recovery worker retry the credit idempotently, or refund the source, while users see a pending status
The debit rolls back automatically because the two shards share one transaction
The user sees the transfer as failed and must start a new one
The money is lost until an operator fixes it by hand
hld:digital-wallet.explanation: A saga is a series of local transactions; there is no shared transaction to roll back. Because the saga state is stored, a recovery worker resumes the credit (idempotent, retried until it succeeds) or runs the compensation. An explicit pending state means nobody sees money disappear.

hld:digital-wallet.prompt: A team uses two-phase commit for every cross-shard transfer. What is the main production risk compared with TCC or a saga?
options: Row locks are held across the coordinator round trip, and participants block if the coordinator dies
It forces eventual consistency, so balances may briefly go negative
It needs each step to be idempotent, which is impossible with locks
It cannot guarantee atomicity, so money may be created or destroyed
hld:digital-wallet.explanation: 2PC does give atomicity, but participants hold locks while waiting for the commit decision, hurting throughput, and a failed coordinator can leave them blocked. TCC and sagas avoid long locks by reserving first or compensating, at the cost of intermediate states.

hld:digital-wallet.prompt: In an event-sourced wallet with CQRS, why must the never-negative balance check read from the write side rather than from the read model?
options: Read models are built asynchronously and can lag, so two transfers could both see enough balance
The write side can answer queries faster than any read model
Read models cannot store balances as integers
Read models are rebuilt from scratch on every query
hld:digital-wallet.explanation: A lagging projection may show a stale balance, letting two concurrent commands both pass the check and overdraw. The write side validates against current state and appends events with an expected sequence number, which gives optimistic concurrency per wallet.

hld:digital-wallet.prompt: Which checks belong in a continuous reconciliation job for the ledger? Select all that apply.
options: Ledger totals match the external provider's settlement files
Each wallet's balance equals the sum of its ledger entries
Provider files are skipped because the internal ledger is the only source of truth
Mismatches are fixed by updating the old ledger entries so history shows the right figures
Every transfer's ledger entries sum to zero
hld:digital-wallet.explanation: The three invariants (zero-sum entries, balance equals entry sum, agreement with the provider) are what catch lost or invented money. Mismatches are repaired with new compensating entries, never by editing history, and external files are checked precisely because the bank may disagree.

hld:digital-wallet.prompt: Which are sound design choices for a wallet service? Select all that apply.
options: Store amounts as integers in minor units, such as cents
Commit to the database, then publish to Kafka in a separate step with no outbox
Write an outbox row in the same DB transaction as the money movement and relay it to Kafka
Keep balances only in a cache and flush them to the database periodically
hld:digital-wallet.explanation: Integers avoid floating-point rounding errors, and the outbox makes the state change and the event atomic. Publishing in a separate step can crash between the two and lose the event, and a cache-only balance can lose acknowledged money on a crash.

hld:digital-wallet.prompt: A client's POST /v1/transfers timed out with no response. To avoid conflicting with the first attempt, it should retry with a fresh Idempotency-Key.
options: True
False
hld:digital-wallet.explanation: A new key looks like a new logical transfer, so if the first attempt actually succeeded the money moves twice. The client should reuse the same key, or query GET /v1/transfers/{id} to learn the outcome of the original attempt.

hld:digital-wallet.prompt: Splitting a hot wallet into sub-balances works well for credits because credits commute, but debits need extra care because the never-negative rule applies to the sum of the sub-balances.
options: True
False
hld:digital-wallet.explanation: A credit can go to any sub-row in any order. A debit may need to draw from several sub-rows, since one sub-row alone may not hold enough while the logical balance does, so it must be done so total funds are never overspent.

hld:digital-wallet.prompt: Assume 300M transfers a day, a peak of 6x the daily average, and about 1,500 transfers per second per shard. What is the minimum number of shards at peak?
options: About 4
About 140
About 14
About 21
hld:digital-wallet.explanation: 300M / 86,400 is about 3,470/s average; x6 is about 20,800/s at peak; / 1,500 per shard is about 13.9, so 14 shards at minimum. 21 would assume 1,000 per shard.

hld:digital-wallet.prompt: Transfers average about 12,000 per second, and balance reads run at about 8x writes. Roughly how many balance reads per second must be served?
options: About 1,500
About 20,000
About 96,000
About 960,000
hld:digital-wallet.explanation: 12,000 x 8 = 96,000 reads/s, served from the wallet row, replicas or caches for non-critical views, never by summing ledger history.

hld:digital-wallet.prompt: The ledger grows by about 700 GB/day, and regulation requires keeping it for 7 years. Roughly how much ledger data is that before replication and indexes?
options: About 5 PB
About 1.8 PB
About 250 TB
About 180 TB
hld:digital-wallet.explanation: 700 GB x 365 is about 255 TB per year; x7 is about 1.8 PB. 250 TB is only one year of data.

hld:digital-wallet.prompt: Why are amounts stored as integer minor units (amount: 2500 for 25.00 USD) rather than floating-point numbers?
options: Integers take noticeably less disk space than floats in every major database
Binary floats cannot represent most decimal fractions exactly, so sums drift
Relational databases cannot build indexes on floating-point columns at all
JSON has no way to carry floating-point numbers between client and server
hld:digital-wallet.explanation: Money needs exact arithmetic; integer cents (or a fixed decimal type) make sums and ledger checks exact. JSON does carry floats, which is exactly how precision bugs sneak in.

hld:digital-wallet.prompt: In a TCC cross-shard transfer, Try placed a hold of 50 on the source wallet, then the destination wallet turns out to be closed. What should happen?
options: The source is debited in full and a refund is promised to the user by email
The hold stays in place indefinitely until a support agent reviews it by hand
Confirm runs anyway, and the money is parked in the closed destination wallet
Cancel runs: the hold returns to the available balance and the transfer fails
hld:digital-wallet.explanation: TCC's Cancel phase undoes the reservation idempotently, so no money moves and nothing is lost. Confirming into a closed wallet strands funds, and leaving holds wastes the user's available balance.

hld:digital-wallet.prompt: The provider's daily settlement file is 1 cent higher than the ledger's total for top-ups. How should this be found and fixed?
options: Match settlement lines to entries by reference id, then post a compensating entry
Ignore it, because a 1 cent difference is below any reasonable materiality level
Edit the most recent top-up ledger entry by 1 cent so the two totals match again
Recompute every balance from scratch and overwrite the wallet table with the results
hld:digital-wallet.explanation: Line-level matching finds the exact cause (a missing, duplicated or rounded item), and a compensating entry fixes it without rewriting history. Editing an existing entry breaks the immutable audit trail.

hld:digital-wallet.prompt: Wallets must move from 50 to 100 physical shards while transfers keep running. Which approach works best?
options: Stop all transfers for a weekend, copy everything, then reopen on the new layout
Change routing from hash mod 50 to hash mod 100 and restart every service at once
Use many logical partitions; move each by copy, catch-up and a brief write pause
Send new wallets to the new shards and leave all existing wallets where they are
hld:digital-wallet.explanation: Logical partitions decouple keys from machines, so a move is a per-partition copy, catch-up and short cutover. Switching mod 50 to mod 100 remaps about half of all wallets at once, and in-flight transfers would hit the wrong shard.

hld:digital-wallet.prompt: Why does the wallet service write events to an outbox table in the same database transaction as the transfer, instead of publishing to Kafka directly after the commit?
options: Kafka cannot accept events directly from an application that also uses a database
The outbox insert makes the whole transfer commit faster than a plain transaction
It avoids the dual-write problem: transfer and event commit or fail together
The outbox table replaces the ledger as the source of truth for every balance
hld:digital-wallet.explanation: Publishing after the commit can fail after the money moved, so the event is lost; publishing first can announce a transfer that rolled back. The outbox commits atomically, and a relay publishes at least once.

hld:digital-wallet.prompt: A user sends 100 USD from a USD wallet to a EUR wallet. How should the ledger record it so that every currency still balances?
options: Debit 100 USD and credit the EUR equivalent as one entry pair that does not sum to zero
Store the amount as a float in a neutral reference currency and convert on every read
Convert both wallets to USD for the duration of the transfer, then convert back after
Route via house USD and EUR accounts at a locked quote, so each currency sums to zero
hld:digital-wallet.explanation: Double entry only balances within one currency, so FX goes through house accounts per currency, with the conversion at a locked quote. A USD debit paired with a EUR credit cannot sum to zero, and reconciliation would flag every FX transfer.

hld:digital-wallet.prompt: Each ledger entry stores balance_after. Select all statements that are correct.
options: It must be computed in the same transaction as the wallet balance update
It can be edited later if a mistake is found, since it is only a convenience field
It lets you read a wallet's balance at any past point without replaying all history
Gaps or jumps between consecutive entries' balance_after values reveal a missing or corrupt entry
hld:digital-wallet.explanation: balance_after makes point-in-time reads cheap and enables chain checks, but it is only trustworthy if written atomically with the balance change. Ledger rows are immutable; mistakes are corrected with compensating entries.

hld:digital-wallet.prompt: The external payment provider sends signed settlement webhooks for top-ups. Select all sound handling practices.
options: Drive the top-up through a status state machine so out-of-order events cannot move it backwards
Deduplicate by the provider's event id, since webhooks can be delivered more than once
Credit the wallet as soon as the user submits the top-up, before the provider confirms
Verify the webhook signature before trusting the payload
hld:digital-wallet.explanation: Authenticate, deduplicate and order-protect webhook processing. Crediting before confirmation invents money that may never arrive.

hld:digital-wallet.prompt: In the event-sourced variant, wallets take periodic snapshots. Select all statements that are correct.
options: Events stay immutable; schema changes are handled with versioned events or upcasters
Snapshots speed up rebuilding state by replaying only events after the snapshot
Once a snapshot exists, older events can be deleted, since the snapshot contains everything
A snapshot must record the last sequence number it includes
hld:digital-wallet.explanation: Snapshots are an optimisation tied to a sequence position, and immutable events need versioning to evolve. Deleting history would destroy the audit trail and the ability to recompute balances at any point in time.

hld:digital-wallet.prompt: Because every transfer's ledger entries sum to zero, the total money across all wallets and external clearing accounts is conserved by construction.
options: True
False
hld:digital-wallet.explanation: True. Each debit has an equal credit, so money only moves between accounts; money entering or leaving the system shows up as entries on external or clearing accounts.

hld:digital-wallet.prompt: A read replica is a safe source for the balance used to approve a transfer, because replication lag is usually under a second.
options: True
False
hld:digital-wallet.explanation: False. Even a small lag can show a stale, higher balance and allow an overdraft. The approval check must use the primary, ideally the conditional UPDATE ... WHERE balance >= amount itself.

hld:stock-exchange.prompt: An exchange handles 500 million orders in a day, all within a 6.5 hour (23,400 s) trading session. What is the approximate average order rate during the session?
options: About 21 thousand per second
About 214 thousand per second
About 500 thousand per second
About 5.8 thousand per second
hld:stock-exchange.explanation: 500M / 23,400 s is about 21.4k orders/s. Dividing by 86,400 s gives 5.8k, but orders only arrive during the session. Peaks at the open or on news are several times higher, which still fits comfortably on a single-threaded engine.

hld:stock-exchange.prompt: A market data feed carries 40,000 incremental book updates per second, and 500 subscribers each receive every update. How many messages per second must be sent if the engine itself sends to each subscriber?
options: 40 thousand
2 million
540 thousand
20 million
hld:stock-exchange.explanation: 40,000 x 500 = 20 million messages per second. That fan-out would swamp the engine, so distribution is moved to multicast or fan-out servers fed by a single outbound stream, keeping the matching engine out of subscriber IO.

hld:stock-exchange.prompt: The book has resting bids A: 100 @ 10.00 (arrived first), B: 100 @ 10.00 (arrived second) and C: 50 @ 9.99. A sell limit order for 150 @ 9.99 arrives. What trades happen?
options: A 100 @ 10.00, then B 50 @ 10.00; B keeps 50 resting
hld:stock-exchange.explanation: Priority is price first (10.00 is better for a seller than 9.99), then time, so A fills fully and B partly. Trades execute at the resting orders' price, 10.00, not the incoming limit. C is untouched because better-priced liquidity covers the whole order.

hld:stock-exchange.prompt: Which structure gives O(1) cancellation of a resting order without scanning the book?
options: A binary search over price levels, then a scan of the level's FIFO list
A hash map from orderId to its node in the doubly linked list at its price level
A single list of all orders sorted by arrival time
A sorted tree keyed by orderId across the whole book
hld:stock-exchange.explanation: The map finds the node directly and the doubly linked list lets it unlink itself in constant time. A level scan is O(n) in the level size, a global list requires scanning, and a tree keyed by orderId is O(log n) and still needs the price level to be updated.

hld:stock-exchange.prompt: A proposed matching engine breaks ties by reading the system clock when each order arrives and processes one book on four threads. What is the main problem?
options: Clock reads are too slow to use on any hot path
Replaying the same input could produce different trades, so fairness, audit and recovery by replay break
Four threads cannot saturate a single core's cache
Orders at different prices would be matched in the wrong order
hld:stock-exchange.explanation: A deterministic engine uses only sequenced events: a sequencer gives each event a global sequence number and journals it, and one thread applies them in order. Clock reads and thread races make the outcome depend on timing, so a replay or a hot standby may diverge from the primary.

hld:stock-exchange.prompt: The primary engine acknowledges orders before the hot standby has received them (asynchronous replication). What is the main risk?
options: Market data sequence numbers will restart from zero
After a failover, the standby may be missing recent orders that were already acknowledged to clients
Orders are matched twice, once on each machine
The standby will match orders differently from the primary
hld:stock-exchange.explanation: Async replication saves microseconds but opens a gap: acknowledged events not yet on the standby are lost if the primary dies. Determinism means the standby matches identically on what it has, so the risk is missing events, not divergence. Sync replication closes the gap at a small latency cost.

hld:stock-exchange.prompt: The standby is promoted after the primary appears dead, but the primary was only paused (for example a long stall) and later resumes. Why is fencing critical?
options: It guarantees the standby has seen every acknowledged order
It compresses the event log to reduce replication traffic
It prevents the old primary from continuing to emit trades alongside the new leader
It speeds up the election so promotion takes microseconds
hld:stock-exchange.explanation: Without fencing, a revived primary and the new leader could both publish executions, a split brain with two conflicting histories. Fencing (an epoch or token that the old primary cannot satisfy) shuts out the stale leader. Replication guarantees are a separate concern.

hld:stock-exchange.prompt: To scale beyond one engine, how should orders be partitioned across sequencer and engine pairs?
options: Round robin across engines, to balance bursts
By symbol, assigning symbol groups to engine pairs
By hash of orderId, to spread load evenly
By account id, so each customer's orders stay together
hld:stock-exchange.explanation: Orders in different symbols never interact, so a symbol is a natural unit of isolation and keeps price-time priority intact inside one engine. Splitting by account, orderId or round robin scatters buy and sell orders for one symbol across engines, so they could never be matched.

hld:stock-exchange.prompt: Select all correct statements about pre-trade risk checks in the exchange design.
options: A price collar rejects orders far from the last trade price
They run before the sequencer, using cheap in-memory account and position state
Trades that breach limits are reversed after matching
Buying power is checked by querying a relational database on each order
hld:stock-exchange.explanation: Risk must be fast and in-memory, and it must run before an order is sequenced so a bad order never reaches the book. A per-order database query would blow the microsecond budget, and trades cannot be undone after the fact because counterparties have already been told they were filled.

hld:stock-exchange.prompt: Select all correct statements about distributing market data.
options: Having the engine push to each subscriber over TCP lowers latency for everyone
Periodic snapshots let a client recover after a gap
Sequence numbers on incremental updates let clients detect gaps
UDP multicast guarantees ordered, retransmitted delivery to every subscriber
hld:stock-exchange.explanation: Multicast is cheap to fan out but unreliable, so clients rely on sequence numbers to detect loss and snapshots (or a replay channel) to recover. Pushing to every subscriber from the engine consumes the engine's resources and adds latency for everyone as subscribers grow.

hld:stock-exchange.prompt: An amend that increases an order's size keeps its original time priority in the queue at its price level.
options: True
False
hld:stock-exchange.explanation: Increasing size is treated like re-entering the order, so it goes to the back of the FIFO queue for that price. Otherwise a participant could claim a front-of-queue position cheaply and then enlarge it, undermining fairness for everyone behind them.

hld:stock-exchange.prompt: Because a single-threaded engine is limited to one core's throughput, matching at around 100,000 orders per second requires a multi-threaded engine.
options: True
False
hld:stock-exchange.explanation: The LMAX article reports roughly 6 million orders per second on one business-logic thread, so 100k/s is far within reach. The hard problems are latency and determinism, and multi-threading would add locks and nondeterministic ordering.

hld:stock-exchange.prompt: The sequenced event log grows by about 100 GB per trading day, and regulators require 7 years of retention. With about 252 trading days a year, roughly how much log is that?
options: About 1.8 PB
About 176 TB
About 256 TB
About 25 TB
hld:stock-exchange.explanation: 100 GB x 252 is about 25 TB per year; x7 is about 176 TB. 256 TB uses 365 days, but the exchange only trades on trading days.

hld:stock-exchange.prompt: An order spends 8 us in gateway decode and risk, 2 us in the sequencer, 3 us matching and 4 us publishing to the outbound path. What is the internal wire-to-wire latency?
options: About 34 us
About 170 us
About 17 us
About 8 us
hld:stock-exchange.explanation: The stages are sequential on the order's path: 8 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 17 us, comfortably inside a well-under-100 us budget. Taking only the largest stage (8 us) ignores that stages add up.

hld:stock-exchange.prompt: The ask side holds 100 @ 10.01, 150 @ 10.02 and 200 @ 10.03. A market buy order for 300 arrives. Which fills result?
options: 300 @ 10.02, the average price
hld:stock-exchange.explanation: A market order walks the book from the best ask: it takes all 100 at 10.01, all 150 at 10.02, then 50 of the 200 at 10.03, each at the resting order's price. Only 100 shares exist at 10.01, so 300 @ 10.01 is impossible.

hld:stock-exchange.prompt: The ask side holds 120 @ 9.99 and 100 @ 10.01. An IOC buy limit order for 200 @ 10.00 arrives. What happens?
options: 120 fill at 9.99 and the remaining 80 rest on the bid at 10.00
Nothing fills, since the whole 200 is not available within the limit
120 fill at 9.99 and the remaining 80 are cancelled
hld:stock-exchange.explanation: IOC fills whatever is available within its limit immediately and cancels the rest; 10.01 is above the 10.00 limit. Resting the remainder is what a plain DAY limit order would do, and 'all or nothing' is FOK.

hld:stock-exchange.prompt: The ask side holds 100 @ 10.01, 100 @ 10.02 and 200 @ 10.03. A FOK buy limit order for 250 @ 10.02 arrives. What happens?
options: 200 fill immediately and the remaining 50 rest on the bid at 10.02
200 fill immediately and the remaining 50 are cancelled right away
250 fill, with the last 50 taken at 10.03 to complete the order
No fills: only 200 are available at or below 10.02, so it is killed
hld:stock-exchange.explanation: Fill-or-kill executes in full immediately or not at all. Only 200 shares are offered at or below 10.02, so it is killed with no trades. Partially filling and cancelling the rest is IOC behaviour.

hld:stock-exchange.prompt: A trader's cancel and an incoming order that would fill the same resting order arrive at nearly the same moment. How does the exchange resolve the race?
options: Sequencer order decides; if the fill came first, the cancel is late or partial
The engine runs both in parallel threads and keeps whichever finishes first
The cancel always wins, whatever the arrival order, to protect the trader
The fill always wins, whatever the arrival order, since trades matter more
hld:stock-exchange.explanation: The sequencer defines one global order, and the deterministic engine applies events in that order, so the outcome is fair and replayable. A fixed 'cancel wins' rule would require reordering events, which breaks determinism.

hld:stock-exchange.prompt: When is a tick-indexed array a better choice than a sorted tree for a symbol's price levels?
options: When a price band bounds the ticks, so each level is a direct O(1) index
When the implementation language has no balanced tree in its library
When prices can range over many orders of magnitude during a session
When nearly all incoming orders are market orders rather than limits
hld:stock-exchange.explanation: An array indexed by price tick gives O(1) access to any level but needs a bounded range of ticks, which price bands provide. For unbounded or very wide ranges the array would be huge and sparse, so a tree's O(log n) is the better trade.

hld:stock-exchange.prompt: A matching engine written in a garbage-collected language allocates a new object for every order and shows p99 latency spikes of several milliseconds every few seconds. What is the most likely cause and fix?
options: Too few symbols per engine; merge engines so each one stays busy and warm
GC pauses; pre-allocate orders and events in pools or a ring buffer instead
The journal is too slow under load; turn journaling off on the hot path
Network jitter between gateways and engine; add more gateways to spread the load
hld:stock-exchange.explanation: Periodic multi-millisecond stalls in an allocating hot path are classic GC pauses; pre-allocation and object reuse, as in the LMAX Disruptor, remove them. Disabling journaling would break durability and replay.

hld:stock-exchange.prompt: A market data client receives incremental update seq 1001 and then seq 1004. What should it do?
options: Distrust its book, fetch a snapshot or retransmission, then reapply increments
Apply 1004 and carry on, since the missing updates were most likely duplicates
Ask the matching engine itself to resend its whole order log from the start
Average updates 1001 and 1004 to estimate the contents of the missing updates
hld:stock-exchange.explanation: Feed sequence numbers exist to detect gaps; applying later increments onto a book that missed updates gives wrong depth. Recovery uses a snapshot or retransmission service, never the engine itself.

hld:stock-exchange.prompt: The exchange must support market-wide halts and opening auctions. Select all statements that are correct.
options: During an auction call period orders are collected without continuous matching
In an opening auction, each order executes at its own limit price in arrival order
Halt and resume are submitted as sequenced events, so replay reproduces exactly when matching stopped
An auction typically uncrosses at a single price chosen to maximise executed volume
hld:stock-exchange.explanation: Putting halts in the sequenced stream keeps the engine deterministic, and auctions collect orders, then execute all crossing orders at one uniform clearing price. Executing each at its own limit would be continuous matching, not an auction.

hld:stock-exchange.prompt: Select all characteristics of an LMAX Disruptor style pipeline in the matching engine.
options: Journaling and replication run in parallel with the business-logic stage
A pre-allocated ring buffer replaces locked queues between stages
Stages coordinate through sequence numbers instead of locks
Each stage allocates a fresh message object per event to avoid sharing memory
hld:stock-exchange.explanation: The ring buffer is allocated once and its slots are reused, which avoids GC and lock contention; consumers track sequences, and durability stages run alongside matching. Per-event allocation is exactly what the design avoids.

hld:stock-exchange.prompt: One very hot symbol alone approaches the capacity of the engine it shares with other symbols. Select all sound responses.
options: Give that symbol its own dedicated sequencer and engine pair
Move the other symbols off its engine to other engine pairs
Hash that symbol's orders across four engines by order id
Optimise the hot path (pinned cores, cache-friendly structures) since one thread can handle millions of events per second
