os:paging-vs-segmentation-page-replaceme.explanation: They shrink page tables and TLB misses, but internal fragmentation grows: on average, half of the last page of each region is wasted, and that is 1 MiB with 2 MiB pages.

os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.prompt: Why does epoll scale better than select for 10,000 connections of which 50 are active?
options: epoll uses more threads
select can only watch sockets, not pipes
epoll reads the data for you
epoll registers fds once and returns only the ready ones, so cost tracks ready events; select copies and scans the whole set every call
os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.explanation: select rebuilds and copies an fd bitmap (capped at FD_SETSIZE, usually 1024) and scans it on return. epoll keeps the interest set in the kernel and fills a ready list via wakeup callbacks.

os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.prompt: With edge-triggered epoll, a handler reads only part of the available data. What happens?
options: epoll reports the fd again on the next epoll_wait
The read blocks until all data is consumed
The kernel discards the leftover bytes
It may never be woken for the leftover bytes, because ET only reports state changes
os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.explanation: With EPOLLET you must use non-blocking fds and read until EAGAIN. Level-triggered mode would keep reporting the fd while data remains.

os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.prompt: epoll can be used to do non-blocking reads from regular files on disk.
options: True
False
os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.explanation: Regular files are always reported ready, so a read can still block on the disk. Node runs fs work on libuv's thread pool, and io_uring offers true async file I/O.

os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.prompt: What is the key difference between epoll and io_uring?
options: They are two names for the same API
io_uring only works for sockets
epoll is asynchronous, io_uring is blocking
epoll is readiness-based (you still call read), io_uring is completion-based with shared submission and completion rings
os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.explanation: io_uring lets you batch many operations, including file I/O, with few or no syscalls and get notified when they complete. It is Linux-only and has had a notable security history.

os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.prompt: A Node server handles 10k idle websockets fine but stalls everyone while parsing a 50 MB JSON body. Why?
options: The websockets exhaust libuv's thread pool
The body is parsed on the thread pool, which is too small
JSON.parse runs synchronously on the single event loop thread, so no other callbacks run until it finishes
epoll cannot handle more than 10k fds
os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.explanation: Idle sockets cost almost nothing with epoll, but any long CPU-bound task blocks the loop. Stream the parse, cap body sizes, or move the work to a worker thread.

os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.prompt: Which statements about I/O models are correct?
options: A non-blocking read on an empty socket returns EAGAIN immediately
select has no limit on the number of fds
Non-blocking I/O alone, without multiplexing, removes the need to poll
Blocking I/O needs roughly one thread per concurrent connection
Multiplexing lets one thread wait on many fds at once
os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.explanation: Without a multiplexer, non-blocking I/O means spinning on reads. select is limited by FD_SETSIZE, typically 1024.

os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.prompt: In which phase of Node's event loop does libuv wait for socket readiness?
options: The timers phase
The poll phase
The check phase
The close callbacks phase
os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.explanation: The loop cycles through timers, pending callbacks, poll, check and close. Poll is where libuv calls epoll_wait (or kqueue or IOCP) and dispatches I/O callbacks. setImmediate runs in check.

os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.prompt: Which I/O scheduler choice is usually right for an NVMe database server?
options: none (or a minimal one such as mq-deadline), because seek reordering buys nothing on flash
Round-robin scheduling of disk heads
Shortest-seek-time-first to maximise throughput
An elevator (SCAN) scheduler to minimise seek time
os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.explanation: Seek-optimising algorithms matter for spinning disks. NVMe devices have no heads and deep internal queues, so the scheduling overhead is better spent elsewhere.

os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.prompt: What is the main weakness of shortest-seek-time-first (SSTF) disk scheduling on an HDD?
options: It only works on SSDs
It needs to know the future request stream
Requests far from the head can starve while nearby requests keep arriving
It ignores the head position entirely
os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.explanation: SSTF maximises throughput greedily but is unfair. SCAN (the elevator) and C-SCAN sweep across the disk to bound waiting.

os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.prompt: Cylinders 0-199, head at 53. Queue: 98, 183, 37, 122, 14, 124, 65, 67. What is the total head movement under SSTF?
options: 208 cylinders
640 cylinders
236 cylinders
299 cylinders
os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.explanation: SSTF order is 65, 67, 37, 14, 98, 122, 124, 183, and the moves add up to 12 + 2 + 30 + 23 + 84 + 24 + 2 + 59 = 236. 640 is FCFS in arrival order.

os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.prompt: Same disk: cylinders 0-199, head at 53 moving toward higher cylinders, queue 98, 183, 37, 122, 14, 124, 65, 67. What is the total head movement under LOOK?
options: 331 cylinders
236 cylinders
299 cylinders
382 cylinders
os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.explanation: LOOK goes up only as far as the last request: 53 to 183 is 130, then it reverses to 14, which is 169, for 299 total. 331 is SCAN, which travels to cylinder 199 before reversing.

os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.prompt: A 7,200 RPM HDD has an 8 ms average seek. Roughly how many random 4 KiB reads per second can it do?
options: About 8,000
About 800
About 7,200
About 80
os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.explanation: Average rotational latency is half a turn: 60 / 7200 / 2 ≈ 4.2 ms. Each random I/O costs about 8 + 4.2 ≈ 12 ms, giving about 80 IOPS. NVMe SSDs reach hundreds of thousands, which is why seek scheduling matters far less there.

os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.prompt: What is the average rotational latency of a 7,200 RPM disk?
options: About 1 ms
About 0.5 ms
About 8.3 ms
About 4.2 ms
os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.explanation: One revolution takes 60 s / 7200 ≈ 8.33 ms, and on average the sector is half a turn away, so about 4.17 ms. 8.3 ms is a full revolution.

os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.prompt: On Linux, write() to a regular file returned successfully. Is the data durable if the machine loses power now?
options: Only if the file is smaller than 4 KiB
Yes, as long as the file was opened read-write
Not necessarily; it may still be in the page cache until fsync or fdatasync
Yes; write() only returns after the disk confirms
os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.explanation: Buffered writes land in the page cache and are flushed later. Databases call fsync (or use O_DSYNC/O_DIRECT) at commit for durability. Without that, power loss can drop acknowledged writes.

os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.prompt: epoll is a reactor-style readiness API. Which describes Windows IOCP and Linux io_uring?
options: Signal-driven I/O based on SIGIO
Proactors; you submit the operation and are told when it has completed
Also reactors; they report when an fd is readable
Blocking I/O with a thread per request
os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.explanation: With readiness APIs you are told an fd is ready and then do the read yourself. With completion APIs you hand over the buffer and receive the finished result. libuv uses IOCP on Windows and epoll/kqueue elsewhere.

os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.prompt: On a busy Linux server, `free` shows little 'free' memory but plenty of 'available'. Why?
options: A memory leak is hiding the free memory
The kernel reserves memory for epoll
Most memory is page cache, which the kernel can reclaim when needed
Swap is counted as free
os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.explanation: Linux uses idle RAM to cache file data. 'available' estimates what can be reclaimed without swapping. Low 'free' on its own is normal, not a leak.

os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.prompt: Several threads call epoll_wait on the same epoll fd. Which flag ensures a single ready socket is handled by only one thread at a time?
options: EPOLLIN
EPOLLET
EPOLLONESHOT
EPOLLRDHUP
os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.explanation: EPOLLONESHOT disables the fd after one event is delivered; the handler re-arms it with epoll_ctl when done. EPOLLET alone can still wake another thread if more data arrives mid-handling. EPOLLEXCLUSIVE targets thundering herds across separate epoll instances.

os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.prompt: A server built on select() starts failing when a new connection gets file descriptor 1024. Why?
options: The kernel caps processes at 1024 sockets
fd_set is a fixed bitmap of FD_SETSIZE (usually 1024) bits
epoll is required once more than 1024 events are pending
TCP has only 1024 ports below the ephemeral range
os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.explanation: select indexes a fixed-size bitmap by fd number, so fds at or above FD_SETSIZE overflow it. poll and epoll avoid this. The per-process fd limit (ulimit -n) is separate and adjustable.

os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.prompt: Inside an fs.readFile callback, code calls setTimeout(a, 0) and then setImmediate(b). Which runs first in Node?
options: Both run in the same tick in source order
It is nondeterministic
b, because the check phase follows the poll phase
a, because timers are checked first
os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.explanation: I/O callbacks run in the poll phase, and the check phase (setImmediate) comes next, before the loop returns to timers. At top level, outside any I/O callback, the order is nondeterministic.

os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.prompt: How does io_uring cut syscall overhead compared with read/write plus epoll?
options: It disables the page cache
Shared submission and completion rings let one syscall, or none with SQPOLL, cover many operations
It runs the application inside the kernel
It turns all files into sockets
os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.explanation: Applications push many submission entries and reap completions from shared-memory rings, batching work into one io_uring_enter. With SQPOLL a kernel thread polls the ring, so no syscall is needed. epoll still needs a syscall per read or write.

os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.prompt: Which practices keep an event-loop server, such as Node, responsive? Select all that apply.
options: Keep CPU-heavy synchronous work off the loop
Offload heavy computation to worker threads
Buffer partial reads and writes instead of assuming whole messages
Use fs.readFileSync in request handlers for simplicity
os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.explanation: Any synchronous work stalls every connection, so keep the loop for I/O and move CPU work to workers. Sockets deliver arbitrary chunks, so you must frame messages. Sync fs calls in handlers block everyone.

os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.prompt: Which statements about HDD scheduling algorithms are correct? Select all that apply.
options: C-SCAN gives more uniform waiting times than SCAN
LOOK reverses at the last pending request rather than at the disk edge
Deadline-style schedulers add per-request expiry times to bound starvation
FCFS minimises total head movement
os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.explanation: C-SCAN serves in one direction then jumps back, evening out waits. LOOK skips empty travel. Deadlines fix SSTF/SCAN-style starvation. FCFS ignores position entirely and usually moves the most.

os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.prompt: Which statements about the Linux page cache are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Writes are buffered and flushed later unless you use fsync or O_SYNC
O_DIRECT bypasses the page cache for that file's I/O
Page cache memory can never be reclaimed by applications
Recently read file data can be served from RAM without disk I/O
os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.explanation: The cache speeds up reads and absorbs writes, and O_DIRECT opts out (some databases manage their own buffers). Clean cache pages are reclaimed whenever applications need memory.

os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.prompt: A read on a non-blocking socket with no data available returns immediately with EAGAIN/EWOULDBLOCK instead of waiting.
options: True
False
os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.explanation: Non-blocking mode never sleeps in read; the caller learns 'not now' and waits for readiness through epoll. That is the building block of event loops.

os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.prompt: Edge-triggered epoll keeps reporting a socket as readable on every epoll_wait while unread data remains in its buffer.
options: True
False
os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.explanation: That describes level-triggered mode. Edge-triggered reports only on a transition, when new data arrives, so you must read until EAGAIN or the remaining data can sit unnoticed.

os:containers-vs-vms.prompt: What is the single most important difference between a container and a VM?
options: VMs cannot have network interfaces
Containers always use more memory than VMs
Containers cannot run Linux binaries
Containers share the host kernel; each VM runs its own guest kernel
os:containers-vs-vms.explanation: A VM virtualises hardware with a hypervisor; a container is processes on the host kernel with a restricted view. Most other differences follow from that.

os:containers-vs-vms.prompt: Which Linux primitives together make up a Docker container?
options: A layered root filesystem (overlayfs) with pivot_root
A hypervisor
Seccomp filters and dropped capabilities
Cgroups, to limit what it can use
Namespaces, to limit what the process can see
A dedicated guest kernel
os:containers-vs-vms.explanation: There is no 'container' object in the kernel; it is a process started with these restrictions. A guest kernel and hypervisor belong to VMs.

os:containers-vs-vms.prompt: What happens when a process in a container exceeds its cgroup memory limit?
options: The kernel reclaims memory in that cgroup and, if that fails, the OOM killer kills a process inside it
The limit is ignored for root processes
The container is paused until memory frees up
The whole host runs out of memory
os:containers-vs-vms.explanation: Cgroups confine the damage to the container, so neighbours are protected. Applications sized from host-level numbers can be surprised by these kills.

os:containers-vs-vms.prompt: Why does a JVM or Node process in a container sometimes size its heap wrongly?
options: It reads host memory (for example /proc/meminfo) rather than the cgroup limit unless it is container-aware
Garbage collectors are disabled in containers
Containers hide all memory information from processes
The cgroup limit is always larger than host memory
os:containers-vs-vms.explanation: Reading host totals leads to a heap larger than the limit and an OOM kill. Modern runtimes read cgroup limits, or you set the heap size explicitly.

os:containers-vs-vms.prompt: A standard Docker container is a strong security boundary for running hostile, untrusted code.
options: True
False
os:containers-vs-vms.explanation: The container reaches the full host syscall surface, and one kernel bug can give host root (runc CVE-2019-5736 is the classic example). For untrusted code use gVisor, Firecracker microVMs or full VMs.

os:containers-vs-vms.prompt: What does the user namespace add to container isolation?
options: Root inside the container maps to an unprivileged uid on the host
It limits CPU usage
It gives the container its own network interfaces
It gives the container its own process tree
os:containers-vs-vms.explanation: uid mapping means escaping as container root lands you as an ordinary user on the host. The pid namespace gives the process tree, net gives interfaces, and cgroups limit CPU.

os:containers-vs-vms.prompt: How does gVisor shrink the attack surface of a shared kernel?
options: It encrypts container memory
It runs every container in a full VM with its own Linux kernel
A user-space kernel (the Sentry) handles the container's syscalls and makes only a small set of host syscalls
It disables all syscalls
os:containers-vs-vms.explanation: Intercepting syscalls costs performance and some compatibility, but the host kernel sees far fewer entry points.

os:containers-vs-vms.prompt: Which of these is a container-hardening practice?
options: Running containers with --privileged for compatibility
Granting all capabilities so apps do not fail
Running as a non-root user and never mounting the Docker socket
Disabling the default seccomp profile
os:containers-vs-vms.explanation: Mounting the Docker socket gives control of the host's container engine, effectively root. The other options widen the attack surface.

os:containers-vs-vms.prompt: Why do containers typically start much faster than conventional VMs?
options: Containers use faster CPUs
Containers skip loading their image
VMs must download their kernel every time
There is no OS to boot; starting a container is starting a process with restrictions
os:containers-vs-vms.explanation: A container starts in milliseconds to about a second. A conventional VM boots a guest kernel and init. Firecracker narrows the gap with a minimal device model.

os:containers-vs-vms.prompt: Which Linux namespace gives a container its own process ID 1?
options: The user namespace
The UTS namespace
The PID namespace
The mount namespace
os:containers-vs-vms.explanation: A PID namespace has its own numbering, so the first process inside is PID 1. UTS isolates the hostname, and mount isolates the filesystem view.

os:containers-vs-vms.prompt: `node server.js` runs as PID 1 in a container with no SIGTERM handler. `docker stop` waits 10 s and then kills it. Why?
options: The kernel does not apply the default action for signals to PID 1 unless it installs a handler
SIGTERM is blocked by the seccomp profile
Node ignores all signals inside containers
docker stop sends SIGHUP, not SIGTERM
os:containers-vs-vms.explanation: PID 1 is special: unhandled SIGTERM is ignored, so Docker escalates to SIGKILL after the timeout. Add a handler, or use an init such as tini (docker run --init), which also reaps zombies.

os:containers-vs-vms.prompt: A host has 64 GiB RAM. Each VM needs 512 MiB of guest OS overhead plus 256 MiB for the app; each container needs only the 256 MiB app. Roughly how many more containers fit than VMs?
options: About 1.5x
About the same
About 10x
About 3x
os:containers-vs-vms.explanation: VMs: 65,536 / 768 ≈ 85. Containers: 65,536 / 256 = 256. That is about 3x, because containers share one kernel instead of booting a guest OS each.

os:containers-vs-vms.prompt: In cgroup v2, what is the difference between memory.high and memory.max?
options: memory.max throttles; memory.high kills
They are aliases
memory.high throttles and reclaims aggressively; reaching memory.max triggers the OOM killer
memory.high applies to swap only
os:containers-vs-vms.explanation: memory.high is a soft limit: the group is slowed down and pushed to reclaim. memory.max is the hard limit, where reclaim fails and the OOM killer runs inside the cgroup.

os:containers-vs-vms.prompt: A Node service runs in a container with a 512 MiB memory limit. What is the safest heap configuration?
options: --max-old-space-size=2048 to avoid GC pauses
No flag; V8 always sizes from the host's total RAM correctly
--max-old-space-size of about 350-400 MiB, leaving headroom for buffers, native memory and stacks
--max-old-space-size=512 so the heap uses the whole limit
os:containers-vs-vms.explanation: The heap is not the only memory: Buffers, native addons, code and thread stacks live outside it. Setting the heap equal to the cgroup limit gets the container OOM-killed before V8 reports heap exhaustion.

os:containers-vs-vms.prompt: How does AWS Firecracker boot microVMs in about 125 ms while still using hardware virtualization?
options: It interprets guest code in user space
It shares the host kernel like a container
It snapshots the host process
A minimal KVM-based VMM with only a few virtio devices and no BIOS or PCI emulation
os:containers-vs-vms.explanation: Firecracker drops most legacy devices and firmware, emulating just virtio net and block, a serial console and little else, so the guest kernel boots almost immediately. Each microVM still has its own kernel behind KVM.

os:containers-vs-vms.prompt: Where does Linux KVM fit in the type 1 / type 2 hypervisor split?
options: A paravirtual device driver for guests
A pure type 2 hypervisor running as a normal app
A kernel module that makes Linux act as a type 1 hypervisor, usually paired with QEMU for devices
A container runtime
os:containers-vs-vms.explanation: KVM exposes CPU virtualization (VT-x/AMD-V) from the host kernel, so Linux itself is the hypervisor; QEMU or Firecracker provide the virtual devices. VirtualBox on a desktop is the usual type 2 example.

os:containers-vs-vms.prompt: A process in a container edits /etc/nginx/nginx.conf, a file that ships in the image. What happens with overlayfs?
options: The file is copied up into the container's writable layer and changed there
The change is written to the host's /etc/nginx/nginx.conf
The write fails because image layers are read-only
The image layer is changed for every container
os:containers-vs-vms.explanation: Image layers are shared and read-only. The first write copies the whole file up into the container's own writable (upper) layer and the edit lands there, so the image and other containers are unaffected, and the change is lost when the container is removed. Files Docker bind-mounts in, such as /etc/hosts and /etc/resolv.conf, are not in the image and skip copy-up.

os:containers-vs-vms.prompt: In a Node Dockerfile, why copy package.json and package-lock.json and run npm ci before copying the rest of the source?
options: It is required for multi-stage builds
The dependency layer stays cached and only rebuilds when the lockfile changes
npm ci requires an empty directory
It makes the final image smaller
os:containers-vs-vms.explanation: Docker reuses a layer until its inputs change. Copying the source first would invalidate the npm ci layer on every code edit. Multi-stage builds are what shrink the image.

os:containers-vs-vms.prompt: Why is running a container with --privileged, or mounting /var/run/docker.sock into it, dangerous?
options: It only slows the container down
Either can give processes in the container root-level control of the host
It disables networking
It prevents the container from being stopped
os:containers-vs-vms.explanation: --privileged grants all capabilities and device access; the Docker socket lets you start a new privileged container that mounts the host filesystem. Both are effectively host root.

os:containers-vs-vms.prompt: What is the purpose of Docker's default seccomp profile?
options: To isolate the hostname
To block risky syscalls and shrink the kernel attack surface
To limit CPU usage
To encrypt container traffic
os:containers-vs-vms.explanation: seccomp filters syscalls, blocking things like kexec_load and mount by default. All containers share the host kernel, so every syscall they cannot make is one less exploit path. CPU limits are cgroups' job.

os:containers-vs-vms.prompt: Which are shared by all containers on one Linux host? Select all that apply.
options: The PID numbers seen inside each container
Each container's root filesystem view
The kernel's CPU scheduler
The host kernel
os:containers-vs-vms.explanation: Containers are processes on one kernel and one scheduler. Mount namespaces give each its own root filesystem view, and PID namespaces give each its own numbering.

os:containers-vs-vms.prompt: You must run untrusted user code from the internet. Which approaches provide meaningful isolation? Select all that apply.
options: Putting it in its own network namespace and nothing more
Firecracker or Kata microVMs, each with its own kernel
Dropping all capabilities and applying seccomp as defence in depth
Running as root in a standard container with a read-only root filesystem
gVisor (runsc), which intercepts syscalls in a user-space kernel
os:containers-vs-vms.explanation: Shrinking or replacing the shared-kernel surface is what matters, plus layered hardening. A read-only filesystem or a separate network namespace alone leaves root with the full syscall surface of the host kernel.

os:containers-vs-vms.prompt: Which resources can cgroups limit? Select all that apply.
options: Memory
Block I/O bandwidth
CPU time
The hostname visible to the container
os:containers-vs-vms.explanation: cgroups account for and limit resources such as CPU, memory, I/O and PIDs. Hostname isolation comes from the UTS namespace; namespaces control what a process sees, cgroups how much it uses.

os:containers-vs-vms.prompt: A Linux container can natively run an OS with a different kernel, because each container ships its own kernel.
options: True
False
os:containers-vs-vms.explanation: Containers share the host kernel; images bring only user-space files. Running a different kernel needs a VM, which is how Docker Desktop runs Linux containers on macOS.

os:containers-vs-vms.prompt: To reach the host, a guest-kernel exploit in a VM usually also has to escape the hypervisor, whose interface is far smaller than the Linux syscall surface.
options: True
False
os:containers-vs-vms.explanation: The guest kernel is the attacker's own; the boundary is the narrow VM-exit and virtual device interface. That smaller surface is why VMs and microVMs are the standard for hostile multi-tenant code.

dbms:acid-isolation-levels.prompt: A transfer moves 100 from account A (balance 500) to account B (balance 200) as a debit statement followed by a credit statement. The process crashes after the debit but before the credit, and the transaction was never committed. Which ACID property is at stake, and what makes the debit disappear after restart?
options: Atomicity: recovery discards the uncommitted debit using undo or by never committing it
Isolation: other sessions are blocked from reading A until the crash is resolved
Consistency: the engine notices the totals no longer add up and repairs B on its own
Durability: the debit was fsynced, so recovery must keep it and replay the credit
dbms:acid-isolation-levels.explanation: Atomicity means all or nothing. Uncommitted work is rolled back (InnoDB undo log, or Postgres never marking the new row versions committed), so both balances stay unchanged. Durability only covers committed data, and the engine cannot know your 'money is conserved' invariant on its own.

dbms:acid-isolation-levels.prompt: A Postgres REPEATABLE READ transaction runs SELECT ... WHERE balance > 300 and gets 2 rows. Another transaction then inserts a matching row and commits. The first transaction runs the same SELECT again. What does it see?
options: 3 rows, because REPEATABLE READ only protects rows that already existed
An error, because Postgres aborts any transaction whose predicate result has changed
2 rows, because Postgres REPEATABLE READ is snapshot isolation and also blocks phantoms
2 rows only if the first query used FOR SHARE, otherwise 3 rows
dbms:acid-isolation-levels.explanation: Postgres REPEATABLE READ takes one snapshot for the whole transaction, so the later insert is invisible: no phantom. That is stronger than the SQL standard requires (which permits phantoms at this level). It still allows write skew.

dbms:acid-isolation-levels.prompt: Two sessions on Postgres at READ COMMITTED each run the pattern below with +10 and +20 respectively, computing the new value in the application. The balance starts at 500. Which change removes the lost update without raising the isolation level or adding retries?
options: Add CHECK (balance >= 0) so the database rejects the second write when the two conflict
Use UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 10 WHERE id = 'A', one atomic statement
Move the sessions to READ UNCOMMITTED so that neither session ever has to wait on the other
Add an index on accounts(id) so the UPDATE finishes faster and the race window shrinks
dbms:acid-isolation-levels.explanation: The final value can be 510 or 520, so one update is lost. An atomic UPDATE takes the row lock and recomputes from the latest committed value. A faster statement only narrows the race, READ UNCOMMITTED behaves like READ COMMITTED in Postgres, and a CHECK constraint says nothing about stale reads.

dbms:acid-isolation-levels.prompt: Two on-call doctors each run a transaction that checks 'at least 2 doctors are on call' and then sets themselves off call. Each transaction updates a different row. Which Postgres isolation level prevents both from committing?
options: READ COMMITTED, because every statement sees the latest committed row
REPEATABLE READ, because the second updater gets a serialization failure on the same row
REPEATABLE READ, because each snapshot is stable for the whole transaction
SERIALIZABLE, because SSI sees the read-write dependency cycle and aborts one transaction
dbms:acid-isolation-levels.explanation: This is write skew: both pass the check on their own snapshot and write different rows, so snapshot isolation (Postgres REPEATABLE READ) allows it and no same-row conflict is raised. Only SERIALIZABLE (SSI) aborts one of them, and the application must retry.

dbms:acid-isolation-levels.prompt: In InnoDB at the default isolation level, transaction T1 runs a plain SELECT count of rows with balance > 300 and gets 2. Transaction T2 inserts a matching row and commits. T1 then repeats the plain SELECT and afterwards runs the same query with FOR UPDATE. What does T1 get?
options: 2 rows for the plain SELECT but 3 for FOR UPDATE, since locking reads see the latest data
2 rows for the plain SELECT, and FOR UPDATE blocks until T2 rolls back
2 rows for both, because REPEATABLE READ freezes every read in the transaction
3 rows for the plain SELECT and 3 for FOR UPDATE, because T2 has already committed its insert
dbms:acid-isolation-levels.explanation: Plain SELECTs read from the snapshot taken at the first read, so they still return 2. Locking reads (FOR UPDATE, UPDATE, DELETE) read the latest committed version, so they see 3. Mixing snapshot and current reads in one transaction can therefore look inconsistent. T2 already committed, so nothing blocks.

dbms:acid-isolation-levels.prompt: A Postgres application running at SERIALIZABLE gets SQLSTATE 40001 (serialization failure) on a statement inside a transaction. What should the application do?
options: Re-send only the failed statement, because earlier statements already took effect
Roll back and rerun the whole transaction from BEGIN, with a bounded number of retries
Lower the isolation level to READ COMMITTED permanently so the error stops appearing
Catch the error and continue with the remaining statements of the same transaction
dbms:acid-isolation-levels.explanation: A serialization failure means the engine aborted this transaction to preserve a serial order. The whole transaction is rolled back, so the application must restart it from the beginning. Retry loops and tolerance for false-positive aborts are the price of SERIALIZABLE.

dbms:acid-isolation-levels.prompt: Which data is the best candidate for relaxing durability (for example Postgres synchronous_commit = off or InnoDB flush_log_at_trx_commit set to 0 or 2) to gain commit latency?
options: Account balances in a payments ledger, where every acknowledged commit must survive a crash
Clickstream analytics events, where losing the last few commits after a crash is acceptable
Unique username claims, where a lost commit could let a duplicate slip in later
Inventory decrements for the last remaining seat on a flight, where overselling is costly
dbms:acid-isolation-levels.explanation: Relaxed flushing risks losing the last few acknowledged commits on a crash, but not corrupting the database. That is fine for analytics events and unacceptable for money, uniqueness claims or scarce inventory, where an acknowledged write must not vanish.

dbms:acid-isolation-levels.prompt: Select all approaches that prevent the on-call doctors write skew on Postgres (both doctors must not be able to go off call at the same time).
options: Run the transactions at SERIALIZABLE and retry on serialization failure
Run the transactions at READ COMMITTED so each statement sees fresh data
Run the transactions at REPEATABLE READ and rely on snapshot isolation
Turn on synchronous_commit so commits are flushed before acknowledging
Lock the on-call rows with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE before the application checks the count
dbms:acid-isolation-levels.explanation: SSI aborts one transaction of the dangerous cycle, and explicit row locks make the two transactions serialize on the rows they read. Snapshot isolation and READ COMMITTED both let each check pass on stale or partial data, and flush settings concern durability, not isolation.

dbms:acid-isolation-levels.prompt: Select all statements that are correct about default and special behavior of Postgres and MySQL/InnoDB isolation levels.
options: InnoDB SERIALIZABLE turns plain SELECTs into SELECT ... FOR SHARE, making it lock-based
Postgres READ UNCOMMITTED behaves like READ COMMITTED, so dirty reads cannot happen
InnoDB defaults to REPEATABLE READ, unlike Postgres which defaults to READ COMMITTED
In Postgres, REPEATABLE READ still allows phantom reads because it follows the SQL standard table
dbms:acid-isolation-levels.explanation: Postgres never exposes dirty reads, and its defaults differ from InnoDB's. InnoDB SERIALIZABLE is lock-based and blocks more. The third statement is wrong: Postgres REPEATABLE READ is snapshot isolation and does prevent phantoms (while permitting write skew).

dbms:acid-isolation-levels.prompt: The C in ACID (consistency) and the C in CAP (consistency) mean the same thing.
options: True
False
dbms:acid-isolation-levels.explanation: ACID consistency means a transaction moves the database between valid states according to declared invariants and your logic. CAP consistency means linearizability: every read sees the latest completed write across replicas. They are unrelated guarantees.

dbms:acid-isolation-levels.prompt: On Postgres at READ COMMITTED, two concurrent sessions each running UPDATE balance = balance + 10 on the same row can still lose one of the increments.
options: True
False
dbms:acid-isolation-levels.explanation: The second UPDATE waits for the first one's row lock, then re-evaluates against the newly committed row version, so both increments apply. The lost update only occurs when the value is read into the application first and written back as a constant.

dbms:acid-isolation-levels.prompt: T1 sets account A to 400 but has not committed. T2 reads A and sees 400. T1 then rolls back. Which anomaly is this, and what is the lowest standard SQL isolation level that prevents it?
options: Non-repeatable read; prevented first at REPEATABLE READ
Phantom read; prevented first at SERIALIZABLE
Dirty read; prevented first at READ COMMITTED
Lost update; prevented first at REPEATABLE READ
dbms:acid-isolation-levels.explanation: T2 read a value that never officially existed, which is a dirty read. READ COMMITTED is the first standard level that forbids it. A non-repeatable read needs the change to be committed between two reads by the same transaction, which is not what happened here.

dbms:acid-isolation-levels.prompt: accounts has CHECK (balance >= 0). A transfer of 600 from A (balance 500) to B runs inside BEGIN ... COMMIT. What happens, and which ACID property is the database enforcing?
options: The debit fails the CHECK and the whole transaction rolls back (consistency)
A goes to -100 and B is credited; the CHECK is only verified at the next VACUUM
The debit is skipped silently and only the credit to B is applied (atomicity)
The debit waits until another deposit makes A large enough (isolation)
dbms:acid-isolation-levels.explanation: Declared constraints are checked on the write, so the debit raises a constraint violation and the transaction must roll back, leaving both rows unchanged. That is the database enforcing consistency for invariants you declared. It never applies half a transaction, and it does not wait for a future deposit.

dbms:acid-isolation-levels.prompt: On Postgres at the default READ COMMITTED, a report runs SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = 'A', then a separate SELECT for B. Between them, the 100 transfer from A (500) to B (200) commits. What total can the report compute?
options: 600, because the report sees the debit but not the credit
800, because it read A before the transfer and B after it
It blocks on the second SELECT until the transfer finishes, then returns 700
700, because the whole transaction reads from one snapshot
dbms:acid-isolation-levels.explanation: READ COMMITTED takes a fresh snapshot per statement. The report reads A = 500 (before) and B = 300 (after), so it computes 800. Fix it with REPEATABLE READ (one snapshot for the whole transaction) or a single statement that sums both rows. MVCC readers never block on writers, so there is no wait.

dbms:acid-isolation-levels.prompt: Postgres runs with synchronous_commit = off for an analytics events table. The server loses power right after several COMMITs returned success. What is the risk?
options: Uncommitted transactions may become visible after restart
Recent acknowledged commits may be lost, but the database stays consistent
Nothing can be lost, because the WAL is still fsynced before COMMIT returns
The data files can be corrupted and need a restore from backup
dbms:acid-isolation-levels.explanation: With synchronous_commit off, COMMIT returns before its WAL record is flushed, so a crash can lose the last few acknowledged transactions. The WAL itself is still flushed in order, so recovery yields a consistent state with no corruption. The wrong guess that WAL is fsynced before returning describes synchronous_commit = on.

dbms:acid-isolation-levels.prompt: In MySQL/InnoDB at the default REPEATABLE READ, T1 and T2 both plain-SELECT balance = 500, then T1 runs UPDATE ... SET balance = 510 and commits, then T2 runs UPDATE ... SET balance = 520 and commits. What is the final balance?
options: 510, because T2's UPDATE matches no rows after T1 commits
T2 fails with a serialization error, so the balance is 510
520, and T1's update is silently lost
530, because InnoDB merges the two increments
dbms:acid-isolation-levels.explanation: InnoDB writes act on the latest committed version and do not raise a conflict error at REPEATABLE READ, so T2 overwrites with 520 and T1's +10 is lost. Postgres REPEATABLE READ would abort T2 with SQLSTATE 40001 (first updater wins). Use an atomic UPDATE balance = balance + 20 or SELECT ... FOR UPDATE.

dbms:acid-isolation-levels.prompt: The app uses optimistic locking: UPDATE accounts SET balance = $1, version = version + 1 WHERE id = $2 AND version = $3. The statement reports 0 rows updated. What should the application do?
options: Retry the identical UPDATE with the same version number until it succeeds
Escalate to SERIALIZABLE for the rest of the session
Treat it as success, because the row already holds a newer value
Re-read the row, recompute the new balance from fresh data and retry
dbms:acid-isolation-levels.explanation: Zero rows means someone else changed the row since you read it, so your computed balance is stale. Re-read, recompute and retry (with a bounded number of attempts). Retrying with the same version can never match, and treating it as success silently drops your change.

dbms:acid-isolation-levels.prompt: A team moves a busy Postgres service from READ COMMITTED to SERIALIZABLE. What are they most likely to observe?
options: Reads stay non-blocking, but some transactions fail with 40001 and need retries
No behavior change, since Postgres SERIALIZABLE is the same as REPEATABLE READ
Every transaction is executed one at a time, so throughput collapses
Plain SELECTs start taking shared locks, so they block concurrent writers on the same rows
dbms:acid-isolation-levels.explanation: Postgres SERIALIZABLE is SSI: snapshot reads plus tracking of read-write dependencies, aborting one transaction in a dangerous cycle (sometimes a false positive). So reads do not block, but the app needs retry loops. Lock-based shared reads describe InnoDB SERIALIZABLE, not Postgres.

dbms:acid-isolation-levels.prompt: Interviewer follow-up: in the on-call doctors write skew, Postgres REPEATABLE READ already aborts a second writer on a concurrent update. Why doesn't that catch this case?
options: The check reads from an index, and index reads are never part of the snapshot
The two transactions commit in the same millisecond, so their order is undefined
Each doctor updates a different row, and snapshot isolation only detects conflicts on the same row
REPEATABLE READ only detects conflicts on INSERT, not on UPDATE
dbms:acid-isolation-levels.explanation: First-updater-wins triggers only when two transactions write the same row. Write skew is two transactions reading overlapping data and writing disjoint rows, so no write-write conflict exists. SERIALIZABLE (SSI) tracks the read-write dependencies and catches it, as does locking the rows read with FOR UPDATE.

dbms:acid-isolation-levels.prompt: Postgres runs at SERIALIZABLE. A long read-only reporting transaction (not declared DEFERRABLE) can never be rolled back with a serialization failure, because it writes nothing.
options: True
False
dbms:acid-isolation-levels.explanation: False. Under SSI a read-only transaction can be part of a dangerous dependency cycle and receive SQLSTATE 40001. Declaring it SERIALIZABLE READ ONLY DEFERRABLE makes Postgres wait for a safe snapshot, after which it cannot fail with a serialization error.

dbms:acid-isolation-levels.prompt: Running the debit and the credit as two separate autocommit statements, instead of inside one BEGIN ... COMMIT, gives up the guarantee that the transfer is all or nothing.
options: True
False
dbms:acid-isolation-levels.explanation: True. In autocommit mode each statement is its own transaction, so a crash between them leaves the debit committed and the credit missing. Atomicity only covers what is inside one transaction.

dbms:acid-isolation-levels.prompt: Select all anomalies that Postgres at its default READ COMMITTED level still allows. Select all that apply.
options: Phantom rows appearing when a range query is repeated
Lost updates when the app reads a value and writes back a computed result
Non-repeatable reads across two statements in one transaction
Dirty reads of another transaction's uncommitted changes
dbms:acid-isolation-levels.explanation: Each statement gets a new snapshot, so later statements see newly committed changes and rows (non-repeatable reads, phantoms), and app-side read-modify-write can lose updates. Dirty reads are impossible in Postgres at any level, even READ UNCOMMITTED.

dbms:acid-isolation-levels.prompt: Select all statements that are correct about which invariants the database enforces for you (the C in ACID). Select all that apply.
options: A foreign key stops a credit row from referencing an account that does not exist
The database automatically ensures total money is conserved across a transfer
A CHECK (balance >= 0) constraint is enforced by the database on every write
A UNIQUE constraint prevents duplicate signups even under concurrent inserts at READ COMMITTED
dbms:acid-isolation-levels.explanation: Declared constraints (CHECK, UNIQUE, foreign keys) are enforced by the engine regardless of isolation level; UNIQUE blocks the second concurrent insert. 'Total money is conserved' is a business invariant the engine does not know about; your transaction logic must keep it.

dbms:acid-isolation-levels.prompt: A hot account row suffers lost updates at READ COMMITTED. Select all targeted fixes that work without raising the isolation level. Select all that apply.
options: A version column checked in the UPDATE's WHERE clause, with a retry on 0 rows
Adding a B-tree index on the balance column
Switching the session to READ UNCOMMITTED so it sees the latest value sooner
SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on the row before computing and writing the new value
A single atomic UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + $1 WHERE id = $2
dbms:acid-isolation-levels.explanation: An atomic UPDATE re-reads the latest row under its row lock, FOR UPDATE serializes the read-modify-write, and a version column detects a concurrent change. READ UNCOMMITTED behaves like READ COMMITTED in Postgres, and an index has nothing to do with concurrency.

dbms:acid-isolation-levels.prompt: Postgres runs with synchronous_commit = on and COMMIT has just returned success for the transfer. The server crashes one millisecond later. Why is the transfer still there after restart?
options: The commit record was flushed to the WAL first, so recovery replays it
A replica always holds a copy, and the primary restores from it on restart
The client driver keeps the transaction in memory and resubmits it automatically
The modified data pages were written to the table files before COMMIT returned
dbms:acid-isolation-levels.explanation: Durability comes from flushing the WAL (including the commit record) before acknowledging; dirty data pages are written later and recovery replays the WAL to rebuild them. Data pages are not forced at commit, which is the whole point of a write-ahead log.

dbms:schema-and-indexing-strategy.prompt: The orders table has hundreds of millions of rows. A hot query is WHERE user_id = ? ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20. Which index serves it best?
options: Two separate indexes, one on user_id and one on created_at
A single index on user_id only
A composite index on (created_at, user_id)
A composite index on (user_id, created_at DESC)
dbms:schema-and-indexing-strategy.explanation: Equality column first, then the sort column: the planner seeks to one user and reads the first 20 entries already in order, with no Sort node. Reversing the order forces a scan over all users' rows, and a user_id-only index still needs a sort of all of that user's orders.

dbms:schema-and-indexing-strategy.prompt: An index exists on (user_id, created_at). Which query gets no efficient seek into a contiguous index range from it?
options: WHERE user_id = 7 ORDER BY created_at
WHERE created_at > '2025-01-01' alone
WHERE user_id = 7 AND created_at > '2025-01-01'
WHERE user_id = 7 with no other filter
dbms:schema-and-indexing-strategy.explanation: Entries are ordered by user_id first, so rows with a given created_at are scattered across every user. That is the leftmost-prefix rule. The other three begin with the leading column and can seek, or read already ordered output.

dbms:schema-and-indexing-strategy.prompt: An ops job runs WHERE status = 'pending' AND created_at < now() - interval '1 hour'. Only a tiny fraction of the table is ever pending and status has about 5 values. Which Postgres index is the best fit?
options: A composite index on (status, created_at) over every row in the table
A partial index on created_at with WHERE status = 'pending'
A separate index on every column of the table
A plain index on status
dbms:schema-and-indexing-strategy.explanation: A partial index stores only the pending rows, so it stays tiny and cheap to maintain, and the query predicate implies the index predicate. A plain status index has poor selectivity for common values, and indexing every column adds write cost for no query benefit.

dbms:schema-and-indexing-strategy.prompt: A write-heavy table has these indexes: the primary key (id), (user_id), (user_id, created_at) and (status). Which is the clearest candidate to drop with no loss of query support?
options: The index on (status), because a status column is never useful for any query
The index on (user_id), because the composite index already serves lookups by user_id
The primary key index, because lookups by id can be served from the other indexes
The index on (user_id, created_at), because it is the widest and costs the most to maintain
dbms:schema-and-indexing-strategy.explanation: Leftmost prefix: (user_id, created_at) also answers WHERE user_id = ?, so (user_id) is redundant and only adds write cost. The status index may be poor but you must prove that with idx_scan, and dropping the PK or the composite loses real query support.

dbms:schema-and-indexing-strategy.prompt: In InnoDB, why is a random UUID primary key typically worse than a monotonically increasing bigint?
options: Rows are clustered by PK, so random inserts land on scattered pages, causing splits and a cold cache
UUIDs cannot be compared in a B+ tree, so every lookup degrades into a full scan of the table
UUID keys disable the buffer pool for the clustered index, so every read goes to disk
Secondary indexes in InnoDB do not store the primary key, so they cannot reference a UUID
dbms:schema-and-indexing-strategy.explanation: InnoDB stores rows in the clustered index in PK order. Random keys insert into arbitrary leaf pages, forcing splits and touching a large part of the tree, while sequential keys append to the right edge. UUIDs compare fine, and secondary indexes do store the PK.

dbms:schema-and-indexing-strategy.prompt: A Postgres Index Only Scan on a covering index (created with INCLUDE) still shows a large number of Heap Fetches. What is the most likely cause and fix?
options: Statistics are stale, so run ANALYZE to refresh the planner's row estimates
The index is missing a needed column, so drop it and rebuild it without the INCLUDE list
The query returns too many rows, so add a LIMIT to avoid touching the heap at all
The visibility map is stale for many pages, so run VACUUM to mark them all-visible
dbms:schema-and-indexing-strategy.explanation: Index Only Scan can skip the heap only for pages marked all-visible in the visibility map; otherwise it must fetch the heap tuple to check visibility. VACUUM updates the map. ANALYZE affects estimates, not heap fetches.

dbms:schema-and-indexing-strategy.prompt: A teammate adds an index because it helps in a quick test on the 50,000-row dev database. What is the right way to decide whether to keep it in production?
options: Keep it if the indexed column appears in a WHERE clause somewhere in the application code
Keep it, since extra indexes only ever speed up reads and never slow anything down
Run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) on production-sized data and check idx_scan in pg_stat_user_indexes
Drop it whenever the index file turns out to be larger than the table itself
dbms:schema-and-indexing-strategy.explanation: A planner can ignore an index at scale that looked fine on tiny data, so verify the plan on realistic volume and measure real usage. Every index taxes inserts, updates, vacuum and cache. Appearing in a WHERE clause says nothing about use, and size alone is not the criterion.

dbms:schema-and-indexing-strategy.prompt: Select all costs that every additional secondary index adds to a write-heavy Postgres table.
options: An UPDATE of an indexed column rewrites index entries and cannot be a HOT update
Slower lookups by primary key
More memory pressure in shared buffers and the OS cache
Each INSERT must also write an entry into the new index
A shorter VACUUM time because dead tuples are indexed
dbms:schema-and-indexing-strategy.explanation: Every insert pays for each index, indexes compete for cache, and updating an indexed column defeats HOT updates. PK lookups are unaffected, and more indexes make VACUUM slower, not faster.

dbms:schema-and-indexing-strategy.prompt: Select all statements that are correct about covering indexes.
options: A covering index is always smaller than the non-covering equivalent
Index Only Scan always avoids every heap access regardless of VACUUM state
In InnoDB a secondary index leaf already holds the primary key, so selecting id from it is free
Postgres 11+ INCLUDE columns let a query be answered with an Index Only Scan without adding them to the sort key
dbms:schema-and-indexing-strategy.explanation: INCLUDE adds payload columns without affecting ordering, and InnoDB secondary leaves carry the PK. Extra columns make the index bigger, not smaller, and Postgres still visits the heap for pages not marked all-visible.

dbms:schema-and-indexing-strategy.prompt: MySQL supports partial indexes, so the same CREATE INDEX ... WHERE status = 'pending' idea works there as in Postgres.
options: True
False
dbms:schema-and-indexing-strategy.explanation: MySQL has no partial indexes. The usual workaround is a composite index such as (status, created_at), which indexes every row and is therefore larger. Postgres partial indexes only help queries whose predicate implies the index predicate.

dbms:schema-and-indexing-strategy.prompt: A Seq Scan node in a plan is always evidence of a missing index.
options: True
False
dbms:schema-and-indexing-strategy.explanation: A sequential scan is often the right choice for small tables or when a large fraction of rows match, since random heap access through an index would be slower. Judge it from EXPLAIN ANALYZE on realistic data, not by the node name.

dbms:schema-and-indexing-strategy.prompt: Given a B-tree index on (a, b, c), which query can return rows in the requested order straight from the index, with no Sort node?
options: WHERE a = 1 ORDER BY b
WHERE a = 1 ORDER BY c
ORDER BY b, a
WHERE b = 1 ORDER BY c
dbms:schema-and-indexing-strategy.explanation: Within a fixed a, entries are sorted by b, so WHERE a = 1 ORDER BY b reads already in order. With only a fixed, c is sorted only within each b, so ORDER BY c needs a sort. Without a leading equality on a, neither b nor (b, a) order exists in the index.

dbms:schema-and-indexing-strategy.prompt: With a B-tree index on (a, b, c), select all queries where the index can narrow the scanned range using its leading column(s). Select all that apply.
options: WHERE a = 1
WHERE a = 1 AND b > 5
WHERE a = 1 AND c = 3
WHERE b = 1 AND c = 3
WHERE b = 1
dbms:schema-and-indexing-strategy.explanation: Any predicate on the leading column a bounds the range; a = 1 AND b > 5 narrows further, and in a = 1 AND c = 3 the c filter is checked inside the a = 1 range. Without a predicate on a, matching b values are scattered across the whole index (leftmost-prefix rule).

dbms:schema-and-indexing-strategy.prompt: On MySQL (no partial indexes) the ops query is WHERE status = 'pending' AND created_at < NOW() - INTERVAL 1 HOUR. Which composite index is the better choice?
options: (created_at, status), because the range column is the most selective one here
(status, created_at): equality first keeps the matching entries contiguous
Two single-column indexes that the optimizer will always merge
(created_at) alone, because status has only 5 values
dbms:schema-and-indexing-strategy.explanation: With status first, all pending rows sit together ordered by created_at, so the engine seeks to status = 'pending' and scans a single tight range. With created_at first, the range covers every status and status becomes a filter over many entries. Index merge is possible but is not guaranteed and usually slower.

dbms:schema-and-indexing-strategy.prompt: Estimate the size of a Postgres B-tree on (user_id bigint, created_at timestamptz) for 300 million orders. Assume ~24 bytes per index tuple plus a 4-byte line pointer, and pages about 90% full.
options: About 1 TB
About 1 GB
About 100 GB
About 10 GB
dbms:schema-and-indexing-strategy.explanation: 300M x 28 bytes = 8.4 GB of entries; at 90% fill that is about 9.3 GB, so roughly 10 GB, before internal pages (a small extra). That is RAM the buffer pool must find for this index to stay hot, which is why each index must earn its place.

dbms:schema-and-indexing-strategy.prompt: In Postgres 16, orders has a primary key plus 4 secondary B-tree indexes. An UPDATE changes total_cents, which appears in one of those secondary indexes. How many new index entries does the update add?
options: 5, one per index, because the update cannot be HOT
0, because Postgres updates index entries in place
1, only in the index that contains total_cents
2, the primary key and the index containing total_cents
dbms:schema-and-indexing-strategy.explanation: Changing an indexed column rules out a HOT update, so the new tuple version gets a new physical location and every B-tree index needs an entry pointing to it. That is why indexing a frequently updated column taxes all indexes on the table, not just one.

dbms:schema-and-indexing-strategy.prompt: Why does a wide primary key, such as a 36-character string UUID, make every secondary index larger in InnoDB?
options: Each secondary index leaf stores the primary key value to locate the row
InnoDB duplicates the entire clustered row into each secondary index leaf
Wide keys force InnoDB to switch secondary indexes to hash structures
InnoDB pads every secondary index key to the length of the primary key
dbms:schema-and-indexing-strategy.explanation: InnoDB tables are clustered on the PK, and secondary index entries locate rows by PK value, so every secondary entry carries a copy of it. A 36-byte key instead of an 8-byte bigint bloats every index and the buffer pool. It does not copy whole rows or change the index type.

dbms:schema-and-indexing-strategy.prompt: status has 5 values: 95% 'completed' and 0.1% 'pending'. When can a plain index on status still be useful in Postgres?
options: Queries for the rare value 'pending', which statistics show is selective
Only after the table is clustered on the status index
Only for WHERE status = 'completed', because it is the most common value
Never, because low-cardinality columns are always ignored by the planner
dbms:schema-and-indexing-strategy.explanation: Postgres keeps most-common-value frequencies, so it knows 'pending' matches few rows and uses the index, while choosing a Seq Scan for 'completed'. Cardinality alone does not decide; selectivity of the value queried does. A partial index on the rare value is usually even better.

dbms:schema-and-indexing-strategy.prompt: For the user-orders query, why prefer CREATE INDEX ON orders (user_id, created_at DESC) INCLUDE (status, total_cents) over adding status and total_cents as trailing key columns?
options: Trailing key columns would break the leftmost-prefix rule for the user_id lookups
Only INCLUDE columns can be read by an Index Only Scan
INCLUDE columns are stored in the heap instead, so the index stays the same size
INCLUDE columns are output-only, so they stay out of the search key and upper pages
dbms:schema-and-indexing-strategy.explanation: The query only filters and sorts on user_id and created_at; status and total_cents are just returned. INCLUDE stores them as payload in leaf tuples, so upper pages stay smaller and no ordering is imposed on them. Key columns can also feed an Index Only Scan, and trailing keys do not break the leftmost prefix.

dbms:schema-and-indexing-strategy.prompt: For WHERE user_id = ? ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20, a Postgres B-tree on (user_id, created_at) in ascending order forces a Sort node because its direction does not match the query.
options: True
False
dbms:schema-and-indexing-strategy.explanation: False. Postgres can scan a B-tree backward, so an ascending (user_id, created_at) index serves ORDER BY created_at DESC for one user with no Sort. Explicit DESC matters for mixed directions across columns, such as ORDER BY a ASC, b DESC.

dbms:schema-and-indexing-strategy.prompt: In Postgres, a partial unique index such as CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ON carts (user_id) WHERE status = 'active' can enforce a business rule (one active cart per user) as well as speed up lookups.
options: True
False
dbms:schema-and-indexing-strategy.explanation: True. A unique index applies only to rows matching its predicate, so it allows many inactive carts but at most one active cart per user, even under concurrent inserts. Indexes are also integrity tools, not only performance tools.

dbms:schema-and-indexing-strategy.prompt: A write-heavy Postgres table has 9 indexes. Select all findings that make an index a safe candidate to drop. Select all that apply.
options: It backs a UNIQUE constraint the app relies on
pg_stat_user_indexes shows idx_scan = 0 over a full business cycle, including month-end jobs
Its columns are a leading prefix of another index on the same table
It is the largest index on the table
It shows zero scans on the primary, though reports run on a read replica
dbms:schema-and-indexing-strategy.explanation: No scans over a representative period and being a redundant prefix (user_id next to (user_id, created_at)) are solid signals. Size is not a reason by itself. Index statistics are per server, so replica usage is invisible on the primary, and a unique index enforces integrity even if never scanned.

dbms:schema-and-indexing-strategy.prompt: A partial index exists: CREATE INDEX ON orders (created_at) WHERE status = 'pending'. Which query can the planner NOT use it for?
options: WHERE status = 'pending' AND created_at < $1 AND total_cents > 0
WHERE status = $1 AND created_at < $2 run as a generic prepared plan
WHERE status = 'pending' AND created_at < now() - interval '1 hour'
WHERE status = 'pending' ORDER BY created_at LIMIT 10
dbms:schema-and-indexing-strategy.explanation: The planner may use a partial index only when it can prove the query's WHERE implies the index predicate. With a generic plan, status = $1 could be any value, so the proof fails. The other queries literally contain status = 'pending', so the implication holds.

dbms:schema-and-indexing-strategy.prompt: Deleting one order takes seconds. order_items.order_id references orders(id) with a foreign key, and there is no index on order_items.order_id. Why is the delete slow in Postgres?
options: The foreign key forces the delete to run at SERIALIZABLE
Postgres scans every index on orders to rebuild them after the delete
Postgres doesn't index the referencing column, so each FK check scans order_items
Postgres must rewrite the whole orders table and all of its indexes after every delete
dbms:schema-and-indexing-strategy.explanation: Postgres indexes the referenced key (orders.id is a PK) but not the referencing column. Each delete must find matching order_items rows, which is a Seq Scan without an index on order_id. Add that index; it also helps the usual join. FKs do not change isolation level.

dbms:schema-and-indexing-strategy.prompt: You ran EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) on production-sized data for the user-orders query. Select all signs that the new index is doing its job. Select all that apply.
options: An Index Scan or Index Only Scan using the intended index
Actual rows close to the estimated rows on each node
A Parallel Seq Scan with several workers
No Sort node above the scan for ORDER BY created_at DESC
A total cost number lower than the one seen on the dev database
dbms:schema-and-indexing-strategy.explanation: The right index, no Sort (order comes from the index) and accurate estimates, ideally with low buffer counts, confirm the design. A Parallel Seq Scan means the index was not used, and cost units from a different database are not comparable.

dbms:btree-vs-lsm.prompt: Why is the LSM write path considered cheap compared with a B+ tree update in place?
options: It writes each row to every level at once so a read needs only a single lookup
It never merges any data, so there is no background work that has to be done later
It appends to a log and a memtable, then flushes sorted immutable files sequentially
It skips the WAL entirely because data files are immutable, so there is nothing to log
dbms:btree-vs-lsm.explanation: Writes go to the WAL and the memtable, and a full memtable is flushed as one sequential SSTable, avoiding random page writes. The cost is deferred: compaction does the merging later, and the WAL is still required because the memtable is in memory.

dbms:btree-vs-lsm.prompt: An LSM engine checks the Bloom filter of an SSTable for a key and gets a negative answer. What does that tell it?
options: The key exists only in the memtable
The key is probably not in that SSTable, and the file must still be read to confirm
The key is definitely not in that SSTable, so the file can be skipped
The key was deleted and a tombstone exists in that SSTable
dbms:btree-vs-lsm.explanation: Bloom filters have no false negatives: a negative is definitive, so the file is skipped, which makes reads for missing keys cheap. A positive may be a false positive and needs a real lookup. They cannot tell about tombstones or the memtable.

dbms:btree-vs-lsm.prompt: A workload is almost all appends of metrics events at very high rate, rarely read by key, and all data expires after 30 days. Which storage design is the best fit?
options: A B+ tree engine keyed by a random UUID so inserts spread evenly across pages
A B+ tree engine with many secondary indexes to support flexible queries later
An LSM engine, ideally with time-window compaction that drops whole expired files
A B+ tree engine with in-place updates, since each row is written only one time
dbms:btree-vs-lsm.explanation: Heavy sequential ingest suits an LSM's append-and-flush path, and time-window compaction (as in Cassandra) lets TTL'd data drop by deleting whole files. A B+ tree would pay random page writes and extra index maintenance for a workload that rarely reads.

dbms:btree-vs-lsm.prompt: A write-heavy ingest cluster runs leveled compaction and compaction IO is saturating the disks, while reads are rare. Which change best matches the trade-off involved?
options: Replace the memtable with an on-disk B+ tree so that no compaction is ever needed
Disable the Bloom filters to free up CPU so compaction runs faster, since reads are rare anyway
Move to size-tiered compaction: lower write amplification, at the price of more files and space
Keep leveled compaction but add a much larger block cache, since cache hits reduce compaction IO
dbms:btree-vs-lsm.explanation: Leveled compaction rewrites data many times as it moves down levels (high write amplification) in exchange for low read and space amplification. Size-tiered does the opposite, which suits write-heavy loads. Removing Bloom filters would hurt reads and not reduce compaction IO.

dbms:btree-vs-lsm.prompt: An InnoDB engine uses 16 KB pages. A single 100-byte row is updated, and nothing else on that page changes before the dirty page is flushed. Ignoring the WAL and the doublewrite buffer, roughly how much larger is the page write than the row change?
options: About 1,640x
About 164x
About 1.6x
About 16x
dbms:btree-vs-lsm.explanation: 16 KB is 16,384 bytes, and 16,384 / 100 is about 164. This page-level write amplification is the B+ tree cost of in-place updates (the WAL, doublewrite and full-page images add more).

dbms:btree-vs-lsm.prompt: A service uses an LSM-backed store as a work queue: items are inserted, consumed and deleted quickly. Reads for the next item get slower over time even though few live rows exist. Why?
options: The WAL grows with every delete and has to be replayed again on each read
Deletes are tombstones that stay until compaction reaches the bottom, so reads must skip them
Bloom filters stop working correctly once any key has been deleted in the table
Memtables grow without bound after deletes, so every read has to scan through memory
dbms:btree-vs-lsm.explanation: A delete in an LSM writes a tombstone, and the shadowed data and tombstone stay until compaction merges them away. Reads have to step over them, so delete-heavy or queue-like patterns degrade. The memtable is flushed when full and the WAL is not read for queries.

dbms:btree-vs-lsm.prompt: Why are range scans typically more expensive on an LSM tree than on a B+ tree?
options: SSTables use hash indexes that do not support ordered iteration of a key range at all
LSM trees cannot read more than one key at a time, so every row costs a separate request
Scans must merge-iterate the memtable and several SSTables, while B+ tree leaves are linked
LSM keys are not kept sorted inside an SSTable, so the scan has to sort them at read time
dbms:btree-vs-lsm.explanation: SSTables are sorted, but the same key range may live in several files and levels, so the scan merges multiple sorted streams (and skips tombstones). A B+ tree reads along a single chain of linked leaf pages.

dbms:btree-vs-lsm.prompt: Select all techniques LSM engines use to limit or reduce read amplification.
options: Flushing the WAL less often
Keeping tombstones longer before compaction
A Bloom filter per SSTable to skip files that lack the key
A block cache over hot SSTable blocks
Leveled compaction, which keeps non-overlapping files per level so a read checks at most one file per level
dbms:btree-vs-lsm.explanation: Bloom filters, caching and leveled compaction all reduce the number of files or blocks a read touches. WAL flush frequency affects durability and write latency, and longer-lived tombstones make reads worse.

dbms:btree-vs-lsm.prompt: Select all statements that are true about the write path of a B+ tree engine such as Postgres or InnoDB.
options: A change modifies the page in memory and appends to the WAL; the dirty page is flushed later
Random-key inserts mostly become sequential disk writes
Page splits can fragment the tree over time
No WAL is needed because pages are updated in place on disk immediately
dbms:btree-vs-lsm.explanation: In-place updates follow the WAL-then-flush pattern and splits cause fragmentation. Random keys produce random page writes (the source of B+ tree write cost), and in-place updates make the WAL more necessary because a crash can leave a half-written page.

dbms:btree-vs-lsm.prompt: An LSM engine still needs a write-ahead log, because the memtable lives in memory and would otherwise be lost on a crash.
options: True
False
dbms:btree-vs-lsm.explanation: Writes are acknowledged after landing in the WAL and the memtable. After a crash the memtable is rebuilt by replaying the WAL, while already flushed SSTables are durable on their own.

dbms:btree-vs-lsm.prompt: Compaction in an LSM is purely background housekeeping that affects disk space but never request latency.
options: True
False
dbms:btree-vs-lsm.explanation: Compaction consumes IO and CPU, and if it falls behind it can cause write stalls and tail-latency spikes. It also bounds read amplification, so it matters for both read and write latency.

dbms:btree-vs-lsm.prompt: A B+ tree has a fanout of about 400 at every level, including about 400 keys per leaf. Roughly how many levels are needed to index 1 billion keys?
options: 2 levels
4 levels
30 levels
8 levels
dbms:btree-vs-lsm.explanation: 400^3 = 64 million is too few, while 400^4 = 25.6 billion covers 1 billion keys, so about 4 levels. High fanout is why B+ trees stay shallow; 30 levels is what a binary tree would need (2^30 is about 1 billion).

dbms:btree-vs-lsm.prompt: In the same 4-level tree (fanout 400, 8 KB pages: 1 root, 400 second-level, 160,000 third-level pages), about how much memory keeps all non-leaf pages cached so a point read needs one disk read?
options: About 3 MB
About 512 GB
About 1.3 GB
About 13 GB
dbms:btree-vs-lsm.explanation: (1 + 400 + 160,000) pages x 8 KB is about 1.28 GB. The 64 million leaf pages (about 512 GB) are the part that does not fit, so a point read costs roughly one leaf read. 3 MB covers only the top two levels.

dbms:btree-vs-lsm.prompt: With leveled compaction and a 10x size ratio between levels, why is a single byte rewritten many times over its lifetime?
options: Merging into the next level rewrites the overlapping files there, at every level
Bloom filters must be rebuilt by rewriting the data they cover
Every read of the key copies it back to the top level so that it stays hot in cache
The WAL is replayed into each level separately on every flush
dbms:btree-vs-lsm.explanation: Moving a file from Ln to Ln+1 merges it with the roughly 10 overlapping files there and writes them all out again; this repeats at each level as data moves down. That is leveled compaction's high write amplification, the price for low read and space amplification. Reads do not rewrite data.

dbms:btree-vs-lsm.prompt: A Cassandra node holds 1 TB of data under size-tiered compaction. Roughly how much free disk should you keep to be safe from a large compaction?
options: About as much free space as data, since a big merge can double usage
About 5%, since compaction works one small file at a time
About 20%, the same as for any database
About 5x the data size, because every level keeps its own full copy of it
dbms:btree-vs-lsm.explanation: Size-tiered merges large SSTables into a new file before deleting the inputs, so in the worst case it temporarily needs space equal to the data being merged, hence the common 'keep about 50% free' guidance. Leveled compaction works on small files and needs far less headroom.

dbms:btree-vs-lsm.prompt: Why does Cassandra keep tombstones for gc_grace_seconds (10 days by default) before compaction may purge them?
options: Because Bloom filters cannot represent deletions until they are fully rebuilt from disk
Because SSTables are immutable and can only be rewritten every 10 days
So that deleted rows can be restored with an undo command during that window
So a replica that missed the delete gets it via repair instead of resurrecting data
dbms:btree-vs-lsm.explanation: If a replica was down during the delete and the tombstone were purged before repair ran, that replica's old value would look newer than nothing and reappear (zombie data). gc_grace_seconds is the window in which repairs must complete. It is not an undo feature.

dbms:btree-vs-lsm.prompt: Why are secondary indexes harder to maintain on an LSM engine than on a B-tree engine?
options: Secondary index files can only ever be compacted together with the primary data files
LSM engines cannot store more than one sorted structure per table
Overwrites are blind writes, so stale index entries aren't removed without an extra read
LSM engines store keys unsorted on disk, so every secondary lookup needs a full scan
dbms:btree-vs-lsm.explanation: LSM writes append the new value without reading the old one. If the indexed attribute changed, the old index entry still points at the key, so the engine must read before write or validate entries at read time. A B-tree update already reads the row in place. SSTables are sorted.

dbms:btree-vs-lsm.prompt: Select all storage engines whose primary on-disk structure is an LSM tree by default. Select all that apply.
options: MySQL InnoDB
PostgreSQL heap with B-tree indexes
RocksDB
SQLite
Pebble (used by CockroachDB)
Apache Cassandra
dbms:btree-vs-lsm.explanation: RocksDB, Cassandra and Pebble (CockroachDB's engine under SQL) are LSM designs. InnoDB, Postgres and SQLite are B-tree family engines that update pages in place.

dbms:btree-vs-lsm.prompt: A key has been written 5 times. The latest value is still in the memtable; older versions sit in 3 SSTables. What does a point read do?
options: Returns the oldest version until compaction merges the files
Fails until the memtable is flushed to an SSTable
Finds the key in the memtable and returns it without consulting the SSTables
Reads all 3 SSTables and the memtable, then returns the value with the largest size
dbms:btree-vs-lsm.explanation: Reads go newest to oldest: memtable first, then SSTables from newest. The first hit is the latest value, so the search stops. Read amplification grows when the key is old or missing and many files must be checked.

dbms:btree-vs-lsm.prompt: LSM engines often compress better than B-tree engines, partly because SSTables are immutable and written once, so blocks can be compressed without leaving room for in-place updates.
options: True
False
dbms:btree-vs-lsm.explanation: True. Sorted, immutable files compress well and never need slack space for updates. B-tree pages are modified in place and kept partly empty to absorb inserts, which limits compression.

dbms:btree-vs-lsm.prompt: In a B+ tree, internal nodes store full rows as well as keys, and that is why the fanout reaches the hundreds.
options: True
False
dbms:btree-vs-lsm.explanation: False. Internal nodes hold only keys and child pointers, which is exactly why hundreds fit in one page and the tree stays shallow. Rows (or row pointers) live in the leaves, which are linked for range scans.

dbms:btree-vs-lsm.prompt: Select all workloads where a B-tree engine (Postgres or InnoDB) is the better default than an LSM engine. Select all that apply.
options: Ingesting a million metric points per second that are rarely read
Frequent short range scans by primary key on a read-mostly table
Read-heavy OLTP with many secondary indexes
A service with strict p99 latency where compaction stalls are unacceptable
An append-only log store keyed by time with data expiring after a week
dbms:btree-vs-lsm.explanation: B-trees give cheap point and range reads, simple secondary indexes and predictable latency without background compaction. Very high-rate ingest and TTL'd append-only data favor an LSM's sequential writes and whole-file expiry.

dbms:btree-vs-lsm.prompt: During a sustained ingest burst, a RocksDB-backed service sees write latency jump to seconds at intervals while the disk is busy. What is the most likely cause?
options: Bloom filters are full and reject new keys
The memtable switched to an unsorted structure under load
Compaction falls behind, L0 files pile up, and RocksDB throttles writes
The B-tree is splitting pages faster than the engine can flush them to disk
dbms:btree-vs-lsm.explanation: When flushes outpace compaction, L0 file count and pending compaction bytes cross thresholds and RocksDB deliberately throttles or stalls writes to protect read performance. Fixes: more compaction threads or IO headroom, or a compaction style with lower write amplification. RocksDB has no B-tree pages.

dbms:btree-vs-lsm.prompt: Select all correct statements about read, write and space amplification. Select all that apply.
options: Size-tiered compaction has lower write amplification than leveled
Per-file Bloom filters remove read amplification for range scans
No design can minimize read, write and space amplification at the same time
B-trees have no write amplification because they update pages in place
Leveled compaction keeps space amplification lower than size-tiered
dbms:btree-vs-lsm.explanation: Leveled trades extra rewrites for low read and space amplification, size-tiered the opposite, and the triangle says you cannot win on all three. In-place B-tree updates still rewrite whole pages (write amplification), and Bloom filters help point lookups, not range scans.

dbms:btree-vs-lsm.prompt: Cassandra stores time-series data that all expires via a TTL after 30 days. Why is time-window compaction a good fit?
options: It buckets data by time, so a fully expired SSTable is just deleted
It switches the table to a B-tree layout once data is older than a day
It keeps all data in the memtable until the TTL passes
It converts tombstones into Bloom filter entries that use no disk space
dbms:btree-vs-lsm.explanation: Time-window compaction compacts within time buckets, so each SSTable holds data from one window. Once every row in it has expired, the whole file is deleted cheaply, avoiding endless merging of tombstones with live data.

dbms:mvcc-nonblocking-reads.prompt: In Postgres, what happens physically when a transaction with id T2 UPDATEs a row?
