options: The row is locked exclusively until T2 commits so readers must wait
Only the changed column is written to a delta table that readers merge later
A new tuple version is inserted with xmin = T2, and the old tuple gets xmax = T2
The row is modified in place and the old values are copied to an undo log
dbms:mvcc-nonblocking-reads.explanation: Postgres never overwrites in place: the heap keeps both versions, and visibility rules decide which one a snapshot sees. Old versions stay in the heap until VACUUM removes them. Keeping old versions in an undo log is the InnoDB model.

dbms:mvcc-nonblocking-reads.prompt: One session sits 'idle in transaction' for hours in Postgres after running a single SELECT at REPEATABLE READ. Why can this cause table and index bloat across the whole database?
options: It blocks autovacuum from even starting on any table in the database until it ends
It holds row locks on every table it has ever read, which stops writers from cleaning up
Its snapshot holds back the xmin horizon, so VACUUM cannot remove newer dead tuples anywhere
It forces every new transaction to share the same snapshot until the session ends
dbms:mvcc-nonblocking-reads.explanation: Dead tuple versions can only be removed once no live snapshot can still see them. The old snapshot pins that horizon cluster-wide. It does not hold locks on read rows, and autovacuum runs but cannot reclaim the pinned versions.

dbms:mvcc-nonblocking-reads.prompt: Two Postgres sessions at READ COMMITTED both run UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 10 WHERE id = 1. The first has not committed yet. What does the second session do?
options: It fails immediately with a serialization error, which the application must retry
It reads the old row version and overwrites it, silently losing the first update
It skips the locked row and reports that zero rows were updated, with no error at all
It waits for the row lock, then re-checks its WHERE clause on the new version and proceeds
dbms:mvcc-nonblocking-reads.explanation: Writers on the same row serialize on the row lock. At READ COMMITTED the waiter then re-evaluates its WHERE clause on the new version and applies the update, so both decrements land. Aborting with 'could not serialize access' happens at REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE.

dbms:mvcc-nonblocking-reads.prompt: The same conflicting UPDATE happens at REPEATABLE READ: transaction 1 updates a row and commits, after transaction 2 already took its snapshot, then transaction 2 tries to update that row. How do Postgres and InnoDB differ?
options: Postgres aborts it with a serialization failure; InnoDB updates the latest version
Both abort transaction 2 with a serialization error and require the application to retry
Postgres lets transaction 2 proceed, while InnoDB aborts it with a deadlock error
Both let transaction 2 proceed against the latest committed version of the row
dbms:mvcc-nonblocking-reads.explanation: Postgres follows first-updater-wins at REPEATABLE READ and aborts the second writer with SQLSTATE 40001. InnoDB's writes use current reads, so the second writer waits then updates the latest committed row without error. That is why a read-modify-write in application code can lose updates in InnoDB unless you use FOR UPDATE or an atomic UPDATE.

dbms:mvcc-nonblocking-reads.prompt: In which case can Postgres perform a HOT (heap-only tuple) update?
options: The UPDATE changes any column as long as autovacuum is enabled
The UPDATE changes an indexed column but the table is small
The UPDATE rewrites the primary key to a smaller value
The UPDATE changes only unindexed columns and the new version fits on the same page
dbms:mvcc-nonblocking-reads.explanation: HOT chains the new version within the page and adds no new index entries, but it needs no indexed column to change and room on the page. That is why a lower fillfactor helps update-heavy tables, and why indexing a frequently updated column makes every update costlier.

dbms:mvcc-nonblocking-reads.prompt: InnoDB needs an older version of a row for a consistent read. How does it find it?
options: It follows the roll pointer into the undo log until it finds a version its read view can see
It scans the heap for tuples whose xmax matches its snapshot, the same way Postgres does
It replays the redo log up to the snapshot timestamp for each row that it reads
It restores the earlier page image from the doublewrite buffer for every single read
dbms:mvcc-nonblocking-reads.explanation: InnoDB updates the clustered record in place and keeps previous versions in the undo log, chained by a roll pointer. The read view tells it which transaction ids count as visible, and the purge thread discards undo records once no view needs them.

dbms:mvcc-nonblocking-reads.prompt: Why is rolling back a huge transaction usually near-instant in Postgres but slow in InnoDB?
options: InnoDB rollbacks always run through the purge thread, which is single-threaded
InnoDB must lock the entire table while a rollback runs, which makes it slow
Postgres just leaves the new tuples uncommitted; InnoDB must apply undo records to revert rows
Postgres skips the WAL for rollbacks, while InnoDB must log every one of them
dbms:mvcc-nonblocking-reads.explanation: Postgres leaves the work as dead tuples for VACUUM to clean up later, so abort is just marking the transaction aborted. InnoDB changed rows in place, so it has to walk the undo log and revert each change. The price in Postgres is bloat and vacuum work.

dbms:mvcc-nonblocking-reads.prompt: Select all mitigations for the operational risk of long-running transactions pinning old snapshots.
options: Run long reporting queries on a read replica
Raise the isolation level to SERIALIZABLE so snapshots are released sooner
Set idle_in_transaction_session_timeout and statement timeouts
Run VACUUM FULL repeatedly on the busy tables
dbms:mvcc-nonblocking-reads.explanation: Timeouts stop forgotten sessions from pinning the horizon, and a replica keeps reports off the primary. SERIALIZABLE does not release snapshots earlier, and repeated VACUUM FULL cannot reclaim versions the pinned snapshot still needs (and takes heavy locks).

dbms:mvcc-nonblocking-reads.prompt: Select all statements that are correct about MVCC.
options: Postgres stores old row versions in an undo log
Two writers updating the same row still conflict on a row lock
Readers do not take row locks to read from their snapshot
MVCC means the database takes no locks at all
VACUUM also freezes old transaction ids to prevent transaction id wraparound
dbms:mvcc-nonblocking-reads.explanation: MVCC removes reader-writer blocking but not writer-writer conflicts, and VACUUM freezing is part of keeping the xid counter safe. Locks still exist (row locks, DDL locks), and old versions live in the heap in Postgres, not in undo (that is InnoDB).

dbms:mvcc-nonblocking-reads.prompt: In Postgres, an UPDATE that changes only an unindexed column modifies the existing tuple in place without creating a new version.
options: True
False
dbms:mvcc-nonblocking-reads.explanation: Every UPDATE creates a new tuple version. If no indexed column changes and the page has room, it is a cheaper HOT update chained within the page, but it is still a new version, and the old one remains until pruned or vacuumed.

dbms:mvcc-nonblocking-reads.prompt: In Postgres, READ COMMITTED takes a single snapshot at the start of the transaction and uses it for every statement.
options: True
False
dbms:mvcc-nonblocking-reads.explanation: READ COMMITTED takes a new snapshot for each statement. REPEATABLE READ and SERIALIZABLE take one snapshot per transaction, which is why only the stricter levels give repeatable reads.

dbms:mvcc-nonblocking-reads.prompt: A Postgres REPEATABLE READ snapshot was taken while xid 100 was in progress. A tuple has xmin = 100 and xmax = 0, and xid 100 has since committed. Is the tuple visible to this transaction?
options: Yes, because xid 100 is committed now
No: xid 100 was still in progress when the snapshot was taken
Only if the tuple sits on a page marked all-visible in the visibility map
Yes, because xmax = 0 means the tuple is live
dbms:mvcc-nonblocking-reads.explanation: Visibility is judged against the snapshot, not the current state: xid 100 is in the snapshot's in-progress list, so its work stays invisible for the whole REPEATABLE READ transaction. xmax = 0 only says nobody deleted it. A READ COMMITTED statement started later would see it.

dbms:mvcc-nonblocking-reads.prompt: A tuple has xmin = 90 (committed long before the snapshot) and xmax = 102. xid 102 was in progress when the snapshot was taken and later committed. What does the snapshot see?
options: Visible, because the deletion by xid 102 is invisible to this snapshot
The read waits until xid 102's row lock is released, then decides visibility
The tuple is invisible, because xid 102 committed before the read
The tuple is invisible, because xmax is set
dbms:mvcc-nonblocking-reads.explanation: The creator (90) is visible, and the deleter (102) is in the snapshot's in-progress list, so from this snapshot's point of view the tuple was never deleted. A set xmax alone means nothing; its transaction must be committed and visible. Readers never wait on row locks.

dbms:mvcc-nonblocking-reads.prompt: Why must Postgres VACUUM freeze old tuples even in a table that only ever receives INSERTs?
options: xids are 32-bit and wrap around, so old xmins must be frozen to stay visible
Freezing removes dead tuples left behind by INSERTs
Frozen tuples are compressed, which keeps insert-only tables small
Freezing is the step that makes newly inserted rows visible to other sessions
dbms:mvcc-nonblocking-reads.explanation: xids are compared modulo 2^32, so about 2 billion transactions later an old xmin would look like it is in the future and the row would vanish. Freezing marks tuples as visible to everyone. If it falls too far behind, Postgres stops assigning xids to protect data. INSERTs create no dead tuples.

dbms:mvcc-nonblocking-reads.prompt: A Postgres cluster commits about 2,000 write transactions per second (read-only transactions get no xid). If freezing never happened, roughly how long until the ~2 billion transaction ID horizon is used up?
options: About 17 minutes
About 12 hours
About 12 days
About 30 years
dbms:mvcc-nonblocking-reads.explanation: 2,000,000,000 / 2,000 per second = 1,000,000 seconds, about 11.6 days. That is why autovacuum's anti-wraparound freezing is non-negotiable on busy systems, and why a long transaction blocking vacuum is dangerous, not just wasteful.

dbms:mvcc-nonblocking-reads.prompt: An update-heavy sessions table only updates last_seen_at (not indexed), yet pg_stat_user_tables shows few HOT updates. What is the best fix?
options: Raise the isolation level to REPEATABLE READ
Lower the table's fillfactor so pages keep room for new versions
Add an index on last_seen_at so the updates can find rows faster
Run VACUUM FULL every hour
dbms:mvcc-nonblocking-reads.explanation: A HOT update requires the new version to fit on the same page. Full pages force the version elsewhere, which needs new index entries. A fillfactor such as 70 to 90 leaves room. Indexing last_seen_at would make HOT impossible, and VACUUM FULL locks the table and refills the pages.

dbms:mvcc-nonblocking-reads.prompt: InnoDB's history list length keeps climbing for hours and consistent reads get slower. What is the most likely cause?
options: Autocommit is enabled, so every statement creates undo
Too many secondary indexes on the busiest table
A long transaction holds an old read view, so purge can't discard undo
The buffer pool is too small to hold the clustered index of the busiest table
dbms:mvcc-nonblocking-reads.explanation: Purge removes undo only when no read view needs it. One old read view (often a forgotten open transaction) pins all undo created since, and consistent reads must walk longer version chains. Find and end it, and add timeouts. Autocommit statements finish quickly and do not pin undo.

dbms:mvcc-nonblocking-reads.prompt: Select all changes that would make an UPDATE of the email column on a Postgres table no longer eligible to be HOT. Select all that apply.
options: The page holding the row has no free space left
The table having a primary key on id
Adding an expression index on lower(email)
Running the update at REPEATABLE READ instead of READ COMMITTED
Adding a B-tree index on email
dbms:mvcc-nonblocking-reads.explanation: HOT needs no B-tree-indexed column to change (an expression index referencing email counts) and room on the same page. Isolation level is irrelevant, and a primary key on an unchanged column does not block HOT.

dbms:mvcc-nonblocking-reads.prompt: A 3-hour report moves to a Postgres streaming replica with hot_standby_feedback = on. What happens to the primary?
options: The replica sends its oldest snapshot upstream, so primary bloat still grows
The primary cancels the report when it vacuums the rows the report needs
The primary pauses writes until the report finishes
Nothing, because a replica's queries are fully isolated from the primary
dbms:mvcc-nonblocking-reads.explanation: hot_standby_feedback prevents query cancellations on the replica by telling the primary not to remove tuples the replica still needs, which moves the bloat problem back to the primary. With it off, the report may be cancelled due to a conflict with recovery. Cancellation happens on the replica, not by the primary.

dbms:mvcc-nonblocking-reads.prompt: Under Postgres MVCC, select all operations that take or wait for row-level locks. Select all that apply.
options: A plain SELECT of a row being updated by another transaction
UPDATE of a row another open transaction has already updated
DELETE of a row
SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on rows to be changed
A plain SELECT inside a REPEATABLE READ transaction
dbms:mvcc-nonblocking-reads.explanation: MVCC removes reader-writer blocking, not writer-writer: UPDATE, DELETE and locking reads take row locks and can wait. Plain SELECTs at any level read a snapshot version and never wait for row locks.

dbms:mvcc-nonblocking-reads.prompt: In Postgres, a plain SELECT can be blocked by a concurrent, uncommitted UPDATE of the same row.
options: True
False
dbms:mvcc-nonblocking-reads.explanation: False. The reader simply uses the last committed version visible to its snapshot; the writer's new version is invisible until it commits. Only another writer (or a locking read like FOR UPDATE) has to wait.

dbms:mvcc-nonblocking-reads.prompt: Plain VACUUM, as autovacuum runs it, usually shrinks the table's files and returns the freed space to the operating system.
options: True
False
dbms:mvcc-nonblocking-reads.explanation: False. Plain VACUUM marks dead space as reusable within the table (free space map); it can only truncate completely empty pages at the end of the file. Returning space generally needs VACUUM FULL or a tool like pg_repack, and VACUUM FULL takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock.

dbms:mvcc-nonblocking-reads.prompt: Select all things a regular (non-FULL) VACUUM does in Postgres. Select all that apply.
options: Takes a lock that blocks normal reads and writes
Updates the visibility map, which enables Index Only Scans to skip heap fetches
Freezes sufficiently old transaction IDs
Records reusable space in the free space map
Removes tuple versions that no running snapshot can still see
Rebuilds every index in sorted order
dbms:mvcc-nonblocking-reads.explanation: Regular VACUUM cleans dead versions, maintains the visibility and free space maps and freezes old xids, all while normal reads and writes continue. Rebuilding indexes is REINDEX, and the blocking exclusive lock belongs to VACUUM FULL.

dbms:mvcc-nonblocking-reads.prompt: Roughly what does a Postgres MVCC snapshot contain?
options: The oldest active xid, the next xid to assign, and the in-progress xids
A full copy of every table page as of the start of the transaction
A list of every row lock currently held by other sessions in the database
The current LSN of the WAL and nothing else
dbms:mvcc-nonblocking-reads.explanation: A snapshot is small: lower and upper xid bounds plus the in-progress list. Combined with each tuple's xmin/xmax and commit status in pg_xact, that decides visibility. Nothing is copied, which is why snapshots are cheap.

dbms:mvcc-nonblocking-reads.prompt: For a read-heavy app with frequent updates, what is the main benefit of MVCC over a design where readers take shared locks?
options: Old row versions take no extra storage
Writers on the same row no longer need to wait for each other
No background cleanup process is needed
Readers never block writers and writers never block readers
dbms:mvcc-nonblocking-reads.explanation: Readers pick a committed version from their snapshot, so reads and writes proceed concurrently. Two writers on one row still serialize, and the costs are extra versions plus cleanup (VACUUM in Postgres, purge in InnoDB).

dbms:two-phase-commit-vs-saga.prompt: In two-phase commit, the coordinator crashes after every participant voted yes but before it sends any commit or abort decision. What is the state of the participants?
options: They commit on their own, since every vote that was collected was a yes
They are in doubt, holding locks until the coordinator recovers or an operator steps in
They abort on their own after a short timeout, since no decision ever arrived
They elect one participant to decide the outcome among themselves using a quorum
dbms:two-phase-commit-vs-saga.explanation: After voting yes a participant gave up the right to decide alone: the coordinator may have decided either way. That blocking is why 2PC is called a blocking protocol. Replicating the coordinator log with consensus (as Spanner does) removes the single point of failure.

dbms:two-phase-commit-vs-saga.prompt: A saga has three steps: reserve a seat (compensable by releasing it), charge the card (compensable by refund) and send a confirmation email (cannot be undone). In which order should they run?
options: Reserve, charge, then send the email last
Send the email first so the customer knows immediately
Email, charge, then reserve, since compensations run in reverse
Charge, email, then reserve, to get the money first
dbms:two-phase-commit-vs-saga.explanation: Put the step that cannot be compensated at the end, after every step that might fail. If it ran earlier, a later failure would leave an email you cannot take back. The compensable steps can run first and be undone by compensating transactions.

dbms:two-phase-commit-vs-saga.prompt: Why is 2PC usually a poor fit when one of the participants is a third-party payment gateway reached over HTTP?
options: Third-party APIs rarely expose prepare/commit and cannot hold locks for the protocol
2PC only supports exactly two participants, so a three-service flow is impossible
HTTP does not allow a second request to be sent after the first one has returned
2PC cannot run over a network because it needs shared memory between participants
dbms:two-phase-commit-vs-saga.explanation: 2PC requires every participant to implement prepare/commit/abort and keep resources locked between phases. Typical external APIs and many NoSQL stores expose none of that, so a saga with compensations (for example a refund) is the practical choice.

dbms:two-phase-commit-vs-saga.prompt: An outbox relay publishes rows from the outbox table to the broker, marking each as sent afterwards. It crashes after publishing a row but before marking it. What is the outcome after restart?
options: The database rolls back the original business transaction
The event is lost, because the broker already saw it
The event is published again, so consumers must deduplicate by event id
The broker rejects the second publish automatically, so no duplicate exists
dbms:two-phase-commit-vs-saga.explanation: The outbox removes the lost-event window of dual writes, but the relay is at-least-once: it will resend an unmarked row. Consumers therefore need idempotent handling keyed by event id.

dbms:two-phase-commit-vs-saga.prompt: A saga has no isolation, and two customers try to book the last hotel room at the same moment. Which saga step design avoids selling it twice?
options: Let both flows run to completion and rely on a refund for the customer who loses
Accept eventual consistency and reconcile any double booking at the end of the day
Run every local transaction at SERIALIZABLE isolation and add no other protection
Reserve the room first with a PENDING status (a semantic lock) that the second flow sees
dbms:two-phase-commit-vs-saga.explanation: A semantic lock such as status = PENDING makes the intermediate state visible and claimable by the first flow. Serializable local transactions only isolate within one step, not across the saga, and compensating the loser later still produces a bad experience.

dbms:two-phase-commit-vs-saga.prompt: A team wants one place to see the state of every in-flight booking and to debug stuck flows easily. Which saga style fits best, and what does it cost?
options: Choreography, at the cost of having to drop idempotency from every handler
Orchestration, at the cost of an extra coordinating component to build and operate
Orchestration, at the cost of needing 2PC between all of the participating services
Choreography, at the cost of every service needing knowledge of the entire flow
dbms:two-phase-commit-vs-saga.explanation: A central orchestrator or workflow engine tracks state and tells each service what to do, so the flow is easy to reason about and monitor. The trade-off is an extra component. Choreography has no central point but makes the flow hard to trace and prone to cyclic dependencies.

dbms:two-phase-commit-vs-saga.prompt: Because of message reordering, a 'cancel hotel reservation' compensation for booking R arrives at the hotel service before the original 'reserve' request for R. What is the correct behavior?
options: Return an error and crash the service so it is redelivered
Ignore the cancel because there is nothing to undo, then process the reserve normally
Record that R is cancelled so the late reserve becomes a no-op
Process the reserve first by buffering cancels in memory until the reserve arrives
dbms:two-phase-commit-vs-saga.explanation: Compensations must tolerate arriving before the action they undo. Persisting a cancel marker keyed by the request id makes the late reserve a no-op. Dropping the cancel would leak a reservation, and in-memory buffering is lost on restart.

dbms:two-phase-commit-vs-saga.prompt: Select all reasons why 2PC is costly across independently owned services.
options: Locks are held across the network for the duration of the protocol
Overall availability depends on every participant (and the coordinator) being up
It requires exactly-once message delivery from the broker
Every participant must support the prepare and commit protocol
It cannot guarantee that all participants reach the same outcome
dbms:two-phase-commit-vs-saga.explanation: Those three are the practical costs: lock duration, multiplied failure probability and participant support. 2PC does guarantee a common outcome (that is its purpose), and it does not rely on a message broker at all.

dbms:two-phase-commit-vs-saga.prompt: Select all measures that make saga steps and compensations safe under at-least-once delivery.
options: Conditional updates, for example only move status from PENDING to CONFIRMED
A unique constraint on the request id so a repeated step is rejected or ignored
Tracking seen message ids only in an in-process memory set
Retrying compensations until they succeed
dbms:two-phase-commit-vs-saga.explanation: Messages can be delivered more than once, so each handler must be repeatable, and compensations must eventually succeed. An in-memory set is lost on restart and not shared between instances, so duplicates slip through.

dbms:two-phase-commit-vs-saga.prompt: Postgres enables prepared transactions by default, so PREPARE TRANSACTION works on a fresh install.
options: True
False
dbms:two-phase-commit-vs-saga.explanation: max_prepared_transactions defaults to 0, which disables the feature until you raise it. Forgotten prepared transactions hold locks and block vacuum, so an external transaction manager must reliably finish them with COMMIT PREPARED or ROLLBACK PREPARED.

dbms:two-phase-commit-vs-saga.prompt: A saga's compensating transaction is a true rollback that restores the database to exactly the state before the step ran.
options: True
False
dbms:two-phase-commit-vs-saga.explanation: Each saga step was already committed locally, so compensation is a new semantic action (refund, release) rather than a rollback. Other transactions may have seen the intermediate state, and some actions cannot be undone at all.

dbms:two-phase-commit-vs-saga.prompt: A 2PC transaction spans 4 participants, each available 99.9% of the time, and needs all of them up. Roughly what is the combined availability, and how much downtime per year is that?
options: 99.6%, about 35 hours a year
96%, about 2 weeks a year
99.99%, about 1 hour a year, because 4 nodes add redundancy
99.9%, about 9 hours a year, because the coordinator retries
dbms:two-phase-commit-vs-saga.explanation: Availabilities multiply when all are required: 0.999^4 is about 0.996, so 0.4% of 8,760 hours is about 35 hours a year. More participants make 2PC less available, not more; redundancy only helps when any one of the nodes is enough.

dbms:two-phase-commit-vs-saga.prompt: In 2PC, how long does a participant hold the row locks it took for the transaction?
options: Until it receives and applies the commit or abort decision
Until it sends its yes vote in phase 1
Only for the duration of each individual statement
Until the coordinator receives all votes, even before any decision
dbms:two-phase-commit-vs-saga.explanation: After voting yes a participant has promised it can commit, so it must keep its locks until phase 2 tells it the outcome. That is why 2PC holds locks across network round trips, and why a slow or dead coordinator leaves locks held.

dbms:two-phase-commit-vs-saga.prompt: A Postgres table is locked and bloat grows, yet pg_stat_activity shows no session that could hold the lock. The system uses an external transaction manager. What should you check first?
options: pg_prepared_xacts, for an orphaned prepared transaction
pg_stat_statements, for a slow query plan
pg_locks for a deadlock between two idle sessions
The autovacuum settings, which might have been disabled on this table
dbms:two-phase-commit-vs-saga.explanation: A transaction after PREPARE TRANSACTION is detached from any session yet keeps its locks and holds back the vacuum horizon. If the transaction manager forgot it, an operator must resolve it with COMMIT PREPARED or ROLLBACK PREPARED. Deadlocks are detected and broken automatically.

dbms:two-phase-commit-vs-saga.prompt: In phase 1 of 2PC, one participant votes no while the others vote yes. What happens?
options: The transaction commits on the majority that voted yes
The yes participants commit and the no participant retries later
The coordinator waits until the no participant changes its vote
The coordinator decides abort, and every participant rolls back
dbms:two-phase-commit-vs-saga.explanation: 2PC is unanimous: any no (or timeout) means abort, and participants that voted yes roll back their prepared work and release locks. Committing on a majority would break atomicity; that is consensus replication, a different problem.

dbms:two-phase-commit-vs-saga.prompt: Why must the 2PC coordinator durably log its commit decision before sending commit messages?
options: Logging first lets the coordinator skip phase 1 on retries
After a crash it must tell in-doubt participants the same outcome
Participants verify the coordinator's log file before committing
The log is needed only for auditing after the transaction finishes
dbms:two-phase-commit-vs-saga.explanation: If it sent commit to some participants and crashed without a record, on recovery it might decide abort for the rest, splitting the outcome. The durable decision is the single source of truth for resolving in-doubt participants. Participants never read the coordinator's log directly.

dbms:two-phase-commit-vs-saga.prompt: Google Spanner uses two-phase commit across shards. How does it avoid the classic 2PC blocking problem?
options: It limits every transaction to a single shard
Each participant and coordinator is a Paxos group, so one crash can't stall it
It skips the prepare phase entirely by relying on TrueTime synchronized clocks
It lets in-doubt participants decide on their own once a timeout has expired
dbms:two-phase-commit-vs-saga.explanation: 2PC blocks when the one coordinator dies holding the decision. Spanner's coordinator and participants are each replicated with Paxos, so another replica takes over with the logged state. TrueTime is for ordering timestamps, not for skipping prepare, and participants still never decide alone.

dbms:two-phase-commit-vs-saga.prompt: A service commits a new order to its database and then publishes OrderCreated to Kafka. The process crashes between the two steps. What is the result?
options: Kafka rolls back the order through its transaction coordinator
The database notices the missing event on restart and aborts the order
The event is published twice when the service restarts and retries
The order exists, but no event is sent, so downstream never learns of it
dbms:two-phase-commit-vs-saga.explanation: This is the dual write problem: two systems, no shared transaction. The DB commit succeeded and the publish never ran. The outbox pattern fixes it by writing the event in the same local transaction and publishing it from a relay.

dbms:two-phase-commit-vs-saga.prompt: Select all drawbacks of choreography-based sagas compared with orchestration. Select all that apply.
options: Adding or reordering a step means changing several services' subscriptions
Services can end up with cyclic event dependencies
A central orchestrator becomes an extra component to run
Every step requires a 2PC between neighboring services
The end-to-end flow is hard to see because it is spread across event handlers
dbms:two-phase-commit-vs-saga.explanation: Choreography spreads the workflow across services reacting to events, so it is hard to trace, prone to cycles and harder to change. An orchestrator as an extra component is a cost of orchestration, and neither style uses 2PC.

dbms:two-phase-commit-vs-saga.prompt: A saga's 'cancel hotel' compensation keeps failing because the hotel service is down. What is the right behavior?
options: Skip that compensation and continue compensating the earlier steps only
Mark the saga as compensated anyway so the rest of the booking flow can finish
Retry the idempotent compensation with backoff, and alert for manual handling
Re-run the forward hotel reservation to cancel it out
dbms:two-phase-commit-vs-saga.explanation: Compensations must eventually succeed, so the saga persists its state and retries (idempotently, with backoff) and escalates to a human after a threshold. Marking it done or skipping it leaves a reserved room nobody pays for.

dbms:two-phase-commit-vs-saga.prompt: A loyalty service awards points when it sees a 'flight reserved' event, but the booking saga later fails at payment and cancels the flight. Which fix best addresses this saga isolation problem?
options: Raise the loyalty service's database isolation to SERIALIZABLE
Make the flight reservation step a 2PC with the loyalty service
Add a delay before awarding points so most failures finish first
Award points only on the final 'booking confirmed' event
dbms:two-phase-commit-vs-saga.explanation: Sagas expose intermediate state, so other flows must act only on committed business outcomes (or check a PENDING semantic lock). A local isolation level cannot see across services, and a delay only makes the bug rarer.

dbms:two-phase-commit-vs-saga.prompt: Select all scenarios where 2PC (XA or Postgres PREPARE TRANSACTION) is a reasonable choice. Select all that apply.
options: A workflow that waits days for a human approval between steps
An order flow that calls a third-party payment API and a partner hotel API
Atomically consuming a message and writing to a database when both support XA in one trust domain
Cross-shard transactions in a system whose coordinator is replicated with consensus
Two databases in one datacenter, owned by one team, with short transactions
dbms:two-phase-commit-vs-saga.explanation: 2PC suits few, co-located, 2PC-capable resources with short transactions, or systems like Spanner that replicate the coordinator. Third-party HTTP APIs cannot participate, and holding locks for days is unacceptable; sagas fit those.

dbms:two-phase-commit-vs-saga.prompt: Even with the outbox pattern, duplicates can reach consumers. Select all places where they can arise. Select all that apply.
options: A consumer processes a message, crashes before committing its offset, and processes it again
The local transaction commits the business row twice for one request
The broker redelivers a message under at-least-once delivery
The relay publishes a row, crashes before marking it sent, and publishes it again
dbms:two-phase-commit-vs-saga.explanation: Outbox removes lost events, not duplicates: the relay, the broker and the consumer can each repeat a delivery, so consumers deduplicate by event ID. The business row and outbox row commit once, atomically, in one local transaction.

dbms:two-phase-commit-vs-saga.prompt: In 2PC, after a participant has voted yes, it may unilaterally abort if the coordinator takes too long to send the decision.
options: True
False
dbms:two-phase-commit-vs-saga.explanation: False. A yes vote is a promise to commit if told to; the coordinator may already have decided commit and told others. Aborting alone could split the outcome, so the participant must wait (in doubt) or ask the coordinator. That is what makes 2PC blocking.

dbms:two-phase-commit-vs-saga.prompt: With the outbox pattern, the business change and the outbox row are written in the same local database transaction, so either both exist or neither does.
options: True
False
dbms:two-phase-commit-vs-saga.explanation: True. That single local transaction is the core of the pattern: it removes the window where the state changes but the event is lost. A relay (poller or CDC such as Debezium) then publishes outbox rows at least once.

dbms:cap-theorem-in-practice.prompt: Which statement is the most accurate way to state the CAP theorem?
options: A system can safely be CA if it is deployed within a single data center
During a partition, a system must pick between linearizability and all live nodes answering
Any distributed database must pick two of consistency, availability and partition tolerance
Availability means reaching 99.99% uptime, and that goal conflicts with strong consistency
dbms:cap-theorem-in-practice.explanation: Partitions are unavoidable in distributed systems, so the real choice is C versus A while one is happening. When the network is healthy you can have both. 'Pick two' is misleading, and A in CAP means every non-failed node responds, not a high uptime percentage.

dbms:cap-theorem-in-practice.prompt: A Dynamo-style store has N = 3 replicas. Which read/write replica counts guarantee that every read quorum overlaps every write quorum (R + W > N)?
dbms:cap-theorem-in-practice.explanation: R + W must exceed N = 3. QUORUM/QUORUM gives 2 + 2 = 4, so the sets overlap. Combinations such as 1 + 2 or 2 + 1 sum to exactly 3, which still allows a read set that misses the latest write, and ONE/ONE (2) favors speed and availability.

dbms:cap-theorem-in-practice.prompt: Two devices add different items to the same shopping cart on opposite sides of a partition in an AP system. Which reconciliation best preserves the user's intent?
options: Reject writes on the side that cannot reach a quorum
Keep the cart from the replica with the most items and delete the other
Merge the two carts by taking the union of items
Keep the cart with the later timestamp (last write wins) and discard the other
dbms:cap-theorem-in-practice.explanation: A cart can be merged safely, so the union keeps both additions and the user is almost never refused. Last write wins silently drops items, and rejecting writes sacrifices availability for something that did not need strong consistency (the Dynamo cart use case).

dbms:cap-theorem-in-practice.prompt: What does the 'ELC' part of PACELC (Else Latency or Consistency) add to CAP?
options: It says that eventual consistency is impossible whenever no partition is present
It says that availability and latency are the same property measured in different units
With no partition, you still trade latency against consistency, e.g. synchronous cross-region writes
It says partitions never occur in a healthy network, so CAP says nothing about normal operation
dbms:cap-theorem-in-practice.explanation: CAP only describes behavior during a partition. PACELC notes that even in normal operation, replicating synchronously for consistency costs latency, while replying earlier risks stale reads. Cassandra and Dynamo lean to latency, Spanner and etcd to consistency.

dbms:cap-theorem-in-practice.prompt: A MongoDB write is acknowledged with w: 1 by the primary, which then fails before replicating it and a secondary is elected. What can happen, and which setting prevents it?
options: The write is lost permanently only when the disk fails
The write is applied twice; idempotent writes prevent this
The write may be rolled back; w: majority (with majority read concern for reads) prevents this
The write is always preserved, because the old primary rejoins and pushes it to the new primary
dbms:cap-theorem-in-practice.explanation: With w: 1 an acknowledgement means only the primary has it, so a failover can roll it back. With w: majority a write survives failover and a primary that loses its majority steps down, leaning consistent. Reads from secondaries can also be stale.

dbms:cap-theorem-in-practice.prompt: A 5-node etcd cluster is split so that 2 nodes cannot reach the other 3. What happens?
options: The 3-node side keeps serving writes; the 2-node side cannot commit or do linearizable reads
The 2-node side wins the election because it happens to contain the old leader
The whole cluster stops serving requests until the partition has healed completely
Both sides keep accepting writes independently and merge their states after healing
dbms:cap-theorem-in-practice.explanation: etcd uses Raft with majority quorum, so only the side with 3 of 5 nodes can elect a leader and commit. The minority refuses requests, which is the CP choice: correctness at the expense of availability for clients on that side.

dbms:cap-theorem-in-practice.prompt: A booking system must never sell the last seat twice, and overselling is worse for the business than a temporary error. During a partition, what should the node on the minority side do?
options: Answer from a stale cache so the user always sees a result
Fail or reject the request (fail closed) until it can reach a quorum
Accept the booking and reconcile duplicates after the partition heals
Accept the booking but mark it unconfirmed so it can be cancelled later
dbms:cap-theorem-in-practice.explanation: When the invariant must never break, favor consistency: the side that cannot confirm the seat with a quorum should refuse. Accepting and reconciling later is the right call for mergeable data like carts, not for scarce inventory.

dbms:cap-theorem-in-practice.prompt: Select all statements that are correct about systems that favor consistency during a partition (CP behavior).
options: Nodes on the side without a quorum refuse or fail some requests
etcd and ZooKeeper behave this way through majority quorums
The system becomes unavailable to every client everywhere
All nodes keep accepting writes and reconcile later
Clients stuck on the minority side see errors or timeouts rather than stale data
dbms:cap-theorem-in-practice.explanation: CP means the minority side fails closed while the majority side can continue. Accepting writes on every node and reconciling later is the AP choice, and the majority side usually remains available, so the whole system is not down.

dbms:cap-theorem-in-practice.prompt: Select all statements that are accurate about CAP in practice.
options: Partitions include slow or dropped packets, not just cut cables
The choice between consistency and availability can be made per operation or per configuration, for example MongoDB write concern
The C in CAP means linearizability, not ACID consistency
A database is simply CP or AP forever, independent of settings
A distributed database can be CA by being careful to avoid partitions
dbms:cap-theorem-in-practice.explanation: Real partitions are often just delays and drops, and many systems expose the choice per request. The idea of a distributed CA system fails because you cannot opt out of partitions, and most systems are tunable rather than strictly CP or AP.

dbms:cap-theorem-in-practice.prompt: The A in CAP is satisfied by any system that achieves 99.99% uptime.
options: True
False
dbms:cap-theorem-in-practice.explanation: CAP availability means every non-failing node must respond to every request, which is a different and stronger property than an uptime percentage.

dbms:cap-theorem-in-practice.prompt: Even with R + W > N, a Dynamo-style quorum system is not guaranteed to be linearizable in all failure cases.
options: True
False
dbms:cap-theorem-in-practice.explanation: Quorum overlap helps a read see the latest acknowledged write when no failures interfere, but sloppy quorums, concurrent writes, hinted handoff and partial writes can still produce stale or non-linearizable reads.

dbms:cap-theorem-in-practice.prompt: A Cassandra keyspace uses N = 5 replicas. With QUORUM reads and QUORUM writes, how many replicas of a key can be down while both still succeed?
dbms:cap-theorem-in-practice.explanation: QUORUM for N = 5 is floor(5/2) + 1 = 3 replicas. With 2 down, 3 remain, which is enough; with 3 down only 2 remain. R + W = 6 > 5, so read and write sets still overlap.

dbms:cap-theorem-in-practice.prompt: Cassandra with N = 3 uses consistency level ONE for both reads and writes. What does a read issued right after a successful write guarantee?
options: No freshness guarantee: it may hit a replica that lacks the write
It blocks until all three replicas have the write
It always returns the new value, because R + W is equal to N here
It returns the new value as long as no replica has failed or lagged
dbms:cap-theorem-in-practice.explanation: R + W = 2, which is not greater than 3, so the read replica and write replica need not overlap and a stale read is possible even with no failures. ONE/ONE buys latency and availability. QUORUM/QUORUM gives the overlap.

dbms:cap-theorem-in-practice.prompt: A single-region Postgres primary replicates asynchronously to two replicas, and a replica is promoted on failover. Which statement best describes it in CAP and PACELC terms?
options: Cleanly AP, because replicas keep serving reads and the app stays up in a partition
Neither cleanly: replica reads can be stale and failover can lose acked writes
CA, because the system is in one region
Cleanly CP, because only one primary ever accepts writes at any given time
dbms:cap-theorem-in-practice.explanation: Async replication favors latency (EL): replicas lag, and a promoted replica lacks writes the old primary acknowledged, so it is not linearizable across failover. It is not AP either, since writes stop while no primary is available. This is Kleppmann's point that CP/AP labels are crude.

dbms:cap-theorem-in-practice.prompt: A Raft group has its leader in us-east and followers in us-west (RTT 70 ms) and eu-west (RTT 80 ms). Ignoring disk time, what is the minimum commit latency for a write from a client in us-east?
options: About 80 ms
About 150 ms
About 0 ms, because the leader is local
About 70 ms
dbms:cap-theorem-in-practice.explanation: A 3-node majority is 2: the leader plus the fastest follower. So a commit needs one round trip to us-west, about 70 ms. Waiting for eu-west too (80 ms) is unnecessary. This is the PACELC 'else latency' cost paid with no partition at all.

dbms:cap-theorem-in-practice.prompt: Network partitions only happen when a cable is cut; long GC pauses or heavy packet loss do not count.
options: True
False
dbms:cap-theorem-in-practice.explanation: False. From the other nodes' point of view, a node frozen in a long GC pause or behind dropped packets is indistinguishable from one on the other side of a cut link. Timeouts are the only signal, so these faults must be handled as partitions.

dbms:cap-theorem-in-practice.prompt: Under PACELC, Cassandra is typically described as PA/EL, while Spanner and etcd are described as PC/EC.
options: True
False
dbms:cap-theorem-in-practice.explanation: True. Cassandra stays available in a partition and favors low latency otherwise (tunable down to ONE). Spanner and etcd refuse to give up consistency in a partition and pay quorum round trips in normal operation.

dbms:cap-theorem-in-practice.prompt: A multi-region AP store accepts the username 'alice' on both sides of a partition. What is the best design for username registration?
options: Route the uniqueness check to a consensus-backed store that fails closed
Keep it AP and resolve duplicates later with last-write-wins
Keep it AP and append a random suffix to the second 'alice' after the partition heals
Increase the replication factor so partitions become impossible
dbms:cap-theorem-in-practice.explanation: Uniqueness is an invariant that cannot be merged afterwards, so that one operation needs a CP path (refuse on the minority side). Profile reads can stay AP. Last-write-wins silently takes the account from one user, and more replicas do not prevent partitions.

dbms:cap-theorem-in-practice.prompt: Cassandra resolves conflicts per cell with last-write-wins on write timestamps. During a partition two clients update the same cell, and one node's clock runs 2 seconds behind. What is the risk?
options: Cassandra pauses writes until the clocks are synchronized
The write with the older timestamp is rejected with an error to the client
A later write can be silently discarded because its timestamp is older
Both values are kept as siblings for the application to merge
dbms:cap-theorem-in-practice.explanation: LWW trusts timestamps, so clock skew can make a later write lose and vanish without any error. Sibling values with app merges are the Riak or Dynamo approach with version vectors, not Cassandra's LWW.

dbms:cap-theorem-in-practice.prompt: After a partition heals, a Riak-style store returns two sibling values for one key. What does that mean, and who resolves it?
options: The replicas are corrupted, and an operator must restore the key from backup
Version vectors found two concurrent writes; the app must merge and write back
One value is stale, and the store will discard it on the next compaction
The read happened during replication, so retrying returns a single value
dbms:cap-theorem-in-practice.explanation: Version vectors detect writes where neither causally follows the other, so the store keeps both instead of guessing. The app merges them, for example a cart union, and writes the result. Retrying returns the same siblings until someone resolves them.

dbms:cap-theorem-in-practice.prompt: A user updates their profile, refreshes, and sees the old value because the read hit a lagging replica. What is the minimal guarantee that fixes this experience?
options: Read-your-writes, e.g. send that user's reads to the primary briefly
Eventual consistency, but with a much shorter replication interval
Serializable isolation on the primary
Linearizability for every read and write across the whole system
dbms:cap-theorem-in-practice.explanation: The user only needs to see their own writes, which is session-level read-your-writes. Route that user to the primary for a short window or pass a version token. Full linearizability is overkill, and faster replication only shrinks the window.

dbms:cap-theorem-in-practice.prompt: Select all faults that a replicated system must treat as a partition or partition-like failure. Select all that apply.
options: Heavy packet loss causing requests between nodes to time out
A planned schema migration on one table
A client sending malformed requests
A cut network link between two datacenters
A node frozen in a 20-second garbage collection pause
dbms:cap-theorem-in-practice.explanation: Cut links, long pauses and packet loss all make nodes unable to reach each other within timeouts, which is exactly what CAP's partition means in practice. Malformed client requests and planned migrations are not communication failures between replicas.

dbms:cap-theorem-in-practice.prompt: Select all design choices that favor availability over consistency during a partition. Select all that apply.
options: Accepting writes on any reachable replica and handing them off later (sloppy quorum)
Serving reads from local secondaries even if they lag
Having a primary step down when it loses contact with the majority
Using consistency level ONE for reads and writes
Requiring a majority quorum before committing any write
dbms:cap-theorem-in-practice.explanation: Sloppy quorums, ONE, and stale local reads keep answering at the cost of freshness or conflicts. Majority commits and stepping down on losing the majority are CP behaviors that refuse requests rather than risk divergence.

dbms:cap-theorem-in-practice.prompt: An interviewer asks, 'Is your design CP or AP?'. Select all elements of a strong answer. Select all that apply.
options: Identify the data that can be reconciled later, such as cart contents
Call the system CA because partitions are rare in one cloud region
Mention the latency cost of consistency even with no partition
Choose consistency per operation instead of labeling the whole system
Name the invariant that must never break, such as no double-selling
dbms:cap-theorem-in-practice.explanation: Good answers tie consistency to specific invariants, accept eventual consistency where merges are safe, decide per operation and acknowledge the PACELC latency cost. CA is not an option for a distributed system, since partitions cannot be opted out of.

dbms:cap-theorem-in-practice.prompt: In a Dynamo-style store with sloppy quorums and hinted handoff (as in the Dynamo paper or Riak), why can a quorum read miss a quorum write even though R + W > N?
options: Write acks may come from fallback nodes outside the key's home replicas
Hinted handoff deletes the original replicas after the partition heals
R + W > N only applies when N is an odd number
Reads always go to a single replica, whatever value R is set to
dbms:cap-theorem-in-practice.explanation: During failures a sloppy quorum counts acks from fallback nodes holding hints, while the read contacts the home replicas, so the overlap argument breaks until hints are handed off. It is one reason even R + W > N is not linearizable. Parity of N is irrelevant.

dbms:debug-slow-query-explain.prompt: A query got slow. EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows a nested loop where the planner estimated 10 rows and the node actually returned 2,000,000. What is the best first move?
options: Raise work_mem to its maximum so that the nested loop can run entirely in memory
Run ANALYZE, raise the statistics target or add extended statistics so estimates match reality
Switch the application's list endpoints from keyset to OFFSET pagination for stability
Add an index on every column that appears in the join condition and the filters
dbms:debug-slow-query-explain.explanation: A huge gap between estimated and actual rows means the planner chose its strategy on bad information, for example stale statistics after a bulk load. Fix the estimates first; indexes or memory settings treat symptoms and may not address why the wrong plan was chosen.

dbms:debug-slow-query-explain.prompt: The query below is slow even though an index exists on orders (user_id, created_at). Why does the plan use a Seq Scan and how is it fixed?
dbms:debug-slow-query-explain.code:
SELECT id, total_cents
FROM orders
WHERE user_id = 42
  AND date(created_at) = '2025-03-01';
options: The function on created_at defeats the index; rewrite the filter as a created_at range
The index is defined on the wrong table, so create an equivalent one on the users table
The query has no LIMIT, so the planner skips indexes; add LIMIT 1 to enable them
Selecting two columns forces a heap scan, so select only id to make the index usable
dbms:debug-slow-query-explain.explanation: A function on the indexed column makes the predicate non-sargable, so the planner cannot seek in the index. Rewrite as created_at >= '2025-03-01' AND created_at < '2025-03-02' (or create an expression index on date(created_at)).

dbms:debug-slow-query-explain.prompt: A nested loop's inner node shows: Index Scan ... (actual time=0.020..0.030 rows=1 loops=50000). Approximately how much time does that node account for in total?
options: About 0.03 ms
About 30 ms
About 15 seconds
About 1.5 seconds
dbms:debug-slow-query-explain.explanation: Actual time in EXPLAIN ANALYZE is per loop, so multiply by loops: 0.030 ms x 50,000 = 1,500 ms, about 1.5 s. Reading the per-loop figure as the total is the classic mistake when judging a nested loop.

dbms:debug-slow-query-explain.prompt: A paginated list uses LIMIT 20 OFFSET 100000 with ORDER BY on an indexed column. Exactly how many rows must the executor produce internally to return that page, and which technique keeps deep pages as cheap as the first?
options: 100,000 rows, then keyset pagination on an indexed sort key to stop the growth
100,020 rows, of which 100,000 are discarded; a larger LIMIT per page fixes it
100,020 rows, of which 100,000 are discarded; keyset pagination on an indexed sort key
20 rows, because LIMIT stops the scan early and the offset costs nothing
dbms:debug-slow-query-explain.explanation: The executor must produce the 100,000 skipped rows and then the 20 returned ones, 100,020 in total, so cost grows with page depth. Keyset (seek) pagination uses WHERE (created_at, id) < (last values) on an index, so every page costs the same. A larger LIMIT does not remove the skipping.

dbms:debug-slow-query-explain.prompt: Every individual query in an endpoint looks fast in EXPLAIN, yet the endpoint is slow. pg_stat_statements shows one tiny SELECT by order_id with 100 calls per request. What is the problem and fix?
options: Stale statistics; run ANALYZE so the planner stops choosing the wrong plan here
N+1 queries: load related rows with a join, batched ANY(...) lookup or eager loading
A missing index on order_id; add one so that every one of those tiny lookups is faster
Lock contention between requests; shorten the transactions so they hold locks briefly
dbms:debug-slow-query-explain.explanation: One query per parent row (N+1) is invisible in a single plan because each query is fast; the signal is a high call count and many round trips. Batch the lookups instead of making each one faster.

dbms:debug-slow-query-explain.prompt: When does the Postgres planner typically pick a Bitmap Heap Scan?
options: A medium fraction of rows matches, or several indexes combine
Exactly one row is expected, so a single index probe will do
The table has no usable index at all on the filtered column
Almost all rows match, so reading the whole table is cheaper
dbms:debug-slow-query-explain.explanation: A bitmap scan collects matching row locations, orders them by page, and fetches in physical order, avoiding random heap access for medium selectivity. A single-row lookup uses an Index Scan, and a predicate matching most rows gets a Seq Scan.

dbms:debug-slow-query-explain.prompt: A plan shows a Seq Scan on a 5 million row table where the filter returns about 60% of the rows. What is the most reasonable response?
options: Treat it as probably correct: reading most of a table sequentially beats random index access
Always replace Seq Scan nodes with Bitmap Heap Scan nodes, since bitmap scans are faster
Partition the table by the filtered column immediately, so the scan touches fewer rows
Add an index on the filtered column and force it with enable_seqscan = off in production
dbms:debug-slow-query-explain.explanation: A seq scan is not automatically wrong. When a large fraction of rows match, an index would add random IO and be slower. Forcing planner settings is brittle; fix the query or the data model if the result set itself is the problem.

dbms:debug-slow-query-explain.prompt: Which join situation favors a Nested Loop over a Hash Join?
options: Both inputs already arrive sorted on the join key because of existing indexes
A tiny outer side (about 10 rows) probing an inner table indexed on the join key
Two very large unsorted tables joined on a plain equality condition between them
A cross join with no join condition, which must produce every possible row pair
dbms:debug-slow-query-explain.explanation: A nested loop probes the inner side once per outer row, so it wins when the outer side is tiny and each probe is an indexed lookup. Large unsorted equi-joins suit hash joins, and sorted inputs suit merge joins. It is terrible if the outer estimate is badly wrong.

dbms:debug-slow-query-explain.prompt: Select all reasons an existing B-tree index on a column might not be used for a predicate.
options: The index is a B-tree
A leading wildcard such as LIKE '%abc'
A function on the column, such as lower(email) = ? against a plain index on email
A column-order mismatch against the leftmost-prefix rule
The predicate uses plain equality on the indexed column
dbms:debug-slow-query-explain.explanation: Leading wildcards, functions without a matching expression index, and skipping the leading composite column all defeat a plain B-tree seek. Equality on an indexed column and the B-tree type are what the index is built for.

dbms:debug-slow-query-explain.prompt: Select all valid ways to eliminate an N+1 query pattern.
options: Add an index on the foreign key and keep one query per parent
Batch the child lookups with WHERE parent_id = ANY(...)
Use a join to fetch parents and children together
Use eager loading in the ORM (include or joinedload) or a DataLoader
Increase the connection pool size so more of the queries run at once
dbms:debug-slow-query-explain.explanation: All three reduce the number of round trips. Indexing the foreign key makes each of the N queries cheaper but still leaves N round trips, and a bigger pool only hides the symptom while adding load.

dbms:debug-slow-query-explain.prompt: EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually executes the statement, so for an UPDATE or DELETE you should wrap it in BEGIN ... ROLLBACK.
options: True
False
dbms:debug-slow-query-explain.explanation: Plain EXPLAIN only shows the planner's estimate, whereas ANALYZE runs the query and reports real times and rows, including side effects for writes. A transaction that you roll back keeps the data unchanged.

dbms:debug-slow-query-explain.prompt: The cost numbers in an EXPLAIN plan are measured in milliseconds.
options: True
False
dbms:debug-slow-query-explain.explanation: Costs are arbitrary planner units, meaningful only when comparing plans for the same query. The real timings appear as actual time (in ms) when you use ANALYZE.

dbms:debug-slow-query-explain.prompt: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) shows 'Buffers: shared hit=12 read=48000' on the scan node, with the default 8 KB page size. Roughly how much data came from outside Postgres shared buffers?
options: About 48 MB
About 3.7 GB
About 96 KB
About 375 MB
dbms:debug-slow-query-explain.explanation: 48,000 pages x 8 KB = 384,000 KB, about 375 MB, while only 12 pages were cache hits. The query is IO-bound on a cold cache; reducing pages touched (better index, covering index) matters more than CPU tuning. 'read' pages may still come from the OS page cache.

dbms:debug-slow-query-explain.prompt: A Hash Join node shows 'Buckets: 65536  Batches: 16  Memory Usage: 4096kB'. What does this indicate, and what is a reasonable fix?
options: The planner chose the wrong join type and must be forced to a nested loop
The index on the join key is corrupted and needs a REINDEX to recover
The hash table is perfectly sized for its input, so no action is needed
It spilled to disk because the hash table exceeded work_mem; raise work_mem
dbms:debug-slow-query-explain.explanation: More than one batch means the build side exceeded work_mem and was partitioned to temporary files. Raise work_mem for that session or query (not globally, since it applies per operation), or shrink the build side with better filters. The join type itself may be fine.

dbms:debug-slow-query-explain.prompt: WHERE email LIKE '%@example.com' is slow, and the B-tree index on email is not used. Which fix lets Postgres use an index for this predicate?
options: Switch the B-tree to a hash index on email
Run ANALYZE on the table so the planner trusts the B-tree
Raise the statistics target on the email column
Create a GIN index with pg_trgm operator classes on email
dbms:debug-slow-query-explain.explanation: A B-tree can only seek on a known prefix; a leading wildcard has none. pg_trgm trigram indexes support LIKE with leading wildcards. An alternative is storing the domain or the reversed string in its own column. Hash indexes only do equality, and statistics do not create a usable access path.

dbms:debug-slow-query-explain.prompt: In MySQL, phone is an indexed VARCHAR column. WHERE phone = 5551234 (a number literal) does a full table scan. Why?
options: The query cache stores the number literal as a string, so the lookup misses
MySQL ignores indexes on VARCHAR columns longer than 10 characters
MySQL casts each phone string to a number, so the string index is unusable
Number literals are always compared with LIKE semantics in MySQL
dbms:debug-slow-query-explain.explanation: Comparing a string column to a number makes MySQL compare numerically, effectively applying a conversion to every column value, which defeats the index (and '0555-1234' style values may even match oddly). Quote the literal so types match. VARCHAR length does not disable indexes.

dbms:debug-slow-query-explain.prompt: A query filters on city = 'Mumbai' AND zip = '400001'. The planner estimates 3 rows, but 4,000 come back, and it picks a poor nested loop. Statistics are fresh. What is the most likely cause and fix?
options: The table needs a VACUUM FULL so that its statistics get rebuilt
Columns are assumed independent; add CREATE STATISTICS on (city, zip)
The query must be rewritten with OR so each column is estimated separately
The zip column needs a hash index instead of the existing B-tree
dbms:debug-slow-query-explain.explanation: By default Postgres multiplies per-column selectivities, but zip almost determines city, so the estimate is far too low. Extended statistics (dependencies or mcv) on both columns teach the planner the correlation. VACUUM FULL does not fix correlation, and OR changes the query's meaning.

dbms:debug-slow-query-explain.prompt: After a nightly bulk load of 20 million rows, morning queries are slow and plans show estimates far below the actual row counts. What is the best first fix?
options: Restart Postgres to clear the plan cache
Raise shared_buffers so the planner sees more data
Add an index on every column used in any WHERE clause of the queries
Run ANALYZE on the loaded tables, as the last step of the load job
dbms:debug-slow-query-explain.explanation: The planner still uses statistics from before the load, so estimates are badly wrong. ANALYZE refreshes them, and running it right after the load avoids waiting for autovacuum's analyze. Restarting or more memory does not update statistics.

dbms:debug-slow-query-explain.prompt: Keyset pagination uses WHERE (created_at, id) < (:last_created_at, :last_id) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20. Why is id included?
options: Postgres requires the primary key in every ORDER BY clause
Comparing whole row tuples is faster than comparing a single timestamp
It makes Postgres use a hash index for the comparison instead of a B-tree
created_at isn't unique, so ties would be skipped or repeated across pages
dbms:debug-slow-query-explain.explanation: If several rows share the last created_at, filtering on created_at < :last alone skips the unseen ones (and <= repeats seen ones). Adding the unique id gives a total order, and a matching index on (created_at, id) keeps every page a cheap seek.

dbms:debug-slow-query-explain.prompt: When is a Merge Join the planner's natural choice?
options: When the outer side has very few rows and the inner side has an index
When one input is small enough to build an in-memory hash table
When both large inputs already arrive sorted on the join key
Only for non-equality joins such as a.x > b.y
dbms:debug-slow-query-explain.explanation: Merge Join walks two sorted inputs in step, so it shines when indexes or earlier steps already provide the order and both sides are large. A tiny outer side with an inner index favors Nested Loop; a small build side favors Hash Join.

dbms:debug-slow-query-explain.prompt: A plan shows Seq Scan on orders (actual rows=120 loops=1), Rows Removed by Filter: 4999880, taking 900 ms. What fraction of rows matched, and what does that suggest?
options: About 0.0024%, so an index on the filter columns is a strong fit
About 24%, so a Bitmap Heap Scan would be the ideal plan
About 2.4%, so the Seq Scan is already the right choice here
It can't be computed without also knowing the estimated cost numbers
dbms:debug-slow-query-explain.explanation: 120 / 5,000,000 = 0.000024, about 0.0024%. Reading 5 million rows to keep 120 is the textbook case for an index (provided the predicate is sargable). A Seq Scan is reasonable only when a large share of rows match.

dbms:debug-slow-query-explain.prompt: Keyset (seek) pagination lets a user jump directly to page 500 as cheaply as loading page 1.
options: True
False
dbms:debug-slow-query-explain.explanation: False. Keyset pages are cheap because each one starts from the last row of the previous page, so there is no way to compute the start of page 500 without walking there. It trades arbitrary page jumps for constant cost per next or previous page.

dbms:debug-slow-query-explain.prompt: In EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS), 'shared read' counts pages not found in Postgres shared buffers, and those pages may still have come from the OS page cache instead of the physical disk.
options: True
False
dbms:debug-slow-query-explain.explanation: True. Postgres only knows whether a page was in its own buffer pool; a 'read' is a request to the kernel, which may be served from the OS page cache. So read counts show work outside shared buffers, not necessarily disk IO. Timing (track_io_timing) helps tell them apart.

dbms:debug-slow-query-explain.prompt: Select all steps of a sound first pass at diagnosing a query that became slow in production. Select all that apply.
options: Compare estimated rows with actual rows on each node
Reproduce it with realistic parameters and production-sized data
Tune it on a small dev database, since plans don't depend on data size
Find the real slow statement via pg_stat_statements or the slow query log
Run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) and read the plan from the innermost nodes
Add indexes on every column in the WHERE clause straight away
dbms:debug-slow-query-explain.explanation: Measure first: the right query, realistic data, an actual plan with buffers, then look for estimate mismatches. Blind indexing adds write cost without evidence, and the planner picks different plans at different data sizes.

dbms:debug-slow-query-explain.prompt: Select all EXPLAIN ANALYZE findings that point to a real problem worth investigating. Select all that apply.
options: A total cost value larger than 1,000
A Seq Scan on a 200-row lookup table
A node estimating 10 rows that actually returns 500,000
A Sort node showing 'Sort Method: external merge  Disk: 250MB'
An Index Only Scan reporting Heap Fetches close to its row count
dbms:debug-slow-query-explain.explanation: Huge estimate errors, sorts spilling to disk and an Index Only Scan forced to the heap (stale visibility map, needs VACUUM) all cost real time. A Seq Scan on a tiny table is optimal, and cost units are arbitrary, so a large number alone means nothing.

dbms:debug-slow-query-explain.prompt: WHERE lower(email) = $1 ignores the plain B-tree index on email. Select all valid fixes. Select all that apply.
options: Run VACUUM FULL so the planner reconsiders the index
Replace the B-tree with a hash index on email
Change the column to citext with a normal index, and query email = $1
Create an expression index on lower(email)
Store emails normalized to lowercase on write, and query email = $1 with the lowercased input
dbms:debug-slow-query-explain.explanation: The index must match the expression in the predicate: index lower(email), use a case-insensitive type, or normalize the stored data so no function is needed. A hash index on raw email has the same mismatch, and VACUUM FULL does not change which expressions an index covers.

dbms:secure-a-production-database.prompt: Why is escaping single quotes not a reliable defense against SQL injection?
options: Quotes are not special characters in SQL, so escaping them accomplishes nothing at all
Escaping only works in the Postgres dialect and breaks down on every other database engine
Escaping makes queries run noticeably slower than the equivalent prepared statement would
It is fragile in numeric and identifier contexts, whereas parameters never mix data into SQL
dbms:secure-a-production-database.explanation: Parameterized queries send the SQL text and the values separately, so the parser never treats a value as syntax. Escaping is textual and fragile: numeric positions have no quotes to escape, identifiers need different rules, and encoding tricks have bypassed it.

dbms:secure-a-production-database.prompt: Why does replacing the interpolation below with a $1 placeholder not work, and what is the safe fix?
options: The driver does not support $1 with SELECT, so escape the value with a regex first
Placeholders cannot bind identifiers; map the input through an allowlist of known columns
Placeholders are only allowed in INSERT statements, so switch to an ORM for every query
Placeholders cannot appear after ORDER BY in Postgres, so strip semicolons from the input
dbms:secure-a-production-database.explanation: Bind parameters carry values, not identifiers or keywords. For dynamic sort fields, look the user's input up in a fixed map of allowed column names and insert only the mapped constant. Stripping characters or regex escaping is the fragile approach.

dbms:secure-a-production-database.prompt: Which of these is still injectable even though the application uses a query builder?
options: knex('users').where({ email })
knex.raw('SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = ?', [email])
client.query('SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = $1', [email])
knex.raw(`SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '${email}'`)
dbms:secure-a-production-database.explanation: Query builders are safe only while you use their parameter binding. A raw fragment built with string interpolation puts the user's text into the SQL, so it is as injectable as concatenation. The other three bind the value separately.

dbms:secure-a-production-database.prompt: What should the application's database role hold on a customer-facing Postgres database?
options: Ownership of every table so that schema migrations run without a second credential
Superuser rights, limited by pg_hba rules to connections from the app subnet only
SELECT on everything plus DDL rights so the app can create missing indexes itself
Only SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE on the tables it needs, with no DDL and no ownership
dbms:secure-a-production-database.explanation: Least privilege limits the blast radius of an injection or leaked credential: no DROP TABLE, no reading other schemas, no COPY ... PROGRAM. DDL belongs to a separate migration role used by the deploy pipeline, and owners also bypass row-level security by default.

dbms:secure-a-production-database.prompt: Disk and volume encryption at rest is enabled on the database. Which threat does it NOT protect against?
options: A stolen disk or volume snapshot taken from the storage layer of the cloud provider
A compromised app credential or SQL injection, since the database decrypts for any valid session
An engineer physically removing drives from a decommissioned server in the data center
A leaked copy of the database backup files written to object storage
dbms:secure-a-production-database.explanation: Encryption at rest protects data on stolen media and backups. Once the database is running, it transparently decrypts for any valid session, so injection or a stolen app password still reads everything. Column-level encryption with keys held outside the database covers more.

dbms:secure-a-production-database.prompt: At 10:42:00 a bad DELETE wiped a table in production. Nightly base backups and continuous WAL archiving are in place. What is the best recovery approach?
options: Restore the most recent nightly backup and accept losing everything since
Run VACUUM FULL, which restores deleted rows
Replay all archived WAL to the latest point so the delete is repeated and then undone by hand
Restore a base backup and replay WAL only up to a target just before the delete, 10:41:59
dbms:secure-a-production-database.explanation: Point-in-time recovery restores a base backup and replays WAL only up to the chosen target, so you lose a second or two of data instead of a day. Replaying everything would re-apply the bad DELETE, and VACUUM does not resurrect deleted rows.

dbms:secure-a-production-database.prompt: A Postgres table has a row-level security policy for tenant isolation, but the application connects as the table's owner. What is the effect?
options: Policies still apply, because row-level security is enforced for every role in the database
Policies apply only to SELECT statements, so inserts and updates are never filtered
The owner bypasses the policies unless FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY is set, so use a non-owner role
The database refuses the connection, because owners may not connect to RLS-protected tables
dbms:secure-a-production-database.explanation: Table owners and superusers are exempt from row-level security by default, so tenant isolation silently disappears if the app connects as the owner. Use a separate non-owner application role (and FORCE for owners where needed).

dbms:secure-a-production-database.prompt: Nightly backups have shown a success status for a year. Which claim about them has still not been verified?
options: That the data can be restored within the required RTO and RPO
That the scheduled backup job actually ran on each of those nights
That the job exited with a success status on every one of its runs
That backup files were produced and written to the storage location
dbms:secure-a-production-database.explanation: A backup is only real once it has been restored. Restore drills reveal corrupt or incomplete backups, missing WAL, wrong keys and recovery times that miss the RTO and RPO. Success status shows only that the job ran.

dbms:secure-a-production-database.prompt: Select all network and transport controls that belong in a hardened production database setup.
options: Use TLS with certificate verification, such as sslmode=verify-full
Rely on sslmode=require alone, which already prevents man-in-the-middle attacks
Open the database port to the internet and depend on a strong password
Place the database in a private subnet with no public IP
Allow inbound connections only from the app tier and a bastion or VPN for admins
dbms:secure-a-production-database.explanation: Private networking, narrow security groups and verified TLS layer the defense. sslmode=require encrypts but does not verify the server certificate, so it does not stop an active attacker, and exposing the port widens the attack surface.

dbms:secure-a-production-database.prompt: Select all practices that belong in secrets handling and auditing for the database.
options: Ship audit logs to a store the database admins cannot alter
Commit database passwords to the repo as long as the repo is private
Keep credentials in a secrets manager and rotate them on a schedule and after any suspected leak
Avoid logging full parameter values that contain secrets or PII
Keep audit logs only on the database host for fast access
dbms:secure-a-production-database.explanation: Managed, rotated credentials, tamper-resistant logs and careful logging all reduce risk. Passwords in a repo leak through clones and history, and logs stored only on the host can be altered or lost by whoever compromises it.

dbms:secure-a-production-database.prompt: Strict input validation, such as allowing only alphanumeric characters, is a sufficient replacement for parameterized queries.
options: True
False
dbms:secure-a-production-database.explanation: Validation is a useful defense in depth, but it is not a structural guarantee: allowlists get loosened, other contexts need different rules, and second-order injection can use stored data later. Parameterized queries remain the primary defense.

dbms:secure-a-production-database.prompt: Encryption at rest protects the data if an attacker obtains a copy of the disk or backup files.
options: True
False
dbms:secure-a-production-database.explanation: That is the threat encryption at rest addresses: stolen disks, snapshots and backups are unreadable without the keys. It does not help against authorized-looking sessions on the running database.

dbms:secure-a-production-database.prompt: A signup form stores the username safely with parameters. Later a nightly report builds SQL by concatenating stored usernames into a query string. What is the risk?
options: Second-order injection: stored data becomes code in concatenated SQL
None, because the data was parameterized when it was first inserted
Only a performance risk, because concatenated queries are not cached
Cross-site scripting in the report's web page
dbms:secure-a-production-database.explanation: Parameterization protects one query, not the data forever. A username like x'; DROP TABLE ... stored safely becomes an attack when another query concatenates it. Every query that uses values, including ones from your own database, must bind them as parameters.

dbms:secure-a-production-database.prompt: The app connects to Postgres with sslmode=require. What protection is still missing compared with sslmode=verify-full?
options: require turns off password authentication for the connection
The server certificate isn't verified, so a MITM can impersonate the server
require only encrypts the query text, not the result rows coming back
Traffic is not actually encrypted at all when sslmode is require
dbms:secure-a-production-database.explanation: require encrypts the connection but accepts any certificate, so an attacker on the path can terminate TLS and relay traffic. verify-full checks the certificate chain against a trusted CA and that the hostname matches. Both encrypt queries and results alike.

dbms:secure-a-production-database.prompt: Postgres row-level security filters on current_setting('app.tenant_id'). The app sits behind PgBouncer in transaction pooling mode and runs SET app.tenant_id = ... at the start of each request. What is the danger?
options: A session SET can stick to a pooled connection and leak to another tenant
