current_setting always returns null on pooled connections
RLS policies are silently ignored whenever PgBouncer sits in front of Postgres
SET is not allowed inside a transaction, so every request fails
dbms:secure-a-production-database.explanation: In transaction pooling, consecutive transactions from one client may run on different server connections, and a session SET persists on whatever connection it ran on. Set it inside each transaction with SET LOCAL or set_config(..., true) so it resets at commit. RLS itself still applies.

dbms:secure-a-production-database.prompt: An injection bug is found. The app role has only SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE on the app's own tables. What can an attacker still do through it?
options: Nothing, because least privilege makes injection harmless
Read and modify any rows in the tables the app role can access
Only read data, because writes are blocked for injected statements
Drop tables and run shell commands with COPY ... PROGRAM
dbms:secure-a-production-database.explanation: Least privilege limits blast radius: no DDL, no superuser features, no other schemas. But the attacker gets exactly the role's rights, so all rows in those tables are exposed to reading and modification. That is why parameterized queries and RLS still matter.

dbms:secure-a-production-database.prompt: A 500 GB base backup restores at about 250 MB/s, and replaying the WAL since that backup takes about 20 minutes. Roughly what recovery time (RTO) should you plan for, before any app checks?
options: About 5 minutes
About 1 hour
About 6 hours
About 1 day
dbms:secure-a-production-database.explanation: 500,000 MB / 250 MB/s = 2,000 s, about 33 minutes, plus 20 minutes of WAL replay gives about 53 minutes, so plan for about an hour. Measure the real number in a restore drill; if it misses the business RTO, use more frequent base backups or a standby replica.

dbms:secure-a-production-database.prompt: WAL archiving runs with archive_timeout = 60s and there is no standby. The primary's storage is destroyed. What is the worst-case data loss (RPO)?
options: Zero, because WAL archiving is synchronous with each commit
Only the transactions that were still uncommitted
Roughly the last minute of commits not yet archived
Everything since the last nightly base backup
dbms:secure-a-production-database.explanation: Archived WAL can be replayed onto the base backup, so you lose only what had not been archived yet: up to about archive_timeout plus any archive lag. Archiving is asynchronous, so zero loss needs a synchronous standby. The base backup alone is not the limit, because WAL bridges the gap.

dbms:secure-a-production-database.prompt: An attacker with admin credentials for the production cloud account deletes the database and every backup in that account. Which control would have saved the data?
options: Encryption at rest on the database volume with a KMS-managed key
Row-level security on the most sensitive tables
Backups in a separate account with immutable (object-locked) retention
Daily instead of weekly backups, stored in the same production account
dbms:secure-a-production-database.explanation: Only backups the compromised identity cannot delete survive: a separate account plus immutability. Encryption at rest, RLS and more frequent backups all live inside the same blast radius and are gone with the account.

dbms:secure-a-production-database.prompt: National ID numbers are encrypted in the application with a KMS-managed key before being stored. What capability do you lose, and how do teams usually get equality lookups back?
options: You lose TLS on those columns; enable column TLS instead
You lose indexing and search; add an HMAC (blind index) column for lookups
You lose backups; restore needs the plaintext, so keep a plaintext copy
Nothing is lost; Postgres decrypts the column transparently for WHERE clauses
dbms:secure-a-production-database.explanation: The database only sees ciphertext, so it cannot index, sort or search by the real value. A deterministic keyed hash (blind index) stored alongside allows exact-match lookups without revealing the value. Keeping a plaintext copy defeats the purpose.

dbms:secure-a-production-database.prompt: An engineer proposes setting log_statement = 'all' on the production database to aid debugging. What is the main security concern?
options: It turns off pgaudit, because both cannot run at once
It grants the logging role read access to every table in the database
Logs may capture secrets and PII from statements and bind parameters
It disables TLS for every connection whose statements are logged
dbms:secure-a-production-database.explanation: Logging every statement records literals and, for extended-protocol queries, parameter values, so secrets and personal data land in log storage with weaker controls, plus huge volume. Prefer targeted auditing (pgaudit on sensitive objects) and redaction.

dbms:secure-a-production-database.prompt: In Postgres you can cap how many concurrent connections a specific role may open with ALTER ROLE ... CONNECTION LIMIT n.
options: True
False
dbms:secure-a-production-database.explanation: True. A per-role connection limit stops a leaked credential or runaway client from exhausting max_connections for everyone. Combine it with a pooler so the app needs few server connections.

dbms:secure-a-production-database.prompt: Making the application role the owner of its tables is harmless as long as the application code never runs DDL.
options: True
False
dbms:secure-a-production-database.explanation: False. An owner can ALTER or DROP its tables and bypasses row-level security unless FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY is set, so an injection or leaked credential inherits those powers. The app role should hold only the DML grants it needs; a separate migration role owns the schema.

dbms:secure-a-production-database.prompt: Select all benefits of a separate migration role, used only by the deploy pipeline, that holds DDL rights. Select all that apply.
options: SQL injection in the app becomes impossible
A leaked app credential cannot alter or drop tables
Schema changes go through one reviewed and auditable path
The runtime app role can be granted DML only, with no DDL
TLS is no longer needed for app connections
dbms:secure-a-production-database.explanation: Splitting roles shrinks what the always-on app credential can do and funnels DDL through the pipeline. It does not replace TLS, and injection is still possible; it just has a smaller blast radius.

dbms:secure-a-production-database.prompt: Select all backup properties that help survive ransomware or a malicious insider with production admin rights. Select all that apply.
options: Snapshots kept in the same account under the same admin role
Copies in a separate account or region that production admins cannot write to
Longer retention of backups that the same admins can still delete
Immutable retention (object lock) for a fixed period
Regular restore drills that prove the backups can be recovered
dbms:secure-a-production-database.explanation: Isolation and immutability keep backups out of the attacker's reach, and drills prove they actually restore. Same-account or deletable backups, however long retained, are deleted along with the database by whoever holds those credentials.

dbms:secure-a-production-database.prompt: A Node.js service uses parameterized pg queries in most places. Select all snippets that are still injectable. Select all that apply.
options: client.query(`SELECT * FROM orders ORDER BY ${req.query.sort}`)
prisma.$queryRaw`SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = ${email}` (tagged template)
client.query(`SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id IN (${ids.join(',')})`) with ids from the query string
prisma.$queryRawUnsafe(`SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '${email}'`)
client.query('SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = $1', [req.params.id])
dbms:secure-a-production-database.explanation: String-built IN lists, queryRawUnsafe with interpolation and an interpolated ORDER BY all put user text into SQL. Use = ANY($1) with an array, bound parameters and an allowlist for sort columns. A $1 placeholder and Prisma's tagged $queryRaw template both send values as parameters.
